# Overview



**Chai-1** is a multi-modal foundation model for molecular structure prediction that achieves state-of-the-art performance across a variety of benchmarks. Developed by Chai Discovery and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Chai-1 enables unified prediction of proteins, small molecules, DNA, RNA, glycosylations, and their complexes — all from a single inference pipeline. Whether you are predicting a monomeric protein, a multi-chain protein-ligand complex, or a glycosylated antibody, Chai-1 treats every entity through a consistent input format and a shared architectural backbone.

![Performance](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/blob/main/assets/performance_barplot.png?raw=true)

For full benchmark details, see the [technical report](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.10.615955).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L10), [chai_lab/__init__.py](/chai_lab/__init__.py#L4-L5)

## What Chai-1 Can Predict

Chai-1 accepts a FASTA-like input format where each entity is labeled with a type and a unique name. The model handles six distinct entity types through a single unified entry point, meaning you do not need separate tools or workflows for different molecular species.

| Entity Type | Input Format | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Protein** | Amino acid sequence (1-letter code) | `AGSHSMRYFSTSVSRPGRGE...` |
| **DNA** | Nucleotide sequence (A/T/G/C) | `ATGCGATC` |
| **RNA** | Nucleotide sequence (A/U/G/C) | `AUGCGAUC` |
| **Ligand** | SMILES string | `CCCCCCCCCCCCCC(=O)O` |
| **Glycan** | Glycan string (monosaccharide notation) | `Man(a1-2)Man(a1-...)` |
| **Modified Residue** | Embedded in sequence as `AAA(MOD)AAA` | `AAA(SEP)AAA` |

The FASTA header syntax uses the pattern `>type|name=identifier` to declare each entity. This convention is parsed by the input validation layer and routed to the appropriate residue tokenizer, enabling a single FASTA file to describe arbitrarily complex multi-modal complexes.

Sources: [examples/predict_structure.py](/examples/predict_structure.py#L17-L31), [chai_lab/data/parsing/structure/entity_type.py](/chai_lab/data/parsing/structure/entity_type.py#L10-L18), [chai_lab/data/dataset/inference_dataset.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/inference_dataset.py#L94-L128)

## Architecture at a Glance

Chai-1's inference pipeline follows a four-stage architecture: **Input Assembly → Feature Embedding → Trunk Recycling → Diffusion Denoising**, followed by confidence prediction and structure ranking. Each stage is modular and operates on well-defined data structures, making the system both extensible and debuggable.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["1. Input Assembly"]
        A[FASTA File] --> B[Entity Parsing & Tokenization]
        B --> C[MSA Generation / Loading]
        B --> D[ESM Embeddings]
        B --> E[Template Processing]
        B --> F[Restraint Loading]
        C & D & E & F --> G[AllAtomFeatureContext]
    end

    subgraph Features["2. Feature Embedding"]
        G --> H[FeatureFactory: 30+ Feature Generators]
        H --> I[Collate & Pad to Batch]
        I --> J[Token Embedder]
    end

    subgraph Trunk["3. Trunk Recycling"]
        J --> K[Trunk Module x N Recycles]
        K --> L[Single & Pair Representations]
    end

    subgraph Diffusion["4. Diffusion Denoising"]
        L --> M[Noise Schedule: 200 Timesteps]
        M --> N[Stochastic Sampler with 2nd-Order Correction]
        N --> O[Atom Coordinates]
    end

    subgraph Output["5. Confidence & Ranking"]
        O --> P[Confidence Head: pAE / pDE / pLDDT]
        P --> Q[Ranking: pTM + ipTM + Clash Score]
        Q --> R[CIF Output + Scores NPZ]
    end
```

The central data structure flowing through the pipeline is the **`AllAtomFeatureContext`**, which bundles structure context, MSA context, template context, embedding context, and restraint context into a single object. This context is padded, collated into a batch, and then transformed by a `FeatureFactory` that orchestrates over 30 feature generators — from residue type one-hot encodings to blocked atom-pair distograms.

Sources: [chai_lab/chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L100-L162), [chai_lab/data/dataset/all_atom_feature_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/all_atom_feature_context.py#L15-L43), [chai_lab/data/collate/collate.py](/chai_lab/data/collate/collate.py#L24-L97)

## Project Structure

The codebase is organized into five core subsystems under `chai_lab/`, plus examples and tests. Understanding this layout is essential for navigating the deeper documentation pages.

```
chai_lab/
├── chai1.py                 # Main inference entry point & orchestration
├── main.py                  # CLI interface (typer-based)
├── __init__.py              # Package version
├── data/                    # Input parsing, feature generation, collation
│   ├── collate/             #   Batch collation & padding
│   ├── dataset/             #   Feature contexts, MSA, embeddings, templates
│   ├── features/            #   FeatureFactory & 30+ feature generators
│   ├── io/                  #   CIF/PDB I/O utilities
│   ├── parsing/             #   FASTA, restraint, glycan, MSA parsers
│   └── sources/             #   RDKit conformer generation
├── model/                   #   Noise schedules & model utilities
├── ranking/                 #   pTM, pLDDT, clash scoring, ranking
├── tools/                   #   Kalign wrapper, rigid transform utilities
└── utils/                   #   Paths, tensor ops, typing, defaults
```

> [!TIP]
> The `chai1.py` file is the single most important file to understand — it contains both the high-level `run_inference` function (which assembles inputs and loops over trunk samples) and the low-level `run_folding_on_context` function (which executes the core model forward pass through embedding, trunk, diffusion, and confidence stages).

Sources: [chai_lab/chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L1-L30), [chai_lab/main.py](/chai_lab/main.py#L1-L49)

## Two Ways to Run Inference

Chai-1 exposes two interfaces for running structure prediction, suited to different levels of customization.

### Command Line Interface

The simplest way to fold a complex is through the `chai-lab fold` command, which is registered as a console script entry point. It accepts a FASTA file and an output directory, with optional flags for MSA generation, template search, and restraints.

```shell
# Basic usage (no MSA, no templates)
chai-lab fold input.fasta output_folder

# With MSA and template server (recommended for best performance)
chai-lab fold --use-msa-server --use-templates-server input.fasta output_folder
```

### Python API

For programmatic control, the `chai_lab.chai1.run_inference` function provides the same functionality with full parameter access. For even deeper control — such as manually constructing an `AllAtomFeatureContext` with custom MSAs, embeddings, or covalent bond specifications — use `chai_lab.chai1.run_folding_on_context`.

```python
from chai_lab.chai1 import run_inference
candidates = run_inference(
    fasta_file=fasta_path,
    output_dir=output_dir,
    num_trunk_recycles=3,
    num_diffn_timesteps=200,
    num_diffn_samples=5,
    use_esm_embeddings=True,
)
```

| Interface | Entry Point | Best For |
|---|---|---|
| CLI | `chai-lab fold` | Quick predictions, scripting, batch jobs |
| Python `run_inference` | `chai_lab.chai1.run_inference` | Programmatic pipelines, parameter sweeps |
| Python `run_folding_on_context` | `chai_lab.chai1.run_folding_on_context` | Custom feature contexts, advanced research |

Sources: [chai_lab/main.py](/chai_lab/main.py#L29-L36), [chai_lab/chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L397-L451), [examples/predict_structure.py](/examples/predict_structure.py#L38-L51)

## Key Configuration Parameters

The inference pipeline exposes several parameters that control the quality–speed tradeoff and the richness of input data.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `num_trunk_recycles` | 3 | Number of times trunk representations are recycled; more recycles improve quality at linear cost |
| `num_diffn_timesteps` | 200 | Denoising timesteps in the diffusion module; fewer steps = faster but lower quality |
| `num_diffn_samples` | 5 | Number of independent structure samples; the best-ranked sample is typically selected |
| `use_esm_embeddings` | True | Use ESM-2 protein language model embeddings as input features |
| `use_msa_server` | False | Query ColabFold MMseqs2 server for MSA generation |
| `use_templates_server` | False | Query server for structural template hits |
| `low_memory` | True | Move model components to CPU between forward passes to reduce GPU memory |

> [!TIP]
> For the best prediction quality, enable both `--use-msa-server` and `--use-templates-server`. The default configuration (ESM embeddings only, no MSA) is optimized for speed and works well for many cases, but MSA and template information substantially improve accuracy for protein complexes.

Sources: [chai_lab/chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L397-L427), [README.md](/README.md#L24-L38)

## Output Artifacts

Each inference run produces a set of output files in the specified directory. For every diffusion sample (indexed 0 through `num_diffn_samples - 1`), the pipeline writes:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `pred.model_idx_N.cif` | Predicted 3D structure in CIF format with pLDDT B-factors (0–100 scale) |
| `scores.model_idx_N.npz` | NumPy archive with `aggregate_score`, `ptm`, `iptm`, `per_chain_ptm`, `per_chain_pair_iptm`, `has_inter_chain_clashes`, `chain_chain_clashes` |
| `msa_depth.pdf` | MSA coverage plot (only if MSA data was provided) |

The **aggregate ranking score** combines interface pTM (80% weight), complex pTM (20% weight), and a clash penalty: `0.8 * ipTM + 0.2 * pTM - 100 * has_clashes`. The `StructureCandidates` object returned by the Python API also provides direct access to per-token pLDDT, per-pair pAE, and per-pair pDE tensors.

Sources: [chai_lab/chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L238-L268), [chai_lab/ranking/rank.py](/chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L93-L109), [chai_lab/chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L966-L1014)

## Unique Capability: Experimental Restraints

Chai-1 uniquely supports **user-specified restraints** as inputs to guide folding. These include contact restraints (specifying which residues should be near each other), pocket restraints (constraining a ligand's binding site), and covalent bond restraints (for ligands with covalent attachments or glycosylated proteins). Restraints are specified in a `.restraints` file and passed via the `--constraint` CLI flag or `constraint_path` Python parameter.

![Restraints](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/blob/main/assets/chailab_restraints_screenshot.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L91-L94), [chai_lab/chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L443-L472)

# Quick Start



Get Chai-1 running in minutes. This page walks you through **installation**, **preparing your first input**, **running a structure prediction**, and **interpreting the output** — everything you need to go from zero to your first predicted structure. No prior experience with Chai-1 is assumed.

![performance](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/blob/main/assets/performance_barplot.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L194), [__init__.py](/chai_lab/__init__.py#L1-L6)

## Prerequisites and Installation

Chai-1 requires **Linux**, **Python ≥ 3.10**, and an **NVIDIA GPU with CUDA and bfloat16 support**. The model weights are downloaded automatically on first use. The table below summarizes the hardware landscape:

| GPU | VRAM | Suitability |
|-----|------|-------------|
| H100 80GB / A100 80GB | 80 GB | ✅ Recommended — handles large complexes comfortably |
| L40S | 48 GB | ✅ Recommended — good for most complexes |
| A10 / A30 | 24 GB | ⚠️ Works for smaller complexes only |
| RTX 4090 | 24 GB | ⚠️ Community-verified for smaller complexes |

> [!TIP]
> Set the `CHAI_DOWNLOADS_DIR` environment variable to control where model weights are stored (e.g., on a mounted drive in Docker). Without it, weights land in your Python site-packages directory.

Install the stable release from PyPI:

```bash
pip install chai_lab==0.6.1
```

Or install the latest development version directly from GitHub:

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab.git
```

The `chai-lab` command-line tool is registered automatically via the `chai-lab` console script entry point, which maps to `chai_lab.main:cli`.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L21-L35), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L73), [Dockerfile.chailab](/Dockerfile.chailab#L1-L85), [requirements.in](/requirements.in#L1-L32)

## Your First Prediction — The Flow

The entire prediction workflow follows a clear pipeline from input to ranked output structures. Here is what happens at each stage:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["📝 Prepare FASTA"] --> B["🚀 Run Inference"]
    B --> C["⚙️ Feature Assembly"]
    C --> D["🔁 Trunk Recycles"]
    D --> E["🌀 Diffusion Denoising"]
    E --> F["📊 Confidence Scoring"]
    F --> G["🏆 Rank & Export CIF"]
```

1. **Prepare FASTA** — Define your protein, ligand, RNA, DNA, or glycan entities in a FASTA-like format.
2. **Run Inference** — Call `chai-lab fold` (CLI) or `run_inference()` (Python).
3. **Feature Assembly** — The system constructs the `AllAtomFeatureContext`, generating ESM embeddings, loading MSAs, and assembling restraints.
4. **Trunk Recycles** — The trunk model iterates on token-level representations (default: 3 recycles).
5. **Diffusion Denoising** — A stochastic denoising process generates 3D atomic coordinates (default: 200 timesteps, 5 samples).
6. **Confidence Scoring** — pAE, pDE, and pLDDT are predicted for each sample.
7. **Rank & Export** — Samples are ranked by aggregate score and written as `.cif` files.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L500-L545), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L700-L830)

## Preparing Input — The FASTA Format

Chai-1 uses a **FASTA-like format** where each entity (protein, ligand, DNA, RNA, or glycan) is specified as a separate entry. The header line encodes the **entity type** and a **unique name**; the sequence line provides the residue string or SMILES.

### Header Syntax

```
>{entity_type}|name={unique_name}
```

### Entity Types and Sequence Formats

| Entity Type | Header Prefix | Sequence Content | Example |
|-------------|--------------|------------------|---------|
| Protein | `protein` | Amino acid one-letter codes | `AGSHSMRYFSTSVSRPGRGE...` |
| Ligand | `ligand` | SMILES string | `CCCCCCCCCCCCCC(=O)O` |
| DNA | `dna` | Nucleotide one-letter codes | `ATCGATCG` |
| RNA | `rna` | Nucleotide one-letter codes | `AUCGAUCG` |
| Glycan | `glycan` | Glycan notation (e.g., `NAG(4-1 NAG)`) | `NAG(4-1 NAG)` |

Modified residues are encoded inline using parenthetical notation within a protein sequence, e.g., `AAA(SEP)AAA` for phosphoserine at that position.

### Complete Example

```fasta
>protein|name=example-of-long-protein
AGSHSMRYFSTSVSRPGRGEPRFIAVGYVDDTQFVRFDSDAASPRGEPRAPWVEQEGPEYWDRETQKYKRQAQTDRVSLRNLRGYYNQSEAGSHTLQWMFGCDLGPDGRLLRGYDQSAYDGKDYIALNEDLRSWTAADTAAQITQRKWEAAREAEQRRAYLEGTCVEWLRRYLENGKETLQRAEHPKTHVTHHPVSDHEATLRCWALGFYPAEITLTWQWDGEDQTQDTELVETRPAGDGTFQKWAAVVVPSGEEQRYTCHVQHEGLPEPLTLRWEP
>protein|name=example-of-short-protein
AIQRTPKIQVYSRHPAENGKSNFLNCYVSGFHPSDIEVDLLKNGERIEKVEHSDLSFSKDWSFYLLYYTEFTPTEKDEYACRVNHVTLSQPKIVKWDRDM
>protein|name=example-peptide
GAAL
>ligand|name=example-ligand-as-smiles
CCCCCCCCCCCCCC(=O)O
```

> [!TIP]
> Every entity must have a **unique name**. Duplicate names will raise an `UnsupportedInputError` at runtime. Keep names descriptive — they are used for chain naming in output CIF files when `fasta_names_as_cif_chains=True`.

Sources: [predict_structure.py](/examples/predict_structure.py#L1-L57), [inference_dataset.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/inference_dataset.py#L1-L80), [1ac5.fasta](/examples/covalent_bonds/1ac5.fasta#L1-L6), [8cyo.fasta](/examples/covalent_bonds/8cyo.fasta#L1-L4), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L340-L365)

## Running Predictions

### Option A: Command Line Interface

The simplest way to fold a complex is via the `chai-lab fold` command:

```bash
chai-lab fold input.fasta output_folder
```

This uses **default settings**: 5 diffusion samples, ESM embeddings enabled, no MSAs, no templates. For improved accuracy, enable MSA and template generation via the ColabFold MMseqs2 server:

```bash
chai-lab fold --use-msa-server --use-templates-server input.fasta output_folder
```

If you host your own ColabFold server, point to it with `--msa-server-url`:

```bash
chai-lab fold --use-msa-server --msa-server-url "https://api.internalcolabserver.com" input.fasta output_folder
```

The CLI also provides utility commands:

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `chai-lab fold` | Run structure prediction |
| `chai-lab a3m-to-pqt` | Convert A3M MSA files to aligned Parquet format |
| `chai-lab citation` | Print citation information |

For full parameter documentation, see [CLI Reference](3-cli-reference).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L37-L65), [main.py](/chai_lab/main.py#L1-L49)

### Option B: Python API

For programmatic control, use the `chai_lab.chai1.run_inference` function. This is the primary entry point for Python-based workflows:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from chai_lab.chai1 import run_inference

candidates = run_inference(
    fasta_file=Path("input.fasta"),
    output_dir=Path("output_folder"),
    # Core inference parameters
    num_trunk_recycles=3,       # Number of trunk recycles
    num_diffn_timesteps=200,    # Diffusion denoising steps
    num_diffn_samples=5,        # Number of structure samples
    seed=42,                    # Reproducibility seed
    device="cuda:0",            # Target GPU device
    # Feature sources
    use_esm_embeddings=True,    # ESM protein embeddings
    use_msa_server=False,       # Auto-generate MSAs via ColabFold
    msa_directory=None,         # Or provide pre-computed MSAs
    use_templates_server=False, # Auto-generate templates
    constraint_path=None,       # Restraints file path
)
```

The returned `StructureCandidates` object provides direct access to predictions and scores:

```python
# Get CIF file paths for all samples
cif_paths = candidates.cif_paths

# Get aggregate confidence scores
agg_scores = [rd.aggregate_score.item() for rd in candidates.ranking_data]

# Load per-sample detailed scores (pTM, ipTM, pLDDT, clash)
import numpy as np
scores = np.load("output_folder/scores.model_idx_0.npz")
```

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L500-L545), [predict_structure.py](/examples/predict_structure.py#L1-L57), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L280-L310)

### Key Inference Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `num_trunk_recycles` | 3 | Iterations of the trunk model; more recycles can improve accuracy at cost of time |
| `num_diffn_timesteps` | 200 | Steps in the diffusion denoising schedule |
| `num_diffn_samples` | 5 | Number of independent structure samples generated |
| `num_trunk_samples` | 1 | Number of independent trunk samples (each generates `num_diffn_samples` structures) |
| `seed` | None | Random seed for reproducibility |
| `device` | `"cuda:0"` | CUDA device string |
| `use_esm_embeddings` | True | Use ESM-2 protein language model embeddings |
| `use_msa_server` | False | Generate MSAs via ColabFold MMseqs2 server |
| `msa_directory` | None | Path to directory with pre-computed `.aligned.pqt` MSA files |
| `use_templates_server` | False | Generate structural templates via ColabFold server |
| `constraint_path` | None | Path to restraints CSV file |
| `low_memory` | True | Optimize for GPU memory by offloading intermediate tensors to CPU |

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L500-L530)

## Understanding the Output

After a successful run, the output directory contains the following files for each of the `num_diffn_samples` predictions:

| File | Content |
|------|---------|
| `pred.model_idx_{N}.cif` | Predicted 3D structure in mmCIF format, with pLDDT as B-factors (0–100 scale) |
| `scores.model_idx_{N}.npz` | NumPy archive with pTM, ipTM, pLDDT, and clash metrics |
| `msa_depth.pdf` | (If MSAs were used) Coverage plot of MSA depth per position |

The **`StructureCandidates`** object returned by `run_inference` provides:

| Attribute | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `cif_paths` | `list[Path]` | Paths to all candidate CIF files |
| `ranking_data` | `list[SampleRanking]` | Ranking scores per candidate, including `aggregate_score` |
| `pae` | `Tensor [candidates, tokens, tokens]` | Predicted Aligned Error matrix |
| `pde` | `Tensor [candidates, tokens, tokens]` | Predicted Distance Error matrix |
| `plddt` | `Tensor [candidates, tokens]` | Per-token pLDDT confidence |
| `msa_coverage_plot_path` | `Path or None` | Path to MSA coverage PDF, if applicable |

Call `candidates.sorted()` to reorder results from highest to lowest aggregate confidence score. The candidate with the **highest `aggregate_score`** is the model's best prediction.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L280-L330), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L960-L1060), [predict_structure.py](/examples/predict_structure.py#L44-L57)

## Common Use Cases at a Glance

The `examples/` directory provides ready-to-run scripts for each scenario. Here is a quick reference:

| Use Case | Example Script | Key Configuration |
|----------|---------------|-------------------|
| Basic folding | `examples/predict_structure.py` | `use_esm_embeddings=True` (defaults) |
| With MSAs (pre-computed) | `examples/msas/predict_with_msas.py` | `msa_directory=Path(...)` |
| With MSAs (auto-generated) | CLI only | `--use-msa-server` flag |
| With templates | `examples/templates/predict_with_templates.py` | `use_msa_server=True, use_templates_server=True` |
| With contact restraints | `examples/restraints/predict_with_restraints.py` | `constraint_path=Path("contact.restraints")` |
| With pocket restraints | `examples/restraints/predict_with_restraints.py` | `constraint_path=Path("pocket.restraints")` |
| Covalent ligands | `examples/covalent_bonds/predict_covalent_ligand.py` | `constraint_path=Path("8cyo.restraints")` |
| Glycosylated proteins | `examples/covalent_bonds/predict_glycosylated.py` | `glycan` entity type + restraints |

Sources: [predict_structure.py](/examples/predict_structure.py#L1-L57), [predict_with_msas.py](/examples/msas/predict_with_msas.py#L1-L46), [predict_with_restraints.py](/examples/restraints/predict_with_restraints.py#L1-L36), [predict_with_templates.py](/examples/templates/predict_with_templates.py#L1-L31), [predict_covalent_ligand.py](/examples/covalent_bonds/predict_covalent_ligand.py#L1-L28)

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Cause | Solution |
|---------|-------|----------|
| `UnsupportedInputError: Too many tokens` | Input exceeds maximum model token limit | Reduce sequence length or number of entities |
| `Output directory is not empty` | `run_inference` requires an empty output directory | Delete or use a new directory path |
| `Duplicate entity name` | Two entities share the same `name=` value | Assign unique names to every entity |
| CUDA out of memory | Complex too large for GPU VRAM | Set `low_memory=True` (default), reduce `num_diffn_samples`, or use a larger GPU |
| MSA server timeout | ColabFold shared server is overloaded | Retry later, or host your own MMseqs2 server and use `--msa-server-url` |
| Weights download failure | Network or storage issue | Set `CHAI_DOWNLOADS_DIR` to a writable path with sufficient disk space |

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L236-L260), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L510-L515), [README.md](/README.md#L78-L85)

# CLI Reference



The `chai-lab` command-line interface provides direct access to Chai-1's structure prediction capabilities without writing Python code. After installing the package (`pip install chai_lab`), the `chai-lab` command becomes available in your shell, exposing three subcommands: **fold** for running structure prediction, **a3m-to-pqt** for converting MSA file formats, and **citation** for printing citation information. This page covers every subcommand, its parameters, defaults, and practical usage patterns.

Sources: [main.py](chai_lab/main.py#L1-L49), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L62-L63)

## Command Tree Overview

The CLI is built on [Typer](https://typer.tiangolo.com/) and registers three subcommands. The entry point `chai-lab` is declared in the package configuration and maps directly to `chai_lab.main:cli`. Each subcommand is a thin wrapper around a core Python function, which means every CLI parameter has an exact counterpart in the Python API — no feature is lost when switching between interfaces.

```
chai-lab
├── fold          → chai_lab.chai1.run_inference
├── a3m-to-pqt    → chai_lab.data.parsing.msas.aligned_pqt.merge_a3m_in_directory
└── citation      → prints Chai-1 technical report citation
```

Sources: [main.py](chai_lab/main.py#L33-L48), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L62-L63)

## `chai-lab fold` — Structure Prediction

This is the primary subcommand. It takes a FASTA file describing your molecular complex and produces a set of predicted 3D structures in CIF format, along with confidence scores. Internally, it calls [`run_inference`](chai_lab/chai1.py#L493-L539), which orchestrates the full pipeline: feature context assembly → trunk recycling → diffusion denoising → confidence prediction → ranking and output.

### Basic Usage

```shell
chai-lab fold input.fasta output_folder
```

By default, the model generates **5 diffusion samples** from a **single trunk pass**, runs **3 trunk recycles**, and uses **200 diffusion timesteps**. It employs ESM embeddings automatically but does **not** search for MSAs or templates unless explicitly requested. The output directory must be **empty** — if it already contains files, the command will fail with an assertion error.

### With MSA and Template Search

For improved prediction quality, enable the ColabFold MMseqs2 server for MSA and template generation:

```shell
chai-lab fold --use-msa-server --use-templates-server input.fasta output_folder
```

If you host your own ColabFold-compatible server, specify its URL:

```shell
chai-lab fold --use-msa-server --msa-server-url "https://api.internalcolabserver.com" input.fasta output_folder
```

> [!TIP]
> The `--use-msa-server` and `--msa-directory` flags are **mutually exclusive** — you cannot specify both simultaneously. The same exclusivity applies to `--use-templates-server` and `--template-hits-path`.

### Full Parameter Reference

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fasta_file` | Path (positional) | *required* | Path to input FASTA file |
| `output_dir` | Path (positional) | *required* | Path to empty output directory |
| `--use-esm-embeddings` | bool | `True` | Use ESM protein language model embeddings |
| `--use-msa-server` | bool | `False` | Generate MSAs via ColabFold MMseqs2 server |
| `--msa-server-url` | str | `https://api.colabfold.com` | URL for custom ColabFold server |
| `--msa-directory` | Path \| None | `None` | Directory of pre-computed `.aligned.pqt` MSA files |
| `--constraint-path` | Path \| None | `None` | Path to restraints file (contacts, pockets, covalent bonds) |
| `--use-templates-server` | bool | `False` | Search for structural templates via ColabFold server |
| `--template-hits-path` | Path \| None | `None` | Path to pre-computed template hits (`.m8` format) |
| `--num-trunk-recycles` | int | `3` | Number of trunk recycling iterations |
| `--num-diffn-timesteps` | int | `200` | Number of diffusion denoising steps |
| `--num-diffn-samples` | int | `5` | Number of structure samples per trunk pass |
| `--num-trunk-samples` | int | `1` | Number of independent trunk passes |
| `--recycle-msa-subsample` | int | `0` | MSA subsampling during recycling (0 = disabled) |
| `--seed` | int \| None | `None` | Random seed for reproducibility |
| `--device` | str \| None | `None` | Torch device string (default: `cuda:0`) |
| `--low-memory` | bool | `True` | Enable CPU offloading to reduce GPU memory usage |
| `--fasta-names-as-cif-chains` | bool | `False` | Use FASTA entity names as CIF chain identifiers |

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L493-L539), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L288-L398)

### Input Limits

The model enforces hard limits on input size. Token counts are padded to the nearest available model size from the set **{256, 384, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048}**, and inputs exceeding 2048 tokens are rejected. Similarly, MSA depth and template count are bounded by internal constants (`MAX_MSA_DEPTH`, `MAX_NUM_TEMPLATES`). Each FASTA entity must have a **unique name** — duplicate entity names trigger an `UnsupportedInputError`.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L232-L254), [utils.py](chai_lab/data/collate/utils.py#L11-L12)

### Output Files

After a successful run, the output directory contains the following files per diffusion sample:

| File | Format | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `pred.model_idx_{N}.cif` | CIF | Predicted 3D structure with pLDDT B-factors (0–100 scale) |
| `scores.model_idx_{N}.npz` | NumPy archive | pTM, ipTM, pLDDT, and clash scores |
| `msa_depth.pdf` | PDF | MSA token coverage plot (only if MSA data was used) |

The `StructureCandidates` object returned by the Python API also exposes `pae`, `pde`, and `plddt` tensors for all candidates, plus a `.sorted()` method that reorders results by descending aggregate confidence score. The highest-scoring candidate is considered the best prediction.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L259-L282), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L940-L1060)

### FASTA Input Format

The FASTA input uses extended headers to declare entity type and name. Each entity occupies one FASTA record with a header pattern of `>{type}|name={identifier}`, followed by the sequence on the next line. Supported entity types are `protein`, `ligand`, `RNA`, and `DNA`. Ligands are specified as **SMILES strings**, and modified residues are encoded inline (e.g., `AAA(SEP)AAA`). Here is a concrete example:

```fasta
>protein|name=receptor
AGSHSMRYFSTSVSRPGRGEPRFIAVGYVDDTQFVRFDSDAASPRGEPRAPWVEQEGPEYWDRETQKYKR
>protein|name=partner
AIQRTPKIQVYSRHPAENGKSNFLNCYVSGFHPSDIEVDLLKNGERIEKVEHSDLSFSKDWSFYLLYYTE
>ligand|name=drug
CCCCCCCCCCCCCC(=O)O
```

Sources: [predict_structure.py](examples/predict_structure.py#L18-L30)

## `chai-lab a3m-to-pqt` — MSA Format Conversion

This utility converts raw `.a3m` MSA files (as produced by tools like MMseqs2 or Jackhmmer) into the `.aligned.pqt` parquet format that Chai-1 consumes. The conversion is performed **per query sequence** — all `.a3m` files in the input directory are assumed to derive from the same query, and they are merged into a single parquet file.

### Usage

```shell
chai-lab a3m-to-pqt /path/to/a3m_directory
```

The command scans the specified directory for files matching `*.a3m`, auto-detects the source database from each filename (e.g., `hits_uniref90.a3m` → UniRef90), and writes the merged result as `{seqhash}.aligned.pqt` into the same directory (or into a custom `--output-directory` if specified). The `seqhash` is a SHA-256 hash of the uppercase query sequence, ensuring deterministic filenames.

### File Naming Convention

| Filename Pattern | Detected Source | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| `hits_uniref90.a3m` / `uniref90_hits.a3m` | `uniref90` | — |
| `hits_uniprot.a3m` / `uniprot_hits.a3m` | `uniprot` | — |
| Any unrecognized pattern | — | Defaults to `uniref90` |

> [!TIP]
> The output `.aligned.pqt` file must follow the `AlignedParquetModel` schema: columns `sequence` (str), `source_database` (str from recognized sources), `pairing_key` (str), and `comment` (str). The first row must always have `source_database == "query"`.

Sources: [aligned_pqt.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/msas/aligned_pqt.py#L200-L241), [aligned_pqt.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/msas/aligned_pqt.py#L33-L41)

## `chai-lab citation` — Citation Information

Prints the BibTeX entry for the Chai-1 technical report to standard output. Use this to quickly grab the citation when writing papers or documentation.

```shell
chai-lab citation
```

Output:

```
@article{Chai-1-Technical-Report,
    title        = {Chai-1: Decoding the molecular interactions of life},
    author       = {{Chai Discovery}},
    year         = 2024,
    journal      = {bioRxiv},
    publisher    = {Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory},
    doi          = {10.1101/2024.10.10.615955},
    ...
}
```

Sources: [main.py](chai_lab/main.py#L17-L31), [main.py](chai_lab/main.py#L34-L36)

## Common Workflows

The following flowchart illustrates how to choose the right CLI flags for common prediction scenarios:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["chai-lab fold"] --> B{Have pre-computed MSAs?}
    B -- Yes --> C["--msa-directory /path/to/pqt"]
    B -- No --> D{Want server MSA search?}
    D -- Yes --> E["--use-msa-server"]
    D -- No --> F[ESM embeddings only, default]
    E --> G{Also need templates?}
    G -- Yes --> H["--use-templates-server"]
    G -- No --> I[MSA only]
    C --> J{Need restraints?}
    F --> J
    H --> J
    I --> J
    J -- Yes --> K["--constraint-path file.restraints"]
    J -- No --> L[Run with defaults]
    K --> M[Structure predictions in output_dir]
    L --> M
```

### Quick Reference: Minimal vs. Full-Featured Commands

| Scenario | Command |
|---|---|
| **Fastest** (ESM only, no MSA) | `chai-lab fold input.fasta output/` |
| **Recommended** (with MSA + templates) | `chai-lab fold --use-msa-server --use-templates-server input.fasta output/` |
| **With restraints** | `chai-lab fold --constraint-path pocket.restraints input.fasta output/` |
| **With local MSAs** | `chai-lab fold --msa-directory ./msas/ input.fasta output/` |
| **Reproducible run** | `chai-lab fold --seed 42 input.fasta output/` |
| **Custom GPU device** | `chai-lab fold --device cuda:1 input.fasta output/` |
| **High-quality (more samples)** | `chai-lab fold --num-diffn-samples 10 --num-diffn-timesteps 400 input.fasta output/` |

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L493-L539), [predict_structure.py](examples/predict_structure.py#L35-L45), [predict_with_msas.py](examples/msas/predict_with_msas.py#L28-L38), [predict_with_restraints.py](examples/restraints/predict_with_restraints.py#L21-L33), [predict_with_templates.py](examples/templates/predict_with_templates.py#L25-L31)

## Python API Equivalence

Every CLI `fold` invocation maps directly to the `chai_lab.chai1.run_inference` function. If you need finer control — such as constructing an `AllAtomFeatureContext` manually or accessing intermediate tensors — switch to the Python API. The following table shows the exact mapping between CLI flags and function parameters:

| CLI Flag | Python Parameter |
|---|---|
| `fasta_file` (positional) | `fasta_file: Path` |
| `output_dir` (positional) | `output_dir: Path` |
| `--use-msa-server` | `use_msa_server: bool` |
| `--msa-directory` | `msa_directory: Path \| None` |
| `--constraint-path` | `constraint_path: Path \| None` |
| `--num-trunk-recycles` | `num_trunk_recycles: int` |
| `--num-diffn-timesteps` | `num_diffn_timesteps: int` |
| `--num-diffn-samples` | `num_diffn_samples: int` |
| `--seed` | `seed: int \| None` |

For advanced use cases beyond the CLI, see [Architecture Overview](7-architecture-overview) for the full pipeline breakdown, or [FASTA Parsing and Entity Types](13-fasta-parsing-and-entity-types) for input format details. To understand how restraints guide folding, refer to [Restraint and Covalent Bond System](17-restraint-and-covalent-bond-system).

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L493-L539), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L288-L398)

## Environment Variables

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `CHAI_DOWNLOADS_DIR` | Override default model weights download location (useful in Docker or mounted-drive setups) |

By default, weights are stored in `<package_root>/downloads`. Set `CHAI_DOWNLOADS_DIR` to redirect downloads to a custom path, e.g., `CHAI_DOWNLOADS_DIR=/tmp/downloads chai-lab fold input.fasta output/`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L74-L80)

# Latest Updates



Chai Discovery has moved fast -- from an open-source structure prediction tool to a unicorn-valued platform with two Big Pharma partnerships in under two years. But while the company's commercial trajectory has accelerated, the open-source `chai-lab` repository tells a quieter, more incremental story of dependency bumps, bugfixes, and usability refinements. Here is what has changed, what hasn't, and what it all means if you are a developer betting on this stack.

---

## From Chai-1 to Chai-3: A Rapid Model Succession

The most consequential development is that Chai-1 is no longer the company's flagship model. In the span of roughly twelve months, Chai Discovery shipped three model generations:

```mermaid
timeline
    title Chai Discovery Model Timeline
    Oct 2024 : Chai-1 released (open-source, "Apache 2.0")
               : Structure prediction SOTA
    Jun 2025 : Chai-2 announced
               : Zero-shot antibody design, ~16% "hit rate"
    Jun 2026 : Chai-3 disclosed via Pfizer deal
               : "Step-change improvements," doubled Chai-2 success rate
```

| Model | Released | Core Capability | Open-Source? | Key Benchmark |
|-------|----------|----------------|--------------|---------------|
| Chai-1 | Oct 2024 | Multi-modal structure prediction | Yes (Apache 2.0) | 77% PoseBusters ligand RMSD success; 75.1% protein-protein DockQ success |
| Chai-2 | Jun 2025 | De novo antibody design | No (partner access) | 16% hit rate across 52 targets; 50% of targets yield at least one binder |
| Chai-3 | Jun 2026 | Antibody design (improved) | No (Pfizer-licensed) | Claims 2x Chai-2 success rate (per [Pfizer license announcement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260602498831/en/Chai-Discovery-Announces-License-Agreement-with-Pfizer-to-Accelerate-Drug-Discovery-with-AI)) |

The critical detail for developers: **Chai-1 remains the only model with publicly available weights and code.** Chai-2 and Chai-3 are commercial-only. The [Chai-2 technical report](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.07.05.663018v1) was posted on bioRxiv in July 2025, and a bibtex entry was [added to the chai-lab README](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/2f7b713d6addd8cd7688ddfd5cb49e138f3e5b78) in August 2025, but no inference code or weights have been released. This bifurcation is structurally significant -- the open-source repo is a structure prediction tool, while the company's commercial value proposition is generative antibody design.

---

## Repository Activity: Steady Maintenance, Not Feature Sprints

The commit log on `chai-lab` since mid-2025 shows a pattern of **maintenance-first engineering**: dependency compatibility, parsing flexibility, and infrastructure hardening. There have been no major architectural changes or new model integrations.

### Dependency and Compatibility Updates

The most common commit type is dependency management -- keeping the package installable on evolving Python/PyTorch ecosystems:

| Commit | Date | What Changed |
|--------|------|-------------|
| [Update rdkit (#416)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/c544fb183e865c4950909444db860a9d50604f66) | Apr 2026 | RDKit version bump |
| [Support newer versions of gemmi (#415)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/61036259c98222160963cb780750e354876ce485) | Mar 2026 | Gemmi compatibility fix |
| [update pandera (#399)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/a01bfdeead343e1c7f369660ec519f12c940e9df) | Sep 2025 | Pandera upgrade (resolving FutureWarning) |
| [Allow torch 2.7 (#383)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/29195b89b1f63fb8a4a78406fc7a58468318ff4a) | Jun 2025 | PyTorch 2.7.1 compatibility |
| [specify kalign version (#375)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/6d1e44d8f2bdd37d96e0ed8d67ca4938d9bff54b) | May 2025 | Pin kalign to avoid version drift |
| [use more generic error (#387)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/0a5a85594a44096aeeba7b6f53f99b53f240de15) | Jul 2025 | Fixed urllib3 NameResolutionError import on older versions |

These are the unglamorous but essential commits that keep `pip install chai_lab==0.6.1` from breaking. The [NameResolutionError fix](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/386) is a good example: Chai was importing `NameResolutionError` from `urllib3.exceptions`, but that class only existed in newer urllib3 versions, causing import failures on AWS instances with older system Python packages.

### Feature and Usability Improvements

A second category of commits improves the input/output ergonomics without changing the model itself:

- **Flexible modification parsing** ([#384](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/dc41706bfc19b8530809c8b88cf7d90a58640b2e)): Support `[]` in addition to `()` for specifying modified residues in FASTA, and relax entity name validation. This directly addresses users who were struggling with custom residue notation.

- **Entity names as chain names** ([#378](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/2a2d4a96e842a73499bacced0db662455b42e886)): Allow FASTA-specified entity names to carry through as chain names in CIF output. Previously, output chains would get generic identifiers, making it harder to map predictions back to inputs.

- **Restraint improvements**: Multiple commits ([#379](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/ac9c1f3edc5c85d0fcb95f465ca1f27bb0481a5f), [#377](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/79dc5b9253c8baae1107ac095bd9693840a72c65)) added support for entity name-based subchains in restraints and improved parsing for edge cases like empty comment fields.

- **Global template cache** ([#371](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/eb63e84536bcbb46c0b675abb6a312ec9d682443)): Introduced `CHAI_TEMPLATE_CIF_FOLDER` envvar for controlling where template CIF files are cached. This is a meaningful operational improvement for Docker deployments and shared compute environments where the default `/downloads` path inside site-packages is not persistent.

### Performance and Infrastructure

Two commits stand out for their impact on operational reliability:

- **Parallel conformer generation with timeout** ([#410](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/af596cbc075a1fce368cec0ab5f31be1090ca7e2)): The previous conformer generation code could hang indefinitely. This fix added parallel processing and a reasonable timeout -- a classic "the process just sits there doing nothing" problem that is devastating in batch workflows.

- **CPU cache for model components** ([#360](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/4d110dd40ee4ae60303c83a21de5ecb2d4a57dd1)): Keeping model components in CPU cache to reduce GPU memory pressure during inference. This is particularly relevant for users running on GPUs with less VRAM (A10, A30, or the consumer-grade RTX 4090 that the README mentions).

---

## PyPI Release History: 0.6.1 and Counting

The current stable PyPI release is **`chai_lab==0.6.1`**, published March 18, 2025. The full release history shows a rapid initial cadence that has since slowed:

| Version | Release Date | Notes |
|---------|-------------|-------|
| 0.0.1 | Sep 9, 2024 | Initial release |
| 0.1.0 | Sep 25, 2024 | First public release alongside Chai-1 |
| 0.2.0 | Oct 21, 2024 | CLI improvements |
| 0.3.0 | Nov 19, 2024 | |
| 0.4.2 | Nov 27, 2024 | Hugging Face model card references this version |
| 0.5.0 | Dec 5, 2024 | |
| 0.5.2 | Dec 24, 2024 | |
| 0.6.0 | Feb 18, 2025 | |
| **0.6.1** | **Mar 18, 2025** | **Current stable release** |

Notably, there has been **no new PyPI release in over a year** despite ongoing commits to `main`. The README still recommends pinning to `0.6.1` and notes that `pip install git+https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab.git` "updates daily to test features that weren't released yet." This gap between commit activity and release cadence suggests that the team is prioritizing stability over feature velocity for the published package, while using the `main` branch as a rolling release for internal and early-adopter testing.

---

## Company Milestones Reshaping the Landscape

The repository exists within a company that has undergone a dramatic transformation. These events do not change the code directly, but they reshape the strategic context for anyone building on Chai-1:

| Date | Event | Significance |
|------|-------|-------------|
| Sep 2024 | $30M seed round (Thrive Capital, OpenAI, Dimension) | Initial funding |
| Oct 2024 | Chai-1 open-source release + [bioRxiv preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.10.615955v2) | Established credibility |
| Jun 2025 | Chai-2 announcement: 16% antibody design hit rate | Shift from prediction to generation |
| Aug 2025 | $70M Series A (Menlo Ventures, Anthology Fund/Anthropic) | Validation from pharma-focused VCs |
| Dec 2025 | $130M Series B at $1.3B valuation (Oak HC/FT, General Catalyst) | Unicorn status; total funding > $225M |
| Jan 2026 | [Eli Lilly partnership](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/yosemiteco_yosemite-is-excited-to-see-eli-lilly-and-activity-7415491352773521408-blcA) (custom model on proprietary data) | First major pharma deployment |
| Jun 2026 | [Pfizer license agreement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260602498831/en/Chai-Discovery-Announces-License-Agreement-with-Pfizer-to-Accelerate-Drug-Discovery-with-AI) (Chai-3 access + custom model) | Chai-3 revealed; validated at scale |

Joshua Meier, Chai's co-founder and CEO, summarized the transition succinctly on LinkedIn: "2025 was the year we proved AI could transform preclinical drug discovery. 2026 will be the year of deployment." The Pfizer deal, in particular, confirmed the existence of **Chai-3** -- a model that "doubles the success rate of its predecessor" and focuses on therapeutic binding, multi-specifics, and hard-to-drug targets. Chai-3 has not been described in any publication and is not available outside the Pfizer agreement.

Forbes also [reported in June 2026](https://www.facebook.com/forbes/posts/1372275921429061) that Chai Discovery is in talks to raise an additional $400M at a $3.4B valuation -- a nearly 3x step-up from the Series B just six months prior.

---

## What the Divergence Means for Developers

Here is the structural tension: the `chai-lab` repository is a **structure prediction** tool (Chai-1), while Chai Discovery's commercial future is **generative molecular design** (Chai-2, Chai-3). These are fundamentally different products. Structure prediction takes a sequence and returns a 3D structure. Generative design takes a target and returns a novel sequence.

**What you get from the open-source repo today** is still remarkably capable. On the PoseBusters protein-ligand benchmark, Chai-1 achieves 77% ligand RMSD success, comparable to [AlphaFold3](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3)'s reported 76%. Its single-sequence mode (no MSAs needed) outperforms AlphaFold-Multimer 2.3 with MSAs on protein-protein interfaces. The restraint system -- pocket restraints, contact restraints, and covalent bond specification -- remains a distinctive feature not available in competing open-source tools.

**What you do not get** is antibody design, miniprotein binder generation, or any of the generative capabilities that have driven the company's recent funding and partnerships. The [About Chai-2 issue](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/412) in the repository -- simply titled "About Chai-2" with the body "I really look forward to use Chai-2. Please please please release it as soon as possible!" -- captures the community sentiment, but there is no indication that generative model weights will be open-sourced.

The practical implication: if you are building a workflow that needs structure prediction of known sequences (protein-protein docking, ligand pose generation, nucleic acid complex modeling), `chai-lab` remains a strong, actively maintained choice. If you need de novo antibody design, you will need to negotiate commercial access.

---

## Notable Technical Changes Worth Tracking

A few recent commits signal directionality worth watching:

1. **Removal of sequence corruption logic** ([#368](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/f824e747b46e73ea78c1153077a5907f6a0c3cca)): D-amino acids are now mapped to `X` rather than to their L-partners, and the residue corruption logic was removed entirely. This is a correctness improvement -- the old behavior silently corrupted D-amino acid information, potentially producing misleading predictions for sequences containing non-standard stereochemistry.

2. **Full Typer CLI** ([#350](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/6d3439a0f41a0f33bb8cc1c3bbacfa36a99b7df9)): Migration to the full `typer` library for CLI argument parsing, replacing ad-hoc argument handling. This makes the CLI more discoverable and consistent.

3. **Bugfix for non-paired MSAs** ([#349](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/bd49ff24d68fe97af7b7a2999b7c7c15fb6fb331)): A subtle but important fix -- incorrect handling of non-paired multiple sequence alignments could silently produce wrong features, degrading prediction quality without raising an error.

---

## Looking Forward

The `chai-lab` repository is in a stable-but-stationary state. The last PyPI release was March 2025. Commits continue to land on `main`, but they are overwhelmingly maintenance-oriented. The company's engineering attention has clearly shifted to Chai-2 and Chai-3, which are not part of this repository.

For developers evaluating whether to build on this stack, the key questions are:

- **Will Chai-1 weights continue to be maintained?** The Apache 2.0 license is irrevocable, but model compatibility with future PyTorch versions is not guaranteed without ongoing maintenance. The torch 2.7 compatibility commit suggests the team is keeping the pipeline alive, but this could change as commercial priorities shift.

- **Will any generative capabilities trickle into the open-source repo?** The restraint system already allows guiding predictions with experimental data. It is conceivable that a simplified version of pocket-restraint-guided design could appear, but nothing has been announced.

- **What about PAE output?** The [open issue requesting PAE matrix extraction](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/411) from CIF files has gone unanswered since December 2025. Chai-1 generates PAE internally but does not write `_ma_qa_metric_local_pairwise` entries to ModelCIF by default. This is a significant gap for users who need confidence metrics for downstream ranking.

The bottom line: `chai-lab` is a well-engineered structure prediction toolkit in a holding pattern while its parent company races toward commercial generative AI. The code works, the license is permissive, and the model is competitive. But if you need capabilities beyond "fold this sequence and give me a structure," you are looking at a commercial conversation, not a pip install.

# Issues and Feedbacks



The chai-lab repository has accumulated 84 open and 144 closed issues as of mid-2026. That's a substantial signal for a project that launched publicly in September 2024. What's revealing is not just the volume, but the *shape* of the complaints: they cluster around a handful of structural gaps that any serious adopter will hit sooner or later. Below, I break down the recurring themes, map how the team has responded, and flag where things still feel unresolved.

## The Issue Landscape at a Glance

```mermaid
quadrantChart
    title chai-lab Issues by Impact and Resolution
    x-axis Low Resolution --> High Resolution
    y-axis Low Impact --> High Impact
    quadrant-1 "Resolved Wins"
    quadrant-2 "Lingering Pain Points"
    quadrant-3 "Minor Friction"
    quadrant-4 "Quick Fixes"
    "PAE not exported": [0.15, 0.85]
    "GPU OOM": [0.60, 0.90]
    "Restraint errors": [0.20, 0.75]
    "Custom modifications": [0.10, 0.80]
    "Website offline": [0.70, 0.50]
    "Template usage": [0.75, 0.65]
    "Bond info loss": [0.15, 0.60]
    "Chai-2 anticipation": [0.05, 0.40]
    "GLIBCXX error": [0.20, 0.30]
    "pandera warning": [0.90, 0.20]
    "Single model prediction": [0.85, 0.35]
    "GPU profiling": [0.15, 0.55]
```

## 1. GPU Hardware: The Elephant in the Room

Chai-1's hardware requirements are not subtle. The README recommends **A100 80GB, H100 80GB, or L40S 48GB**, and notes that A10/A30 "will work for smaller complexes." Consumer-grade RTX 4090 (24GB) is mentioned as having been "reported to work." That language is doing a lot of heavy lifting.

The most notorious open issue is [CUDA out of memory (#17)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/17), where users on 2080 Ti (11GB), A100 40GB partitions, and even some A100 80GB setups all hit OOM errors. One commenter discovered that the issue was related to protein sequence length:

> "If I use the full sequence ~1500 it crash. Then I only put ~900 (remove 600), it worked." -- [@lonelu](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/17)

The issue was eventually closed by contributor Alex Rogozhnikov in January 2025, likely related to the [keep model components in CPU cache (#360)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/4d110dd40ee4ae60303c83a21de5ecb2d4a57dd1) commit, which offloads model components to CPU when not actively needed. This is a pragmatic fix, but the fundamental tension remains: **this is a large model that demands serious GPU memory, and there is no multi-GPU parallelism.**

The hardware story gets more complicated on non-NVIDIA terrain. [GLIBCXX_3.4.31 (#422)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/422) reports an `ImportError` on systems with outdated `libstdc++`, a classic dependency hell problem that bites users on older CentOS or HPC cluster environments. And [Inquiry about chai-1 support for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (#381)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/381) shows users trying to run on the newest RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell cards -- the answer is yes, but you may need bleeding-edge PyTorch and CUDA builds.

Meanwhile, [Error applying restraints (#413)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/413) specifically surfaces on **AMD GPUs via PyTorch ROCm**, where a padding-length mismatch error occurs in the restraint feature generator. This is a reminder that the chai-lab codebase is tested against NVIDIA CUDA first, and ROCm compatibility is essentially community-verified.

**Bottom line**: If you're not on an A100/H100 with current CUDA, expect friction. The team has made memory optimizations (CPU caching, conformer timeout in [PR #410](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/af596cbc075a1fce368cec0ab5f31be1090ca7e2)), but there's no magic bullet for running large complexes on budget hardware.

## 2. The Restraint System: Powerful but Perilous

Chai-1's restraint feature is arguably its most differentiated capability compared to [AlphaFold 3](https://deepmind.google/technologies/alphafold-3/) and [Boltz](https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz). You can specify pocket restraints, contact restraints, and covalent bonds to guide folding with experimental priors. But the implementation has sharp edges.

The most fundamental confusion was documented in [Using constraints seems to have little to no effect (#204)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/204), where a user specified **intra-chain** contact restraints and saw zero effect. Contributor Kevin Wu explained:

> "The restraints in Chai-1 are trained as **inter**-chain contacts; based on the line you've provided, it looks like you're trying to specify an **intra**-chain contact. Intra-chain contacts are more akin to structure templates, which you may be able to hack into the `TemplateContext`."

This is a critical documentation gap. The restraint system *silently ignores* intra-chain restraints rather than raising an error. Users waste compute cycles thinking the model is using their data when it isn't.

Then there are the outright bugs. [Error on run with restraints: Expected unique residue but found 0 (#376)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/376) reports an error with pocket restraints where the model can't resolve a residue identifier -- yet the run continues and produces output anyway, leaving users unsure whether their restraints were actually applied. And [Error applying restraints (#413)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/413) shows a padding-length mismatch when using restraints on ROCm, suggesting the feature generator has platform-specific behavior.

On the documentation side, [Source for Pocket Restraint Docs (#418)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/418) reveals that even the restraint documentation figure in the repository assets appears to have no attributable source, with a user noting they "am unable to find a source, besides some X posts that also showcase the same figure."

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User specifies restraint] --> B{Inter-chain?}
    B -->|Yes| C{Valid residue IDs?}
    B -->|No| D[Silently ignored - no warning]
    C -->|Yes| E{Correct format?}
    C -->|No| F["Error: Expected unique residue but found 0"]
    E -->|Yes| G[Restraint applied]
    E -->|No| H["Error: padding length mismatch"]
    D --> I[User thinks restraint is working]
    F --> J[Run continues anyway - ambiguous]
    
    style D fill:#ff9,stroke:#333
    style I fill:#f99,stroke:#333
    style J fill:#f99,stroke:#333
```

**Bottom line**: The restraint system is one of Chai-1's killer features, but it needs better guardrails. At minimum, intra-chain restraints should produce a warning. At best, they should be supported or the documentation should clearly state the limitation upfront.

## 3. Output Fidelity: What You See Isn't Always What You Get

Two persistent issues reveal that Chai-1's output format drops important information that downstream tools expect.

### PAE: Present in Computation, Absent in Output

[Extract PAE matrix from .cif file (#411)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/411) documents that Chai-1's ModelCIF output contains `_ma_qa_metric_local` entries (per-residue confidence) but **not** the `_ma_qa_metric_local_pairwise` entries that encode the Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) matrix. This is confirmed by [Missing PAE File in Python Prediction Mode (#348)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/348), which has accumulated 4 comments from users hitting the same wall.

The PAE matrix is essential for understanding inter-domain or inter-chain prediction confidence. Its absence means you can't distinguish between "both chains are well-predicted and correctly oriented" and "both chains are well-predicted but may be mis-positioned relative to each other" -- precisely the distinction that matters most for docking and complex prediction.

This is not a model limitation; the PAE is computed internally. It's an export gap. As [ChimeraX's ModelCIF PAE recipe](https://rbvi.github.io/chimerax-recipes/modelcif_pae/modelcif_pae.html) demonstrates, other tools in the ecosystem *do* write and read this field.

### Bond Information Loss in Small Molecules

[chai-1 prediction causes loss of atomic bond information (#417)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/417) reports that when predicting small molecule ligands, double bonds are reduced to single bonds in the output CIF. This is a known class of problem with diffusion-based structure predictors: the diffusion module predicts atom coordinates, not bond orders, so bond type information must be reconstructed from the input chemistry. When that reconstruction fails, you lose aromaticity and double-bond character -- information that's critical for downstream drug design workflows.

| Output Metric | Status | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| pLDDT (per-residue confidence) | Exported | Low |
| pTM / ipTM | Exported | Low |
| PAE (pairwise aligned error) | **Not exported** | **High** |
| Bond order (small molecules) | **Lost** | **High** |
| Chain naming | Configurable (since [PR #378](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/2a2d4a96e842a73499bacced0db662455b42e886)) | Medium |

**Bottom line**: For a model marketed as SOTA for drug discovery, losing PAE and bond orders in the output is a significant gap. These aren't edge cases -- they're core to how practitioners evaluate and use predictions.

## 4. Custom Chemistry: The CCD Wall

[Prediction with custom nucleotide/amino acid modifications (#423)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/423) is the most recent open issue and arguably the most forward-looking. A user wants to predict structures containing phosphorothioated nucleotides and other modifications that **have no CCD (Chemical Component Dictionary) code**. They've generated custom CIF files in the minimal CCD format used by AlphaFold 3 and Boltz, and ask:

> "Similarly to AF3 and Boltz, is there a way to update the list of CCD codes to include my custom ones, so I can predict sequences like ATG(PSC-min)GGTA?"

This is a real architectural limitation. Chai-1's input parsing resolves modification codes against the CCD, and there's currently no mechanism to extend the dictionary with user-provided entries. The recent [More flexible modification parsing (#384)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/dc41706bfc19b8530809c8b88cf7d90a58640b2e) commit broadened the parsing syntax (supporting `[]` in addition to `()` for modification specification), but didn't add custom CCD support.

Related issues include [Custom residue modification and covalent constraints (#366)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/366) and [Will ligand input as ccdcode be optional? (#382)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/382), both pointing at the same wall: the CCD is a fixed dependency, and the growing world of therapeutic oligonucleotides with non-standard chemistry doesn't fit neatly inside it.

**Bottom line**: For a tool used in drug discovery, extensibility of the chemistry dictionary is not optional. This is an area where [Boltz](https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz) currently has no advantage either, making it an opportunity for chai-lab to differentiate.

## 5. Infrastructure Fragility

Several issues reveal that getting chai-lab running is harder than it should be:

- **[Website is offline (#408)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/408)**: The `chaiassets.com` domain that serves conformer data files went offline on December 1, 2025, blocking inference entirely. This is a single-point-of-failure in the dependency chain: the model downloads conformer reference data at runtime from an external host, and when that host disappears, you're stuck. Five comments on this issue suggest it affected many users.

- **[HTTPError URL not found (#404)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/404)**: Another runtime download failure, this time with no details provided beyond a screenshot of the error.

- **[NameResolutionError (#386)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/386)**: A breaking import error caused by `urllib3.exceptions.NameResolutionError` not existing in older `urllib3` versions. Fixed quickly in [PR #387](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/0a5a85594a44096aeeba7b6f53f99b53f240de15) by switching to a more generic exception class, but the pattern is clear: **dependency version constraints are loosely specified**, and churn in transitive dependencies breaks chai-lab in unpredictable ways.

- **[pandera warning (#398)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/398)**: A `FutureWarning` from pandera about deprecated import paths. Non-fatal, but it signals that the dependency pinning strategy needs attention. Fixed the same day in [PR #399](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/a01bfdeead343e1c7f369660ec519f12c940e9df).

The [Global template cache folder + envvar (#371)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/eb63e84536bcbb46c0b675abb6a312ec9d682443) commit is a step in the right direction -- it adds a `CHAI_TEMPLATE_CIF_FOLDER` environment variable for controlling where template CIF files are cached, avoiding repeated downloads from RCSB. More of this kind of "make downloads optional and cacheable" thinking would help.

## 6. The Template System: Documented but Undocumented

[How to use structural templates? (#101)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/101) was opened in October 2024 and remained open for seven months before being closed. The original poster wanted to dock two proteins where one had a known structure, and couldn't find examples of how to provide template features. This is a common pattern: the README explains *that* you can provide templates, but the *how* is scattered across example scripts and source code.

The more recent [IntCastingNaNError (#402)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/402) shows a user crafting a custom `.m8` template hits file by hand to force Chai-1 to use a specific PDB structure as a template, only to hit a NaN error during parsing. The root cause was likely a formatting mismatch between the hand-crafted m8 file and what the parser expects, but the error message was unhelpful.

**Bottom line**: Template usage is a power-user feature with power-user documentation requirements that haven't been met. The addition of `CHAI_TEMPLATE_CIF_FOLDER` in [PR #371](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/eb63e84536bcbb46c0b675abb6a312ec9d682443) helps, but what's really needed is a worked example with a custom (non-RCSB) template.

## 7. Throughput and Scalability: The Virtual Screening Question

Two closed issues point at a class of use case that chai-lab isn't optimized for:

- **[Virtual Screening (#380)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/380)**: A user asked whether protein features could be cached when folding multiple ligands against the same protein, to speed up virtual screening workflows. They even offered to submit a PR with guidance. No response from the team was documented in the issue.

- **[How to predict only one model instead of five? (#385)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/385)**: A straightforward request to reduce the default 5-sample prediction to 1 for batch processing speed. The `--num-diffn-samples` flag exists but isn't prominently documented.

- **[Feature Request: GPU Profiling (#414)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/414)**: A request for built-in GPU profiling to identify memory hot spots, referencing the [PyTorch Profiler](https://pytorch.org/blog/introducing-pytorch-profiler-the-new-and-improved-performance-tool/). Closed immediately without implementation.

These issues collectively point at a tension: **Chai-1 is designed for accuracy-first single-complex prediction, but many drug discovery workflows need throughput-first batch processing.** The architecture doesn't currently support feature caching, and there's no built-in tooling for profiling or optimizing memory usage.

## 8. The Chai-2 Elephant

[About Chai-2 (#412)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/412) is just one sentence -- "I really look forward to use Chai-2. Please please please release it as soon as possible!" -- but it represents a broader dynamic. Chai Discovery [announced a $130M Series B](https://www.chaidiscovery.com) and has published the [Chai-2 technical report](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2025/07/06/2025.07.05.663018) on bioRxiv demonstrating zero-shot antibody design with ~20% experimental hit rates. Yet the Chai-2 code and model weights are **not open source** and are only available through a [trial application](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/391).

This creates a fork in the community: chai-lab (the open-source repo) remains Chai-1 only, while Chai-2 lives behind a proprietary access wall. As [Boolean Biotech's comparison](https://blog.booleanbiotech.com/alphafold3-boltz-chai1) noted, Chai-1 is already "inference only" -- no training code -- and now the next generation is further restricted. This trajectory is worth watching.

## Response Pattern: How the Team Engages

Looking at commit history and issue closure patterns, the chai-lab team is responsive but selective:

| Category | Typical Response | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Dependency breakage | Fast (days) | [NameResolutionError](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/386) fixed in hours |
| Parsing/formatting | Moderate (weeks) | [Modification parsing](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/dc41706bfc19b8530809c8b88cf7d90a58640b2e) |
| Feature requests | Slow or silent | [GPU Profiling](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/414) closed without action |
| Architecture gaps | No public response | [PAE export](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/411) open since Dec 2025 |
| Documentation gaps | Minimal | [Template usage](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/101) took 7 months |

The contributors -- primarily **Alex Rogozhnikov** (dependency fixes, memory optimization), **Kevin Wu** (restraint system, parsing, template handling), and **Jack Dent** (CLI, dependency updates) -- are clearly iterating on the codebase, but the GitHub issue tracker feels more like a support forum than a product roadmap. Many open issues receive no maintainer response at all.

## Summary: Where Chai-1 Stands with Its Users

The community feedback paints a picture of a model with genuine technical strengths -- SOTA benchmarks, commercial-friendly licensing, unique restraint capabilities -- but with operational rough edges that matter in practice:

1. **Hardware access remains the #1 gate.** No multi-GPU support, and memory optimization is incremental rather than transformative.
2. **The restraint system needs documentation and guardrails.** Silently ignoring intra-chain restraints is a design smell.
3. **Output completeness is a trust issue.** Missing PAE and bond orders undermine confidence for drug discovery workflows.
4. **Custom chemistry support is the next frontier.** The CCD wall will only get taller as oligonucleotide therapeutics grow.
5. **Infrastructure reliability needs hardening.** Runtime downloads from external hosts are fragile.

The good news is that many of these are fixable without architectural changes. The bad news is that with Chai-2 going proprietary, the open-source community's leverage for getting these fixes is diminishing. If you're building on chai-lab, pin your versions, cache your dependencies, and test your restraints carefully.

# About Contributors



The people behind chai-lab are not your typical open-source maintainers tinkering on weekends. They are the core of **Chai Discovery**, a San Francisco-based applied AI lab that has raised over **$225 million** in total financing ([General Catalyst Series B announcement](https://www.generalcatalyst.com/stories/our-investment-in-chai-discovery)), landed partnerships with **Pfizer** and **Eli Lilly**, and shipped two consecutive state-of-the-art models — Chai-1 for structure prediction, Chai-2 for de novo antibody design — in under two years. The repo itself is the open-source inference engine for Chai-1, released under Apache 2.0, and the commit log tells the story of a small, intensely focused team.

Let us meet them.

---

## The Founders

The four co-founders — Joshua Meier, Jack Dent, Matthew McPartlon, and Jacques Boitreaud — form a tightly knit unit whose professional histories intertwine across Harvard, big tech, and biotech. As [General Catalyst's investment memo](https://www.generalcatalyst.com/stories/our-investment-in-chai-discovery) puts it: their partnership was **"a decade in the making."**

### Joshua Meier — Co-Founder & CEO

Josh is the public face and corresponding author of both the [Chai-1 preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.10.615955v2) and the [Chai-2 preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.07.05.663018v1). His career arc reads like a microcosm of the AI-for-biology movement itself:

- **Harvard** — Studied chemistry and computer science, where he met Jack Dent on their first day of CS classes.
- **OpenAI** — Joined during the GPT-1/GPT-2 era. As Josh told *GEN*: *"We really had a front-row seat to language modeling and everything that was happening there."* The experience prompted a career-defining question: *"If these AI models can understand natural language processing, why can't they understand the real natural language, like DNA and proteins?"*
- **Meta (Facebook AI)** — Co-led development of **ESM1**, the first transformer protein-language model. This work on evolutionary scale modeling fundamentally changed how the field thinks about replacing MSAs with learned representations.
- **Absci** — Served as Chief AI Officer, where he and Matt McPartlon pioneered early de novo antibody design research and contributed to multiple drugs now in the clinic.

Josh's commit footprint in chai-lab is selective but meaningful — he authored [chai-2-bibtex (#394)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/2f7b713d6addd8cd7688ddfd5cb49e138f3e5b78), a citation utility, reflecting his role as the publication-facing lead. On X, he [described](https://x.com/joshim5/status/1917600000000000000) Chai-2's antibody hit rates as something he had *"only dreamed of"* for his entire career.

### Jack Dent — Co-Founder & President

Jack's trajectory is the most unusual of the four. As revealed in a [LinkedIn podcast appearance](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/sabrina-halper-00535716a_new-episode-with-jack-dent-co-founder-of-activity-7463323129533100033-aPpp), he **cold-emailed Stripe as a teenager** and joined the company, spending several years building out new product and engineering teams. His X profile simply reads: [Co-Founder @chaidiscovery](https://x.com/jackdent).

In chai-lab, Jack's contributions reflect his product-engineering instincts. He authored [Use full typer (#350)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/6d3439a0f41a0f33bb8cc1c3bbacfa36a99b7df9), migrating the CLI framework, and the recent [Update rdkit (#416)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/c544fb183e865c4950909444db860a9d50604f66) — dependency hygiene work that is thankless but critical for a package users install across wildly heterogeneous HPC environments. He was also the one who [engaged with the Hugging Face community](https://x.com/jackdent/status/1862200000000000000) to get Chai-1 on the Hub, and who [responded promptly](https://x.com/jackdent/status/1300000000000000000) when a user flagged a broken terms-of-service link.

The podcast anecdote that Sam Altman apparently asked Josh and Jack to start Chai **years before they actually did** is telling. They waited — Jack building systems muscle at Stripe, Josh deepening domain expertise — until the timing was right. That patience shows in the repo's engineering quality.

### Matthew McPartlon — Co-Founder

Matt is the least public-facing founder but arguably the most scientifically central to Chai-2's breakthrough. His quote in [Pharm Exec](https://www.pharmexec.com/view/menlo-ventures-led-70-million-series-a-fundraiser-chai-discovery-transform-molecular-design) captures the vision:

> *"Before Chai-2, the process was not unlike searching a giant bunch of keys for the right fit for a lock but there are millions of keys. Now, it's like having a master locksmith design exactly the right shape key, based only on your description of the lock. A company had spent more than three years and over $5m on a problem. With Chai-2, we were able to find an experimentally validated solution within two weeks."*

Matt's background runs parallel to Josh's: **Absci**, where he served as tech lead for de novo antibody design modeling. Before that, the [Menlo Ventures announcement](https://menlovc.com/perspective/revolutionizing-antibody-design-with-ai-why-were-backing-chai-discovery) describes him as one of the *"top researchers at the intersection of biology and artificial intelligence."* He is a co-author on both the Chai-1 and Chai-2 preprints but does not appear in the chai-lab commit log — his contributions sit upstream in model architecture and training, not inference infrastructure.

### Jacques Boitreaud — Co-Founder

Jacques led AI at **Aqemia**, a French small-molecule drug discovery company, where he productionized ML tools for molecular design — making research prototypes robust, scalable, and reliable enough for real-world deployment. That productionization ethos is visible in the chai-lab codebase: Jacques authored the early [PR to write predictions in CIF format](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/pull/45), which Jack Dent [publicly acknowledged](https://x.com/jackdent/status/1300000000000000000) as a response to community feedback. He is a co-author on both preprints.

---

## The Core Engineers

Beyond the founders, two names dominate the chai-lab commit history: **Alex Rogozhnikov** and **Kevin Wu**. Between them, they account for the majority of commits in the past year.

### Alex Rogozhnikov — The Infrastructure Architect

Alex is, by any measure, the most prolific contributor to chai-lab's day-to-day development. His [personal blog](https://arogozhnikov.github.io/about) describes him as a machine learning methodologist with a **PhD in mathematics and physics from Moscow University**, additional master's degrees from MSU's CS faculty, Higher School of Economics, and Yandex School of Data Analysis.

But Alex is best known in the broader ML community as the creator of **[einops](https://github.com/arogozhnikov/einops)** — the tensor manipulation library that has become a de facto standard in PyTorch codebases worldwide, with ~4 million monthly PyPI downloads and 9,500+ GitHub stars. In his own [retrospective on einops](https://arogozhnikov.github.io/2023/07/13/retrospective-thoughts-on-einops.html), he describes it as *"engineering art"* — a system shaped by hard constraints. That same sensibility is visible in his chai-lab work.

His commits tell a clear story: Alex is the person who keeps the inference pipeline from falling over. A representative sample:

| Commit | What it does |
|--------|-------------|
| [keep model components in CPU cache (#360)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/4d110dd40ee4ae60303c83a21de5ecb2d4a57dd1) | Memory optimization — offloading model components to CPU |
| [remove seq corruption logic, do not map D-AAs to their L-partners (#368)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/f824e747b46e73ea78c1153077a5907f6a0c3cca) | Correctness fix for D-amino acid handling |
| [use more generic error, that is also available in old urllib3 (#387)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/0a5a85594a44096aeeba7b6f53f99b53f240de15) | Compatibility fix for older environments |
| [Minimized version of #409 (parallel processing of conformers + reasonable timeout) (#410)](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/commit/af596cbc075a1fce368cec0ab5f31be1090ca7e2) | Fixed process hanging on conformer generation |

The pattern is unmistakable: **compatibility, robustness, memory management, and dependency hygiene**. Alex is the reason chai-lab runs on A100s and RTX 4090s alike without mysterious crashes. He also opened the GitHub issues [How do I get A100 GPU? #69](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/69) and [Feature request: support larger crop sizes #153](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/153), showing he thinks about user experience from the inside out.
