## Commit Velocity and Team Rhythm

The commit history reveals a telling pattern about how this team operates:

```mermaid
timeline
    title chai-lab Commit Rhythm (2024-2026)
    Sep 2024 : Chai-1 public release<br>Jack & "Jacques)" drive initial infra
    Oct 2024-Mar 2025 : Kevin Wu dominates<br>Restraints, FASTA parsing, caching
    Apr-May 2025 : Alex Rogozhnikov takes over<br>Memory optimization, D-amino acid fixes, kalign
```

The team clearly works in focused sprints rather than a steady drip of commits. Long silences correspond to periods when the team is heads-down on model development (Chai-2, Chai-3), with bursts of open-source activity when they surface to integrate fixes and push releases.

## What the Team's Background Explains About the Repo

Several characteristics of chai-lab that users frequently encounter — and occasionally frustration-vent in issues — become more legible when you understand who built it:

**The product-engineering DNA** (Jack from Stripe, Josh from OpenAI) explains why chai-lab has a clean CLI, a web interface, and an Apache 2.0 license rather than the non-commercial license typical of academic bioinformatics tools. This is infrastructure built for adoption.

**The Absci lineage** (Josh and Matt) explains the restraint system. Absci's whole thesis was AI-driven antibody design, and the ability to constrain folding with experimental data is what distinguishes Chai-1 from pure structure prediction tools like AlphaFold3. Kevin Wu's extensive restraint work is a direct continuation of that lineage.

**The production-ML DNA** (Alex from einops, Jacques from Aqemia) explains the obsessive attention to dependency compatibility, memory management, and timeout handling. These are people who have seen what happens when research code meets real infrastructure.

**The small team size** (~25 people total, far fewer working on open-source inference) explains why some issues linger. As Josh acknowledged to *GEN*: *"We're a small team, but we've got a lot of work to do."* The open issues about [custom nucleotide modifications](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/423), [PAE extraction](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/411), and [bond information loss](https://github.com/chaidiscovery/chai-lab/issues/417) are not signs of neglect — they reflect the reality of a team whose commercial priorities (Chai-2, Chai-3, Pfizer, Lilly) pull in a different direction from the open-source inference engine.

---

## The Bigger Picture

Chai Discovery's contributor story is ultimately about a team that made a very specific bet: that foundation models for biology would hit an inflection point where they become useful across the board for drug discovery. As Josh [told *GEN*](https://www.genengnews.com/topics/artificial-intelligence/chais-the-limit-for-ai-antibody-designer-after-130m-series-b-funding): *"We made a bet that these language models would reach an inflection point... five years from now, this is just how everyone is going to be discovering drugs."*

The chai-lab repo is the open-source expression of that bet. It is maintained by a team that could easily have kept it proprietary — and indeed, Chai-2 and Chai-3 are not open-source — but chose to release Chai-1 freely. Whether that openness continues as the company's commercial pressures mount remains an open question. For now, the commit log tells the story of a small, technically elite team moving fast and shipping real infrastructure.

That the repo's most active maintainer is also the author of einops — one of the most widely used ML utilities in the PyTorch ecosystem — is not a coincidence. It is a signal about the caliber of engineering that serious AI-for-biology demands.

# Architecture Overview



Chai-1 is a unified deep learning system for **multi-chain molecular structure prediction** — it folds proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, and glycans into joint 3D structures from sequence inputs alone. The architecture follows a **four-stage pipeline**: input parsing and context assembly, feature embedding and token representation, iterative trunk refinement with recycling, and diffusion-based structure generation with confidence scoring. Each stage is decoupled into dedicated modules that communicate through typed data contexts, enabling both CLI-driven inference and programmatic exploration.

![Chai-1 Performance](chaidiscovery/chai-lab/blob/main/assets/performance_barplot.png?raw=true)

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L1-L109), [main.py](chai_lab/main.py#L1-L49)

## High-Level Pipeline Architecture

The end-to-end inference flow is orchestrated by `run_inference`, which delegates to `make_all_atom_feature_context` for data preparation and `run_folding_on_context` for model inference. The system loads **five exported TorchScript model components** — `feature_embedding.pt`, `token_embedder.pt`, `trunk.pt`, `diffusion_module.pt`, and `confidence_head.pt` — each wrapped in a `ModuleWrapper` that handles device migration and crop-size dispatching via `forward_{crop_size}` methods.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["Input Data System"]
        FASTA["FASTA File"] --> PARSE["FASTA Parsing<br/>& Entity Typing"]
        PARSE --> CHAINS["Chain Objects"]
        CHAINS --> CTX["AllAtomFeatureContext"]
        MSA["MSA Sources"] --> CTX
        ESM["ESM Embeddings"] --> CTX
        TPL["Templates"] --> CTX
        RST["Restraints"] --> CTX
    end

    subgraph FeatureEng["Feature Engineering"]
        CTX --> COLLATE["Collate & Pad"]
        COLLATE --> FF["FeatureFactory<br/>(30+ generators)"]
        FF --> BATCH["Batched Tensors"]
    end

    subgraph Model["Model Inference"]
        BATCH --> FE["Feature Embedding"]
        FE --> TE["Token Embedder"]
        TE --> TRUNK["Trunk<br/>(w/ Recycling)"]
        TRUNK --> DIFF["Diffusion Module<br/>(Denoising)"]
        DIFF --> CONF["Confidence Head"]
    end

    subgraph Output["Output & Evaluation"]
        CONF --> RANK["Ranking & Scoring"]
        RANK --> CIF["CIF Output"]
        RANK --> SCORES["pTM / pLDDT / PAE"]
    end

    style Input fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#2d7d2d
    style FeatureEng fill:#e8e8f4,stroke:#2d2d7d
    style Model fill:#f4e8e8,stroke:#7d2d2d
    style Output fill:#f4f4e8,stroke:#7d7d2d
```

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L498-L572), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L579-L716)

## Core Data Model: Context Objects

The architecture is built around a hierarchy of **immutable context objects** that encapsulate different modalities of input data. The central hub is `AllAtomFeatureContext`, which aggregates six distinct contexts — each independently paddable, serializable to dicts, and carrying typed tensor data. This design ensures that every model component receives exactly the data it needs through a well-defined interface rather than ad-hoc parameter passing.

| Context | Purpose | Key Fields | Source Module |
|---------|---------|------------|---------------|
| **AllAtomStructureContext** | Atom-level coordinates, masks, residue indices, bond info | `atom_coords`, `atom_exists_mask`, `token_residue_index` | [all_atom_structure_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/structure/all_atom_structure_context.py) |
| **MSAContext** | Multiple sequence alignment tokens, deletions, pairing keys | `tokens`, `mask`, `deletion_matrix`, `pairing_key_hash` | [msa_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/msas/msa_context.py) |
| **TemplateContext** | Structural template hits from homologous structures | Template distograms, unit vectors, residue types, masks | [context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/templates/context.py) |
| **EmbeddingContext** | Pre-computed ESM protein language model embeddings | `esm_embeddings` (shape: `num_tokens × 2560`) | [embedding_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/embeddings/embedding_context.py#L14-L26) |
| **RestraintContext** | User-specified distance/pocket restraints and covalent bonds | Pairwise constraint tensors | [restraint_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py) |
| **AllAtomFeatureContext** | **Aggregate container** for all above contexts | `chains`, plus all five contexts above | [all_atom_feature_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/all_atom_feature_context.py#L24-L39) |

> [!TIP]
> The `AllAtomFeatureContext.pad()` method cascades padding through every sub-context — tokens are padded to the nearest `AVAILABLE_MODEL_SIZES` bucket (256, 384, …, 2048), and atoms scale proportionally at 23 atoms per token. This ensures that the exported TorchScript models, which are compiled for fixed sizes, always receive correctly shaped input.

Sources: [all_atom_feature_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/all_atom_feature_context.py#L24-L96), [embedding_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/embeddings/embedding_context.py#L14-L51), [collate/utils.py](chai_lab/data/collate/utils.py#L13-L39)

## Feature Generation System

Features are produced by a **registry of 30+ `FeatureGenerator` instances** collected into a `FeatureFactory`. Each generator declares a `FeatureType` (the output slot it fills) and an `EncodingType` (how raw data is encoded). The factory's `generate()` method iterates all registered generators against the collated batch, producing a dictionary of named tensors that the model consumes.

The `FeatureType` enum defines **seven feature slots** that correspond to the model's input channels. Each slot carries distinct geometric and semantic information:

| FeatureType | Dimensionality | Description | Example Generators |
|-------------|---------------|-------------|-------------------|
| `TOKEN` | Per-token | Single-token properties | `ResidueType`, `ESMEmbeddings`, `RelativeEntity` |
| `TOKEN_PAIR` | Token×Token | Pairwise token relations | `RelativeSequenceSeparation`, `TokenDistanceRestraint` |
| `ATOM` | Per-atom | Single-atom properties | `AtomElementOneHot`, `AtomNameOneHot`, `RefPos` |
| `ATOM_PAIR` | Atom×Atom (blocked) | Pairwise atom relations | `BlockedAtomPairDistogram`, `BlockedAtomPairDistances` |
| `MSA` | MSA depth × Tokens | Multiple sequence alignment | `MSAFeatureGenerator`, `MSADeletionValueGenerator` |
| `TEMPLATES` | Templates × Tokens | Structural templates | `TemplateDistogramGenerator`, `TemplateUnitVectorGenerator` |
| `RESIDUE` / `PAIR` | Legacy slots | Internal use | — |

> [!TIP]
> The `EncodingType` controls how raw integer or float data is cast for model consumption. `ONE_HOT` and `OUTERSUM` modes append a mask class (index = `num_classes`) for padding positions; `IDENTITY` mode reserves its last channel as a binary mask flag. This unified masking strategy ensures that every feature tensor is self-describing about which positions are valid.

Sources: [feature_type.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_type.py#L1-L17), [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L58-L114), [feature_factory.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L16-L27), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L172-L236)

## Model Component Architecture

The model is decomposed into **five exported TorchScript components**, each loaded on demand and moved between CPU and GPU to manage memory. The `ModuleWrapper` and `_component_moved_to` context manager implement a transient device migration pattern — a component is moved to GPU for computation, then immediately back to CPU, avoiding repeated disk I/O for large model weights.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Embedders
        FE["feature_embedding.pt<br/>Embeds raw features<br/>into TOKEN, TOKEN_PAIR,<br/>ATOM, ATOM_PAIR, MSA, TEMPLATES"]
        TE["token_embedder.pt<br/>Projects atom-level info<br/>into token representations"]
    end

    subgraph Trunk
        TR["trunk.pt<br/>Iterative refinement<br/>with MSA & template attention<br/>(recycled N times)"]
    end

    subgraph Generation
        DM["diffusion_module.pt<br/>Denoises atom positions<br/>(stochastic sampler,<br/>200 timesteps default)"]
        CH["confidence_head.pt<br/>Predicts PAE, PDE, pLDDT"]
    end

    FE --> TE
    TE --> TR
    TR --> DM
    DM --> CH

    TR -.->|recycled reprs| TR
    TE -.->|structure inputs| DM
```

The **feature embedder** splits each output into two halves along the channel dimension — one for the trunk pathway and one for the structure/diffusion pathway. This dual-output design means that the token embedder and trunk operate on one set of embeddings while the diffusion module receives a parallel set, allowing specialized representations for iterative refinement versus coordinate generation.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L679-L738), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L115-L148), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L844-L885)

## Inference Flow: From Context to Structure

The `run_folding_on_context` function implements the complete inference trajectory in a precise sequence. Understanding this flow is essential for navigating the codebase:

1. **Collation**: The `Collate` class pads the `AllAtomFeatureContext` to the nearest model size bucket, computes blocked atom-pair indices for local attention, and runs all feature generators to produce the full feature dictionary. [collate.py](chai_lab/data/collate/collate.py#L29-L97)

2. **Feature Embedding**: Raw features are projected through `feature_embedding.pt`, producing embedded representations for each feature slot. Each slot's output is **split in half** — one half feeds the trunk, the other feeds the structure module. [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L687-L698)

3. **Bond Feature Injection**: `TokenBondRestraint` features are generated separately (due to export constraints) and projected through `bond_loss_input_proj.pt`, then **added** to the token pair representations for both trunk and structure pathways. [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L705-L715)

4. **Token Embedding**: The `token_embedder.pt` consumes embedded token, pair, and atom features along with blocked atom-pair data, producing three outputs: `token_single_initial_repr`, `token_single_structure_input`, and `token_pair_initial_repr`. [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L721-L738)

5. **Trunk Recycling**: The trunk iterates `num_trunk_recycles` times (default 3), receiving both initial and recycled representations. On each recycle, MSA features can be subsampled. The trunk outputs updated `token_single_trunk_repr` and `token_pair_trunk_repr`. [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L748-L777)

6. **Diffusion Denoising**: Starting from pure noise (scaled by σ_max), the diffusion module iteratively denoises atom coordinates using a **stochastic sampler** with configurable churn (S_churn=80), second-order updates, and power-interpolation noise scheduling. [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L806-L885)

7. **Confidence Prediction**: The `confidence_head.pt` predicts per-atom pLDDT, per-token-pair PAE, and per-token-pair PDE for each of the `num_diffn_samples` generated structures. [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L894-L915)

8. **Ranking & Output**: Each sample is ranked using an aggregate score: `0.2 × pTM + 0.8 × ipTM − 100 × has_inter_chain_clashes`. Results are written as CIF files and `.npz` score archives. [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L94-L99)

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L579-L1059), [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L56-L112), [diffusion_schedules.py](chai_lab/model/diffusion_schedules.py#L13-L48)

## Memory Management Strategy

The codebase implements an explicit **CPU offloading strategy** to support inference on GPUs with limited memory. The `_component_moved_to` context manager caches loaded TorchScript modules in a global `_component_cache` dict, moving each component to GPU only during its forward pass and back to CPU immediately afterward. The `low_memory` flag (default `True`) controls whether intermediate embeddings are returned to CPU between stages. Additionally, `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` is called after the trunk recycling loop and after the diffusion loop to release fragmented GPU memory before subsequent operations.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L151-L166), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L648-L649), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L779-L780), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L887-L888)

## Input Data System Overview

The input pipeline converts raw FASTA files into the `AllAtomFeatureContext` through a multi-step process. Each entity in the FASTA file is parsed according to its type (protein, DNA, RNA, ligand, glycan), tokenized into residue-level tokens, and assembled into `Chain` objects. External data sources — MSA, ESM embeddings, templates, and restraints — are loaded or generated and merged into the context. The following table summarizes the five data modalities and their entry points:

| Modality | Entry Point | Default Behavior | User Control |
|----------|-------------|-----------------|--------------|
| **MSA** | `get_msa_contexts()` / `generate_colabfold_msas()` | Empty if no source specified | `--use-msa-server` or `--msa-directory` |
| **ESM Embeddings** | `get_esm_embedding_context()` | Enabled by default (CPU) | `--no-use-esm` |
| **Templates** | `get_template_context()` | Empty if no source specified | `--use-templates-server` or `--templates-path` |
| **Restraints** | `load_manual_restraints_for_chai1()` | Empty if no constraint file | `--constraint-path` |
| **Covalent Bonds** | `get_atom_covalent_bond_pairs_from_constraints()` | Parsed from restraint file | Embedded in `.restraints` file |

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L338-L495), [inference_dataset.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/inference_dataset.py#L94-L177)

```
chai_lab/

│   │   ├── msas/             ← MSA generation (ColabFold) and loading
│   │   ├── structure/        ← All-atom tokenization, chain, bond utilities
│   │   └── templates/        ← Template alignment and loading
│   ├── features/             ← Feature generation framework & 20+ generators
│   │   └── generators/       ← Individual feature generator implementations
│   ├── io/                   ← CIF/PDB output, RCSB utilities
│   ├── parsing/              ← FASTA, glycan, restraint, MSA, template parsing
│   └── sources/              ← RDKit integration for ligand conformers
├── model/
│   ├── diffusion_schedules.py← Noise schedule (power interpolation)
│   └── utils.py              ← Attention blocking, quaternion math, augmentation
├── ranking/                  ← Structure scoring: pTM, pLDDT, clash detection
├── tools/                    ← External tool wrappers (kalign, rigid transforms)
└── utils/                    ← Paths, tensor ops, plotting, typing, defaults
```

Sources: [Project structure](chai_lab/)

# Feature Context Assembly



Feature Context Assembly is the critical orchestration layer in Chai-1's inference pipeline that transforms raw input sequences into a fully resolved, padded, and batched tensor dictionary ready for model consumption. It bridges the gap between heterogeneous input sources — FASTA sequences, MSAs, templates, ESM embeddings, and restraints — and the unified feature tensors that the model's forward pass expects. Understanding this assembly process is essential for anyone extending Chai-1's input capabilities or debugging data pipeline issues.

## The Assembly Architecture at a Glance

The assembly follows a strict three-phase pipeline: **context construction** (per-system), **collation** (cross-system), and **feature generation** (batch-wide). Each phase has a clear contract — contexts produce typed dataclasses, collation handles padding and stacking, and feature generation applies encoding transformations to produce the final tensor dictionary.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Phase1["Phase 1: Context Construction"]
        A[FASTA Input] --> B[Chain Tokenization]
        B --> C[AllAtomStructureContext]
        A --> D[MSA Generation / Loading]
        D --> E[MSAContext]
        A --> F[Template Search / Loading]
        F --> G[TemplateContext]
        A --> H[ESM Embedding Computation]
        H --> I[EmbeddingContext]
        A --> J[Restraint Parsing]
        J --> K[RestraintContext]
    end

    subgraph Phase2["Phase 2: Collation"]
        L["AllAtomFeatureContext<br/>aggregates all sub-contexts"]
        C --> L
        E --> L
        G --> L
        I --> L
        K --> L
        L --> M["Pad to AVAILABLE_MODEL_SIZES"]
        M --> N[Stack into Batch Dict]
    end

    subgraph Phase3["Phase 3: Feature Generation"]
        O["FeatureFactory.generate"]
        N --> O
        O --> P["Encoded Feature Tensors<br/>by FeatureType"]
    end

    Phase1 --> Phase2
```

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L214-L399), [all_atom_feature_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/all_atom_feature_context.py#L26-L96), [collate.py](/chai_lab/data/collate/collate.py#L23-L98)

## The Central Data Structure: AllAtomFeatureContext

**AllAtomFeatureContext** is the unified container that aggregates every sub-context for a single molecular system. It is a frozen dataclass produced by the dataset layer and consumed by the collation layer. Its design enforces a clean separation: metadata fields (like `chains`) travel alongside the batch but are never padded or stacked, while all sub-contexts implement a `pad()` method and a `to_dict()` method that standardize their representation for batched tensor operations.

| Sub-Context | Role | Key Fields | Max Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `AllAtomStructureContext` | Token/atom coordinates, residue types, chain IDs, bond indices | `token_residue_type`, `atom_ref_pos`, `atom_covalent_bond_indices` | n_tokens × 23 atoms |
| `MSAContext` | Multiple sequence alignment rows, deletion matrices, pairing keys | `tokens`, `mask`, `deletion_matrix`, `pairing_key_hash` | 16,384 depth |
| `TemplateContext` | Structural templates with backbone frames and distograms | `template_restype`, `template_distances`, `template_unit_vector` | 4 templates |
| `EmbeddingContext` | Pre-computed ESM protein embeddings | `esm_embeddings` | n_tokens × 2560 |
| `RestraintContext` | Contact, pocket, and docking restraints | `docking_restraints`, `contact_restraints`, `pocket_restraints` | Unbounded lists |

The `to_dict()` method merges all sub-context dictionaries into a single flat dictionary, where tensor keys follow a naming convention like `msa_tokens`, `template_restype`, and `esm_embeddings`. This flattened representation is what the collator stacks across the batch dimension. The `pad()` method delegates to each sub-context's own padding logic, ensuring that every tensor within a batch shares the same spatial dimensions before stacking.

> [!TIP]
> The `profile_msa_context` is a second `MSAContext` distinct from `msa_context`. The main MSA context carries the full depth alignment (up to 16,384 rows), while the profile MSA context provides a compressed summary used for profile-based feature generation like `MSAProfileGenerator`. Both are padded and batched identically but serve different feature generators downstream.

Sources: [all_atom_feature_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/all_atom_feature_context.py#L26-L96), [all_atom_structure_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/structure/all_atom_structure_context.py#L25-L96), [msa_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/msas/msa_context.py#L19-L168), [context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/templates/context.py#L35-L120), [embedding_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/embeddings/embedding_context.py#L10-L52), [restraint_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py#L29-L71)

## Context Construction: From FASTA to AllAtomFeatureContext

The `make_all_atom_feature_context` function in `chai1.py` is the entry point for context construction during inference. It orchestrates a deterministic sequence of steps, each producing one sub-context:

1. **Input parsing and validation** — `read_inputs` parses the FASTA file, identifies entity types (protein, ligand, RNA, DNA, glycan), and validates uniqueness of entity names.

2. **Chain tokenization** — `load_chains_from_raw` converts each input into an `AllAtomEntityData`, then tokenizes it via `AllAtomResidueTokenizer` to produce `Chain` objects wrapping `AllAtomStructureContext`. Failed tokenizations are silently dropped.

3. **Structure merging** — Individual chain structure contexts are merged via `AllAtomStructureContext.merge`, producing a single unified structure context with reindexed tokens and atoms across all chains. Token count validation (`raise_if_too_many_tokens`) occurs here.

4. **MSA assembly** — Depending on configuration, MSAs are either generated via ColabFold server, loaded from a directory, or left empty. The `get_msa_contexts` function produces the main `MSAContext`, while a profile MSA is derived separately.

5. **Template loading** — Template contexts are built from MMseqs2 search results or pre-loaded template files, producing a `TemplateContext` with up to 4 structural templates.

6. **ESM embedding** — Optionally, ESM-2 embeddings are computed for protein sequences and wrapped in an `EmbeddingContext`.

7. **Restraint parsing** — If a restraint file is provided, `load_manual_restraints_for_chai1` parses it into a `RestraintContext` containing contact, pocket, or docking constraints.

The final `AllAtomFeatureContext` is assembled by passing all sub-contexts to its constructor. Notably, `EmbeddingContext` is optional (`None` if ESM is disabled), and `RestraintContext.empty()` is used when no restraints are specified.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L293-L399), [inference_dataset.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/inference_dataset.py#L172-L246), [restraint_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py#L82-L137)

## Collation: Padding, Stacking, and Batch Preparation

The `Collate` dataclass transforms a list of `AllAtomFeatureContext` objects into a single batched dictionary. This is a two-stage process implemented in `_collate` and `_post_collate`.

**Stage 1 — Pad and Stack (`_collate`)**: First, `get_pad_sizes` determines the maximum token and atom counts across all feature contexts in the batch. Token padding snaps up to the nearest entry in `AVAILABLE_MODEL_SIZES = [256, 384, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048]`, while atom padding uses the formula `23 × n_tokens` (each token can have up to 23 atoms). Each context is padded independently via `AllAtomFeatureContext.pad`, then all padded contexts are converted to dicts and stacked along a new batch dimension using `torch.stack`.

**Stage 2 — Post-Collation (`_post_collate`)**: After stacking, the collator computes auxiliary data structures needed by the model: block-based atom pair indices (`block_q_atom_idces`, `block_kv_atom_idces`) and their corresponding masks. These enable the model's blocked attention pattern over atom pairs, which is critical for memory efficiency at large token counts. Finally, the `FeatureFactory.generate` method is called on the entire batch to produce the encoded feature tensors.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Input
        FC1[FeatureContext 1]
        FC2[FeatureContext 2]
        FC3[FeatureContext 3]
    end

    subgraph Pad
        PS["get_pad_sizes<br/>→ nearest AVAILABLE_MODEL_SIZE"]
        P1[.pad n_tokens, n_atoms]
        P2[.pad n_tokens, n_atoms]
        P3[.pad n_tokens, n_atoms]
    end

    subgraph Stack
        D1[to_dict]
        D2[to_dict]
        D3[to_dict]
        ST[torch.stack<br/>→ batch dim 0]
    end

    subgraph PostCollate
        BA[Block Atom Pair Indices]
        FF[FeatureFactory.generate]
    end

    FC1 --> P1
    FC2 --> P2
    FC3 --> P3
    PS --> P1
    PS --> P2
    PS --> P3
    P1 --> D1
    P2 --> D2
    P3 --> D3
    D1 --> ST
    D2 --> ST
    D3 --> ST
    ST --> BA
    ST --> FF
```

| Model Size | Max Tokens | Max Atoms (23×) | Typical Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | 256 | 5,888 | Small single proteins |
| 384 | 384 | 8,832 | Medium proteins |
| 512 | 512 | 11,776 | Protein-ligand complexes |
| 768 | 768 | 17,664 | Multi-chain assemblies |
| 1024 | 1,024 | 23,552 | Large complexes |
| 1536 | 1,536 | 35,328 | Very large complexes |
| 2048 | 2,048 | 47,104 | Maximum capacity |

Sources: [collate.py](/chai_lab/data/collate/collate.py#L23-L98), [collate_utils.py](/chai_lab/data/collate/utils.py#L10-L40)

## FeatureFactory: The Encoding Engine

`FeatureFactory` is a lightweight orchestrator that maps named feature generators to their outputs. It holds a `dict[str, FeatureGenerator]` and its `generate` method simply iterates over all registered generators, calling each one's `generate` method on the batch dictionary. The resulting `dict[str, Tensor]` is stored under the `"features"` key in the final batch.

Each `FeatureGenerator` is an abstract base class that declares three critical properties:

- **`ty` (FeatureType)** — Determines the tensor's structural role: `TOKEN` (per-token features), `TOKEN_PAIR` (pairwise token features), `MSA` (alignment features), `TEMPLATES` (template features), `ATOM` (per-atom features), or `ATOM_PAIR` (pairwise atom features).

- **`encoding_ty` (EncodingType)** — Determines the numerical encoding strategy: `ONE_HOT` (categorical → one-hot vectors), `RBF` (radial basis functions for distances), `FOURIER` (positional encodings), `IDENTITY` (pass-through with masking), `ESM` (pre-computed embeddings), or `OUTERSUM` (outer sum of one-hot encodings).

- **`mask_value`** — A computed property that returns the appropriate fill value for masked positions, varying by encoding type. For one-hot encodings, it returns `num_classes` (an extra "mask" class); for RBF/Fourier, it returns `-100.0`; for identity, it uses a dedicated mask channel where the last position is 1 for masked items.

The full set of feature generators registered in Chai-1's `feature_factory` spans 29 named generators, organized by their feature type:

| FeatureType | Generator Names | Count |
|---|---|---|
| TOKEN | `ResidueType`, `ESMEmbeddings`, `IsDistillation`, `TokenBFactor`, `TokenPLDDT`, `ChainIsCropped` | 6 |
| TOKEN_PAIR | `RelativeSequenceSeparation`, `RelativeTokenSeparation`, `RelativeEntity`, `RelativeChain`, `MissingChainContact`, `TokenDistanceRestraint`, `TokenPairPocketRestraint` | 7 |
| ATOM | `AtomRefPos`, `AtomRefCharge`, `AtomRefMask`, `AtomRefElement`, `AtomNameOneHot` | 5 |
| ATOM_PAIR | `BlockedAtomPairDistogram`, `InverseSquaredBlockedAtomPairDistances` | 2 |
| MSA | `MSAOneHot`, `MSAHasDeletion`, `MSADeletionValue`, `MSADeletionMean`, `MSAProfile`, `IsPairedMSA`, `MSADataSource` | 7 |
| TEMPLATES | `TemplateMask`, `TemplateUnitVector`, `TemplateResType`, `TemplateDistogram` | 4 |

> [!TIP]
> The `DockingConstraintGenerator` is registered with `include_probability=0.0` and `structure_dropout_prob=0.75`, meaning docking restraints are effectively disabled during standard inference. This is a training-time feature for data augmentation. If you need to enable docking restraints at inference, you must modify the generator's configuration or create a custom feature factory.

Sources: [feature_factory.py](/chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L1-L27), [base.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L11-L114), [feature_type.py](/chai_lab/data/features/feature_type.py#L1-L17), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L165-L253)

## Sub-Context Padding Semantics

Each sub-context implements padding with domain-specific semantics that go beyond simple zero-filling. Understanding these semantics is critical for interpreting masked values in downstream feature tensors.

**AllAtomStructureContext** pads tokens by extending `token_exists_mask` with `False` entries and filling token-level fields with neutral values (e.g., gap residue type for `token_residue_type`). Atom-level fields follow a similar pattern: `atom_exists_mask` and `atom_is_not_padding_mask` are extended with `False`, and coordinate fields (`atom_ref_pos`, `atom_gt_coords`) are zero-filled. Covalent bond indices are preserved as-is since they reference atoms within the non-padded region.

**MSAContext** pads along both the token dimension (columns) and the depth dimension (rows). Token padding fills with the gap token (`:`), `NO_PAIRING_KEY` for pairing hashes, zero deletions, and `False` mask. Depth padding adds empty rows with identical fill values. The `sequence_source` field is padded with `MSADataSource.NONE` to ensure padded MSA rows are not attributed to any search source.

**TemplateContext** pads templates with null residue types (gap character `-`), zero masks for pseudo-beta and backbone frames, and zero distance/unit-vector tensors. The `template_mask` property (derived as `template_restype != gap`) correctly identifies non-null templates after padding.

**EmbeddingContext** zero-pads the ESM embedding matrix along the token dimension, producing `esm_embeddings` of shape `[max_tokens, 2560]` with zero vectors for padding positions.

**RestraintContext** is a notable exception — its `pad()` method is a no-op, returning the same object unchanged. This is because restraints are stored as Python lists of dataclasses, not tensors, and are processed by feature generators that handle their own indexing into the token space.

Sources: [all_atom_structure_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/structure/all_atom_structure_context.py#L25-L200), [msa_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/msas/msa_context.py#L90-L130), [context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/templates/context.py#L108-L200), [embedding_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/embeddings/embedding_context.py#L30-L42), [restraint_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py#L44-L48)

## The End-to-End Data Flow

Tracing the complete path from a FASTA file to the model-ready batch reveals how each component participates in the assembly:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant make_context as make_all_atom_feature_context
    participant chains as load_chains_from_raw
    participant msa as MSA Pipeline
    participant tmpl as Template Pipeline
    participant esm as ESM Pipeline
    participant restraint as Restraint Parser
    participant aafc as AllAtomFeatureContext
    participant collate as Collate
    participant ff as FeatureFactory

    User->>make_context: FASTA file + config
    make_context->>chains: parse + tokenize
    chains-->>make_context: list[Chain]
    make_context->>msa: protein sequences
    msa-->>make_context: MSAContext (main + profile)
    make_context->>tmpl: protein sequences
    tmpl-->>make_context: TemplateContext
    make_context->>esm: protein sequences
    esm-->>make_context: EmbeddingContext
    make_context->>restraint: constraint file
    restraint-->>make_context: RestraintContext
    make_context->>aafc: assemble all sub-contexts
    aafc-->>collate: AllAtomFeatureContext

    collate->>collate: get_pad_sizes → pad each context
    collate->>collate: to_dict + torch.stack
    collate->>collate: compute block atom pair indices
    collate->>ff: FeatureFactory.generate(batch)
    ff-->>collate: dict[str, Tensor] features
    collate-->>User: final batch dict
```

The final batch dictionary contains three top-level keys: `"inputs"` (the stacked, padded raw tensors from all sub-contexts), `"features"` (the encoded feature tensors produced by the FeatureFactory), and additional block-attention indices (`block_atom_pair_q_idces`, `block_atom_pair_kv_idces`, `block_atom_pair_mask`). The model's forward method receives this complete dictionary and dispatches features by their `FeatureType` to the appropriate embedding modules.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L293-L399), [collate.py](/chai_lab/data/collate/collate.py#L36-L98), [feature_factory.py](/chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L14-L21)

## Next Steps

With the feature context fully assembled and batched, the pipeline proceeds to the embedding and attention stages. To understand how raw features are transformed into model inputs:

- **[Feature Embedding and Token Embedding](9-feature-embedding-and-token-embedding)** — How each FeatureType is embedded and combined into the trunk's input representations.
- **[Feature Generator Base Design](18-feature-generator-base-design)** — Deep dive into the `FeatureGenerator` ABC and how to create custom generators.
- **[Token and Atom Feature Generators](19-token-and-atom-feature-generators)** — Detailed breakdown of per-token and per-atom feature encoding logic.

# Feature Embedding and Token Embedding



The Feature Embedding and Token Embedding stages form the critical bridge between raw, heterogeneous input features and the structured latent representations that feed Chai-1's trunk recycler and diffusion module. Together, they transform a dictionary of disparate feature tensors—each with its own encoding scheme, dimensionality, and semantic domain—into unified **token single**, **token pair**, and **atom** representations ready for iterative attention. Understanding this two-stage pipeline is essential for anyone extending the feature set, debugging representation quality, or reasoning about what information is available to downstream modules.

## From Raw Features to Typed Tensors: The FeatureFactory

Every inference run begins with a **FeatureFactory** that orchestrates the generation of all raw features. The factory is a simple name-to-generator registry: each registered `FeatureGenerator` knows how to extract its input keys from a batch dictionary, compute its feature tensor, and cast it to the correct dtype via its `EncodingType`. The factory's `generate` method iterates over all generators and returns a flat dictionary of named tensors.

```python
# The factory is constructed once in chai1.py with ~30 generators
feature_factory = FeatureFactory(feature_generators)
# ... later, inside Collate._post_collate:
raw_batch["features"] = self.feature_factory.generate(raw_batch)
```

Each generator declares two orthogonal axes of identity: its **FeatureType** (the semantic domain it belongs to) and its **EncodingType** (how the raw data is numerically represented). These two axes determine how the downstream feature embedder will process the tensor.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L118-L186), [feature_factory.py](/chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L1-L27), [collate.py](/chai_lab/data/collate/collate.py#L77-L85)

## Feature Types and the Semantic Domain Taxonomy

The `FeatureType` enum partitions all features into six semantic domains. This taxonomy is not merely organizational—it directly governs how the feature embedder routes and concatenates tensors:

| FeatureType | Shape Pattern | Description | Example Generators |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TOKEN` | `[B, N, ...]` | Per-token single features | `ResidueType`, `ESMEmbeddings`, `MSAProfile` |
| `TOKEN_PAIR` | `[B, N, N, ...]` | Per-token-pair features | `RelativeSequenceSeparation`, `RelativeEntity`, `RelativeChain` |
| `ATOM` | `[B, A, ...]` | Per-atom single features | `AtomRefPos`, `AtomRefCharge`, `AtomRefElement` |
| `ATOM_PAIR` | `[B, A_block, ...]` | Blocked atom-pair features | `BlockedAtomPairDistogram` |
| `MSA` | `[B, D, N, ...]` | MSA depth × token features | `MSAFeatureGenerator`, `MSAHasDeletion` |
| `TEMPLATES` | `[B, T, N, ...]` | Template features | `TemplateDistogram`, `TemplateUnitVector` |

Here `B` is batch size, `N` is number of tokens, `A` is number of atoms, `D` is MSA depth, and `T` is number of templates. The feature embedder consumes all of these in a single forward pass, concatenating within each domain before applying domain-specific linear projections.

Sources: [feature_type.py](/chai_lab/data/features/feature_type.py#L1-L17)

## Encoding Types and the Mask Convention

Each `FeatureGenerator` also declares an `EncodingType` that determines both the raw dtype and the masking strategy:

| EncodingType | Input Dtype | Masking Strategy | Used By |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ONE_HOT` | `long/int` | Mask index = `num_classes` (extra class) | `ResidueType`, `RelativeSequenceSeparation`, `RelativeTokenSeparation`, `RelativeEntity`, `RelativeChain` |
| `IDENTITY` | `float` | Extra channel appended; 1 = masked | `AtomRefCharge`, `MSADeletionValue`, `MSAProfile` |
| `RBF` | `float16/32/bf16` | -100.0 sentinel | `BlockedAtomPairDistogram`, `TokenDistanceRestraint` |
| `FOURIER` | `float16/32/bf16` | -100.0 sentinel | `RefPos` |
| `ESM` | `float` | 0.0 (zero vector) | `ESMEmbeddings` |
| `OUTERSUM` | `long/int` | Mask index = `num_classes` | Pairwise one-hot combinations |

The critical insight is that **masking is baked into the feature tensor itself** before it ever reaches the neural network. For `ONE_HOT`-encoded features, masked positions receive an additional class index beyond the valid range; for `IDENTITY`-encoded features, an extra binary channel is concatenated where `1` indicates a masked position. This convention allows the feature embedder to learn how to handle missing data without requiring separate mask tensors per feature.

> [!TIP]
> When adding a new feature generator, the `can_mask` parameter controls whether an extra channel is appended for `IDENTITY`-type features. Setting `can_mask=False` (the default for most pair features) means the generator asserts its data is always present—use this only for structurally guaranteed features like relative positions.

Sources: [base.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L1-L114)

## The Feature Generators: Token-Level Features

Token-level features capture the per-residue identity and context. The most important generators in this domain are:

**ResidueType** — A 32-class one-hot encoding of the residue type (20 standard amino acids + gap + unknown + nucleotide types + special tokens). It reads `token_residue_type` from the batch and produces a `[B, N, 33]` tensor (32 classes + 1 mask class). This is the primary sequence identity signal.

**ESMEmbeddings** — A pass-through of precomputed ESM-2 embeddings with encoding type `ESM`. These 768-dimensional (or 1280-dimensional, depending on the ESM model used) vectors provide a rich, pretrained representation of each residue's biochemical context. The generator simply reads `esm_embeddings` from the batch and returns it as-is.

**MSAProfile** — The marginal distribution over residue types computed from the full (unsubsampled) MSA. This is an `IDENTITY`-encoded feature of dimension `num_res_ty` (typically 32), computed via `scatter_add` over the MSA depth dimension. It provides a coevolutionary summary that complements the raw MSA features fed to the MSA stream.

**MSADeletionMean** — The mean deletion count at each position across the MSA depth, scaled by `2/π · arctan(d/3)`. This is a scalar `IDENTITY`-encoded feature that signals insertion/deletion pressure at each residue.

Sources: [residue_type.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/residue_type.py#L1-L35), [esm_generator.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/esm_generator.py#L1-L35), [msa.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/msa.py#L84-L167)

## The Feature Generators: Pair-Level Features

Pair-level features encode the relational structure between tokens—the spatial, sequential, and organizational relationships that the pair representation must capture.

**RelativeSequenceSeparation** — Binned relative residue index between tokens *i* and *j*, but only within the same chain. For inter-chain pairs, a special bin index is assigned. The default configuration uses 65 bins (offset range ±32), producing a 67-class one-hot (65 + inter-chain + mask). This is the primary within-chain positional signal.

**RelativeTokenSeparation** — Similar to above but operates on absolute token index rather than residue index, and additionally masks out inter-residue and inter-chain positions (setting them to a dedicated class `2*r_max+2`). With `r_max=32`, this yields a 67-class one-hot. The distinction from `RelativeSequenceSeparation` is that token index accounts for multi-token residues (e.g., modified residues with multiple tokens).

**RelativeEntity** — A 3-class one-hot derived from `entity_id`: same entity (class 0), previous entity (class 1), or next entity (class 2). Inspired by AlphaFold-Multimer's Algorithm 5, this feature informs the model whether two tokens belong to the same polypeptide chain, the same ligand entity, or different entities entirely.

**RelativeChain** — A 6-class one-hot (with `s_max=2`) encoding the relative chain ID *within* the same entity. Inter-entity positions are assigned a dedicated class. This captures homo-oligomeric symmetry: chains that are copies of the same entity receive distinct relative-chain labels.

**BlockedAtomPairDistogram** — An RBF-encoded distance histogram between atom pairs in a blocked (sparse) format. This is the primary geometric signal entering the atom-pair stream, providing a coarse-grained representation of 3D proximity between atom blocks.

Sources: [relative_sep.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_sep.py#L1-L63), [relative_token.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_token.py#L1-L54), [relative_entity.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_entity.py#L1-L48), [relative_chain.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_chain.py#L1-L55)

## Stage 1: The Feature Embedder

The feature embedder (`feature_embedding.pt`) is the first learned component in the inference pipeline. It takes the raw feature dictionary produced by the `FeatureFactory` and projects each semantic domain into a unified embedding space. Critically, it processes all domains in a single forward pass:

```python
with _component_moved_to("feature_embedding.pt", device) as feature_embedding:
    embedded_features = feature_embedding.forward(
        crop_size=model_size,
        move_to_device=device,
        return_on_cpu=low_memory,
        **features,
    )
```

The output is a dictionary keyed by `FeatureType` names, each containing an embedded tensor. The inference code then splits specific outputs into **trunk** and **structure** pathways:

```python
token_single_input_feats = embedded_features["TOKEN"]
token_pair_input_feats, token_pair_structure_input_feats = embedded_features[
    "TOKEN_PAIR"
].chunk(2, dim=-1)
atom_single_input_feats, atom_single_structure_input_feats = embedded_features[
    "ATOM"
].chunk(2, dim=-1)
block_atom_pair_input_feats, block_atom_pair_structure_input_feats = (
    embedded_features["ATOM_PAIR"].chunk(2, dim=-1)
)
template_input_feats = embedded_features["TEMPLATES"]
msa_input_feats = embedded_features["MSA"]
```

The `.chunk(2, dim=-1)` pattern is architecturally significant: the feature embedder produces embeddings with **double width** for `TOKEN_PAIR`, `ATOM`, and `ATOM_PAIR` domains. The first half feeds the trunk (iterative refinement), while the second half is held aside for the structure module (diffusion conditioning). This bifurcation ensures that the diffusion module receives geometrically grounded input even before trunk recycling begins.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L636-L663)

## Bond Features: A Separate Projection

Bond features are handled outside the main feature embedder due to TorchScript export limitations. The `TokenBondRestraint` generator produces a raw bond feature tensor, which is then projected by a dedicated `bond_loss_input_proj.pt` module:

```python
bond_ft_gen = TokenBondRestraint()
bond_ft = bond_ft_gen.generate(batch=batch).data
with _component_moved_to("bond_loss_input_proj.pt", device) as bond_loss_input_proj:
    trunk_bond_feat, structure_bond_feat = bond_loss_input_proj.forward(
        return_on_cpu=low_memory,
        move_to_device=device,
        crop_size=model_size,
        input=bond_ft,
    ).chunk(2, dim=-1)
token_pair_input_feats += trunk_bond_feat
token_pair_structure_input_feats += structure_bond_feat
```

The projected bond features are **additively merged** into the token-pair representations for both the trunk and structure pathways. This residual-style integration means the bond signal acts as a bias on the pair representation without disrupting the primary feature embedding.

> [!TIP]
> The additive merge (`+=`) for bond features means that if no covalent bond restraints are provided, `bond_ft` will be all-zeros, and the projection will add a near-zero bias. This graceful degradation ensures the pipeline works identically with or without covalent bond specifications.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L669-L684)

## Stage 2: The Token Input Embedder

The token input embedder (`token_embedder.pt`) is the second learned component. It takes the feature-embedded representations and cross-domain information (atom features aggregated to token level, block atom-pair features) and produces the **initial token representations** that seed the trunk:

```python
with _component_moved_to("token_embedder.pt", device) as token_input_embedder:
    token_input_embedder_outputs = token_input_embedder.forward(
        token_single_input_feats=token_single_input_feats,
        token_pair_input_feats=token_pair_input_feats,
        atom_single_input_feats=atom_single_input_feats,
        block_atom_pair_feat=block_atom_pair_input_feats,
        block_atom_pair_mask=block_atom_pair_mask,
        block_indices_h=block_indices_h,
        block_indices_w=block_indices_w,
        atom_single_mask=atom_single_mask,
        atom_token_indices=atom_token_indices,
        crop_size=model_size,
    )
token_single_initial_repr, token_single_structure_input, token_pair_initial_repr = (
    token_input_embedder_outputs
)
```

This module performs the critical **atom-to-token aggregation**: atom-level single features are pooled to token-level using the `atom_token_indices` mapping, and block atom-pair features are similarly condensed. The output is a triple:

| Output | Shape | Destination |
|---|---|---|
| `token_single_initial_repr` | `[B, N, D_trunk]` | Trunk single representation (seed for recycling) |
| `token_single_structure_input` | `[B, N, D_struct]` | Structure module single input (diffusion conditioning) |
| `token_pair_initial_repr` | `[B, N, N, D_trunk]` | Trunk pair representation (seed for recycling) |

Notice that `token_pair_structure_input_feats` (from the feature embedder) is *not* produced by the token embedder—it flows directly to the structure module. The token embedder thus owns the initial trunk representations and the structure single input, while the structure pair input bypasses it entirely.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L688-L714)

## End-to-End Data Flow

The following diagram summarizes the complete pipeline from raw batch to initial representations:

```mermaid
flowchart TD

```

## Key Architectural Observations

**Dual-pathway design**: The `.chunk(2, dim=-1)` pattern at the feature embedder output creates a hard split between trunk and structure pathways at the *earliest possible stage*. This means the trunk and diffusion module never share a projection layer—only raw feature generators. This design choice likely improves training stability by preventing gradient interference between the iterative refinement trunk and the denoising diffusion module.

**Bond features as additive bias**: By projecting bond features separately and adding them to the token-pair representation, the architecture treats covalent bond information as a *perturbation* on the pair representation rather than a first-class feature. This is consistent with the observation that most proteins don't need covalent bond restraints, and the model must degrade gracefully in their absence.

**MSA bypasses the token embedder**: The embedded MSA and template features flow directly to the trunk module—they are not processed by the token input embedder. This means the token embedder's job is specifically to fuse atom-level geometric information with token-level sequence and pair information, while the trunk handles the MSA/template attention streams independently.

**Feature embedder is JIT-compiled with crop-size dispatch**: The `ModuleWrapper.forward` method selects a different compiled function based on `crop_size`, which means the feature embedder (and token embedder) are compiled separately for each supported model size. This is a performance optimization that avoids dynamic shape overhead at inference time.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L44-L60), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L636-L714)

## What Comes Next

The initial representations produced by the token input embedder—`token_single_initial_repr` and `token_pair_initial_repr`—become the starting point for the trunk's iterative refinement loop. The structure-pathway representations (`token_single_structure_input`, `token_pair_structure_input_feats`, `atom_single_structure_input_feats`, `block_atom_pair_structure_input_feats`) are held constant and later used to condition the diffusion module. To understand how these representations evolve through recycling and attention, proceed to [Trunk Recycling and Attention](10-trunk-recycling-and-attention). For details on the individual feature generators that produce the raw inputs, see [Token and Atom Feature Generators](19-token-and-atom-feature-generators) and [Pairwise and Restraint Feature Generators](20-pairwise-and-restraint-feature-generators).

# Trunk Recycling and Attention



The trunk is the iterative reasoning core of Chai-1's inference pipeline — a module that refines token-level single and pair representations through repeated passes, each enriched by MSA, template, and recycled prior-state information. This page examines the recycling loop mechanics, the blocked local attention pattern that governs atom-pair interactions, and the MSA subsampling strategy that stabilizes later recycles. Understanding this stage is essential because the quality of trunk outputs directly determines the fidelity of the downstream diffusion denoising and confidence prediction.

## Architectural Position of the Trunk

The trunk occupies the central position in Chai-1's three-stage inference pipeline: feature embedding → token embedding → **trunk recycling** → diffusion denoising. It receives four categories of input: (1) initial single and pair token representations from the token embedder, (2) recycled single and pair representations from the previous trunk pass, (3) MSA and template features, and (4) token-level masks. Its outputs — refined `token_single_trunk_repr` and `token_pair_trunk_repr` — are consumed by both the diffusion module and the confidence head.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Pre-Trunk
        FE["Feature Embedding<br/>(feature_embedding.pt)"]
        TE["Token Embedder<br/>(token_embedder.pt)"]
    end

    FE -->|"TOKEN, TOKEN_PAIR,<br/>ATOM, ATOM_PAIR, TEMPLATES, MSA"| TE
    TE -->|"token_single_initial_repr<br/>token_pair_initial_repr<br/>token_single_structure_input"| RECYCLE

    subgraph Recycle_Loop["Trunk Recycling Loop (×num_trunk_recycles)"]
        RECYCLE["Trunk Module<br/>(trunk.pt)"]
        MSA_SUB["MSA Subsampler<br/>(optional, per-recycle)"]
        MSA_SUB -->|"subsampled MSA<br/>feats + mask"| RECYCLE
    end

    TE -->|"token_single_initial_repr<br/>token_pair_initial_repr"| RECYCLE
    RECYCLE -->|"token_single_trunk_repr<br/>token_pair_trunk_repr"| RECYCLE
    RECYCLE -->|"refined single & pair repr"| DIFF["Diffusion Module"]
    RECYCLE -->|"refined single & pair repr"| CONF["Confidence Head"]

    style RECYCLE fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff,stroke:#2c5f8a
    style MSA_SUB fill:#6ab0f3,color:#fff,stroke:#4a90d9
```

The initial representations serve as a fixed reference across all recycles, while the recycled representations evolve with each iteration. This dual-input design — constant anchor plus mutable state — prevents representation drift while allowing iterative refinement.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L708-L746), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L689-L706)

## The Recycling Loop

The recycling loop is the trunk's defining mechanism. On each iteration, the trunk module receives both the **initial** representations (immutable across recycles) and the **current** recycled representations (output of the previous pass). The loop executes `num_trunk_recycles` times (default: 3), and the recycled representations are initialized to the initial representations before the first iteration.

The core loop is straightforward in structure but critical in effect:

```python
token_single_trunk_repr = token_single_initial_repr
token_pair_trunk_repr = token_pair_initial_repr
for _ in range(num_trunk_recycles):
    # Optional: subsample MSA for this recycle
    subsampled_msa_input_feats, subsampled_msa_mask = None, None
    if recycle_msa_subsample > 0:
        subsampled_msa_input_feats, subsampled_msa_mask = (
            subsample_and_reorder_msa_feats_n_mask(msa_input_feats, msa_mask)
        )
    # Run trunk with both initial and recycled representations
    (token_single_trunk_repr, token_pair_trunk_repr) = trunk.forward(
        token_single_trunk_initial_repr=token_single_initial_repr,
        token_pair_trunk_initial_repr=token_pair_initial_repr,
        token_single_trunk_repr=token_single_trunk_repr,  # recycled
        token_pair_trunk_repr=token_pair_trunk_repr,  # recycled
        msa_input_feats=...,
        msa_mask=...,
        template_input_feats=template_input_feats,
        template_input_masks=template_input_masks,
        ...
    )
```

> [!TIP]
> The trunk's dual-input convention — separate `initial` and `recycled` representation arguments — is architecturally significant. The initial representations anchor the model to its first-pass understanding, preventing runaway drift across recycles. The recycled representations carry cumulative refinements. When debugging trunk behavior, inspect both streams independently: if the recycled stream diverges significantly from the initial stream after early recycles, it may indicate unstable attention patterns or excessive MSA noise.

| Parameter | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `num_trunk_recycles` | 3 | Number of iterative trunk passes; more recycles improve quality at linear compute cost |
| `num_trunk_samples` | 1 | Number of independent trunk samples (each with full recycle loop); multiple samples capture stochastic variation |
| `recycle_msa_subsample` | 0 | When > 0, stochastically subsample MSA rows to this depth per recycle; 0 disables subsampling |

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L708-L746), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L478-L484)

## Blocked Local Attention for Atom Pairs

Chai-1 employs a **blocked local attention** pattern for atom-pair interactions, avoiding the quadratic cost of full atom-pair attention. The mechanism is governed by two structural parameters: `num_key_atoms=128` (KV block size) and `num_query_atoms=32` (query stride), configured during collation.

### Block Index Computation

The function `get_qkv_indices_for_blocks` partitions the atom sequence into non-overlapping query blocks of size `stride` (32), each attending to a centered local KV block of size `kv_block_size` (128). For a query block starting at position `q_start`, the KV block spans from `q_start + (stride - kv_block_size) // 2` to `q_start + (stride - kv_block_size) // 2 + kv_block_size`. Given stride=32 and kv_block_size=128, this offset is `(32 - 128) // 2 = -48`, meaning each query block's KV context extends 48 positions before and 80 positions after the query block's start — a heavily backward-biased local window that prioritizes upstream structural context.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Sequence["Atom Sequence"]
        direction LR
        Q1["Q Block 1"]
        Q2["Q Block 2"]
        Q3["Q Block 3"]
        QN["..."]
    end

    subgraph KV_Context["KV Context Windows (centered, overlapping)"]
        KV1["KV1: positions -48..+80 relative to Q1"]
        KV2["KV2: positions -48..+80 relative to Q2"]
        KV3["KV3: positions -48..+80 relative to Q3"]
    end

    Q1 --> KV1
    Q2 --> KV2
    Q3 --> KV3
```

### Boundary Handling

When the centered KV block extends beyond sequence boundaries (near the start or end of the atom sequence), the implementation uses modular wrapping (`kv_indices % sequence_length`) combined with a **wrapping mask** that nullifies out-of-bounds positions. This ensures that (a) index computation never fails, and (b) attention weights never attend to wrapped-around atoms, preserving the local attention semantics.

```python
# Mask out positions where kv_indices gets wrapped
kv_mask = (kv_indices < sequence_length) & (kv_indices >= 0)
kv_indices = kv_indices % sequence_length  # Safe indexing, masked later
```

The block atom-pair mask is then computed as the logical AND of the query-side atom mask, the KV-side atom mask, and the wrapping validity mask, producing a `Bool[Tensor, "b bl bl_q bl_kv"]` tensor that gates attention computation.

> [!TIP]
> The 128/32 KV/Q ratio means each query atom attends to 128 local key atoms with 4:1 compression. This is not merely a memory optimization — the local window encodes an inductive bias that structural interactions are spatially local at the atom level, which is consistent with the physics of interatomic forces. When adapting the model to unusually long-range interaction scenarios, consider that the 128-atom KV window covers roughly 5–6 residues of backbone context.

Sources: [utils.py](/chai_lab/model/utils.py#L14-L57), [collate.py](/chai_lab/data/collate/collate.py#L64-L85)

## MSA Subsampling During Recycling

When `recycle_msa_subsample > 0`, each trunk recycle applies stochastic MSA row subsampling. This serves two purposes: (1) it reduces memory and compute for deep MSAs, and (2) it introduces controlled stochasticity that can improve generalization across recycles by presenting different evolutionary information at each pass.

### Subsampling Algorithm

The subsampling function `_subsample_msa_rows` selects `select_n_rows` rows from the MSA using a **size-biased random scoring** strategy. Each MSA row receives a score equal to its non-padding residue count multiplied by a random weight, and the top-scoring rows are selected. This biases selection toward larger, more informative MSA hits while maintaining stochastic diversity.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    INPUT["MSA mask<br/>(1, depth, tokens)"]
    SCORE["Score = row_coverage × random_weight<br/>(biased toward larger hits)"]
    SORT["Sort scores ascending,<br/>select last N rows"]
    REORDER["Move selected rows to top,<br/>pad remaining depth with zeros"]
    OUTPUT["Subsampled MSA features + mask"]

    INPUT --> SCORE --> SORT --> REORDER --> OUTPUT
```

After selection, the MSA features are reordered so selected rows appear first, while the mask is truncated and zero-padded to maintain the original depth dimension. A critical invariant: every selected row must have nonzero coverage — empty rows are never sampled.

| Aspect | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Selection bias | Larger MSA hits (more non-padding residues) are preferentially selected |
| Ordering | Selected rows maintain their original relative order |
| Padding | Mask is zero-padded to original depth; features retain full depth with unselected rows shifted to the end |
| Default depth | `select_n_rows = 4096` when enabled |
| Inactive when | Input MSA depth ≤ `select_n_rows`, or `recycle_msa_subsample = 0` |

Sources: [utils.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/msas/utils.py#L11-L87), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L714-L722)

## Model Size Gating and Static Graph Export

The trunk (along with all other exported modules) is compiled as a **TorchScript static graph** for specific token counts. The available model sizes are `[256, 384, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048]`, and inputs are padded to the nearest size during collation. The trunk's forward method is dispatched via `forward_{crop_size}`, meaning each model size has its own compiled graph.

This design has a direct consequence for the trunk's attention patterns: the blocked local attention indices are pre-computed during collation (not inside the trunk itself), and the specific block structure depends on the padded sequence length. The `get_qkv_indices_for_blocks` function requires that the sequence length be exactly divisible by the query stride (32), which is guaranteed by the padding strategy.

| Model Size | Max Tokens | Max Atoms (23×tokens) |
|---|---|---|
| 256 | 256 | 5,888 |
| 384 | 384 | 8,832 |
| 512 | 512 | 11,776 |
| 768 | 768 | 17,664 |
| 1024 | 1,024 | 23,552 |
| 1536 | 1,536 | 35,328 |
| 2048 | 2,048 | 47,104 |

Sources: [utils.py](/chai_lab/data/collate/utils.py#L11-L40), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L678-L685)

## Device Management and Memory Strategy

The trunk module uses the `_component_moved_to` context manager for transient device placement. Within each recycle iteration, the trunk module is moved to the compute device (typically CUDA), the forward pass executes, and then the module is moved back to CPU. This pattern is critical for the `low_memory=True` inference mode, where only one model component resides on GPU at any time.

The recycling loop itself operates on CPU-resident representations when `low_memory=True` — the `move_to_device` parameter inside `trunk.forward()` handles the transient GPU transfer of input tensors, and `return_on_cpu` ensures outputs come back to CPU. After all recycles complete, `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` is called explicitly to release fragmented GPU memory before the diffusion stage begins.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L60-L78), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L748-L749)

## Data Flow Summary

The following table traces the complete tensor lifecycle through the trunk recycling stage, from token embedder output to diffusion module input:

| Tensor | Shape Pattern | Origin | Destination |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_single_initial_repr` | `(1, n_tokens, d_single)` | Token embedder | Trunk (constant across recycles) + Diffusion + Confidence |
| `token_pair_initial_repr` | `(1, n_tokens, n_tokens, d_pair)` | Token embedder | Trunk (constant across recycles) |
| `token_single_trunk_repr` | `(1, n_tokens, d_single)` | Initialized from initial, updated each recycle | Trunk (recycled) → Diffusion + Confidence |
| `token_pair_trunk_repr` | `(1, n_tokens, n_tokens, d_pair)` | Initialized from initial, updated each recycle | Trunk (recycled) → Diffusion + Confidence |
| `msa_input_feats` | `(1, depth, n_tokens, d_msa)` | Feature embedding | Trunk (optionally subsampled per recycle) |
| `template_input_feats` | `(1, n_templates, n_tokens, d_template)` | Feature embedding | Trunk (constant across recycles) |
| `block_atom_pair_mask` | `(1, n_blocks, 32, 128)` | Collation | Trunk (pre-computed, constant) |

After the recycling loop concludes, the trunk's output representations are split into two streams: the `token_single_trunk_repr` and `token_pair_trunk_repr` flow into the diffusion module alongside the structure-specific input projections (`token_single_structure_input`, `token_pair_structure_input_feats`), while the same trunk representations also feed the confidence head. This bifurcation means the trunk must produce representations that serve both coordinate generation and quality estimation — a dual objective that recycling helps to satisfy.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L689-L746), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L752-L775)

## What Comes Next

With the trunk's refined representations in hand, the pipeline proceeds to stochastic structure generation. The [Diffusion Denoising Process](11-diffusion-denoising-process) page details how these representations guide the iterative denoising of atom coordinates from Gaussian noise. For the memory implications of running multiple trunk samples and diffusion steps, see [Memory Management and Device Strategy](24-memory-management-and-device-strategy). The noise schedule governing the diffusion process is covered in [Diffusion Noise Schedule](25-diffusion-noise-schedule).

# Diffusion Denoising Process



The diffusion denoising process is the generative core of Chai-1: it transforms pure noise into physically plausible all-atom 3D coordinates. Unlike autoregressive or VAE-based structure generation, Chai-1 adopts a **score-based diffusion framework** rooted in the Elucidating the Design Space (EDM) methodology of Karras et al., implementing a stochastic sampler with optional second-order correction. The process takes the trunk's learned representations—token-level single and pair features—and iteratively refines a noisy atom coordinate field across hundreds of timestep steps, ultimately producing multiple independent structure samples ranked by a downstream confidence head.

## Architecture Context: Where Diffusion Fits

The diffusion module sits at the terminal position of the inference pipeline, consuming the fused output of the trunk recycles. Before a single denoising step executes, the model has already assembled features, embedded tokens, and recycled the trunk representations. The diffusion module is the **only stage that directly produces atom coordinates**, making it the singular generative bottleneck in the entire architecture.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Upstream["Upstream Pipeline (Pre-Diffusion)"]
        A[Feature Context Assembly] --> B[Feature Embedding]
        B --> C[Token Input Embedder]
        C --> D[Trunk Recycles x N]
    end
    
    subgraph Diffusion["Diffusion Denoising Process"]
        D --> E["Static Diffusion Inputs<br/>token_single/pair reprs<br/>atom_single/pair feats"]
        E --> F["Noise Schedule<br/>σ₀ → σₙ"]
        F --> G["Initial Atom Positions<br/>σ₀ · 𝒩(0, I)"]
        G --> H{"Denoising Loop<br/>t = 0..T-1"}
        H --> I[Center + Random Augmentation]
        I --> J["Stochastic Noise Injection<br/>σ̂ = σ(1 + γ)"]
        J --> K["First Denoise Call<br/>dᵢ = (x̂ - D(x̂,σ̂)) / σ̂"]
        K --> L["Euler Step<br/>x ← x̂ + (σₙₑₓₜ - σ̂) · dᵢ"]
        L --> M{"Second Order?"}
        M -->|Yes| N["Second Denoise Call<br/>dᵢ' = (x - D(x,σₙₑₓₜ)) / σₙₑₓₜ"]
        N --> O["Corrected Step<br/>x ← x + (σₙₑₓₜ - σ̂)(dᵢ'+dᵢ)/2"]
        M -->|No| P[Next Step]
        O --> P
        %% 在子图内部完成循环闭环，避免跨图连线破坏子图内部逻辑
        P --> H
    end
    
    subgraph Downstream["Downstream Pipeline (Post-Diffusion)"]
        %% 建立子图内部独立节点接收外部输入
        Q_in["Final σ → 0"] --> Q["Denoised Atom Positions"]
        Q --> R["Confidence Head<br/>pAE / pDE / pLDDT"]
        R --> S[Ranking & CIF Output]
    end

    %% 跨子图连接：从 Diffusion 的 P 指向 Downstream 的 Q_in
    P --> Q_in

    style Diffusion fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#e94560,stroke-width:2px,color:#eee
    style Upstream fill:#16213e,stroke:#0f3460,color:#eee
    style Downstream fill:#16213e,stroke:#0f3460,color:#eee
```

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L782-L888), [diffusion_schedules.py](chai_lab/model/diffusion_schedules.py#L1-L49)

## Static Diffusion Inputs: The Condition Field

Before the iterative denoising loop begins, Chai-1 assembles a **frozen condition dictionary** called `static_diffusion_inputs`. This dictionary remains constant across all denoising timesteps and all diffusion samples—it is the structural context the denoiser conditions on. The inputs bifurcate along two axes: **structure-specific pathways** (used exclusively by the diffusion module) and **shared representations** (originating from the trunk's recycled output).

| Input Key | Source | Shape Pattern | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_single_initial_repr` | Token embedder (structure split) | `(1, N_tokens, D)` | Per-token identity prior before trunk |
| `token_pair_initial_repr` | Feature embedder (structure split) | `(1, N_tokens, N_tokens, D)` | Pairwise geometric prior |
| `token_single_trunk_repr` | Trunk output (after recycles) | `(1, N_tokens, D)` | Refined single representation |
| `token_pair_trunk_repr` | Trunk output (after recycles) | `(1, N_tokens, N_tokens, D)` | Refined pair representation |
| `atom_single_input_feats` | Feature embedder (structure split) | `(1, N_atoms, D)` | Per-atom conditioning features |
| `atom_block_pair_input_feats` | Feature embedder (structure split) | `(1, N_blocks, N_q, N_kv, D)` | Local block atom-pair features |
| `atom_single_mask` | Input collation | `(1, N_atoms)` | Valid atom mask |
| `atom_block_pair_mask` | Block pair computation | `(1, N_blocks, N_q, N_kv)` | Valid block-pair mask |
| `token_single_mask` | Input collation | `(1, N_tokens)` | Valid token mask |
| `block_indices_h/w` | Block index computation | `(N_blocks, N_q/kv)` | Attention block indices |
| `atom_token_indices` | Input collation | `(1, N_atoms)` | Atom-to-token mapping |

A critical architectural detail: the feature embedding output is **split in half** along the channel dimension. One half feeds the trunk pathway (`token_pair_input_feats`, `atom_single_input_feats`); the other half feeds the structure/diffusion pathway (`token_pair_structure_input_feats`, `atom_single_structure_input_feats`). This partition ensures the diffusion module receives a dedicated feature channel that the trunk does not overwrite during recycling, preserving a clean information pathway from raw features to coordinate generation.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L688-L716), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L788-L804)

## Noise Schedule: Power-Law Sigma Trajectory

The denoising trajectory is governed by a **sigma schedule**—a monotonically decreasing sequence of noise levels that the sampler traverses from high noise (pure chaos) to near-zero noise (clean structure). Chai-1 implements this via `InferenceNoiseSchedule`, which produces sigma values through a **power-law interpolation** between `s_max` and `s_min`.

The interpolation formula is:

```
σ(t) = σ_data · [ t · s_min^(1/p) + (1-t) · s_max^(1/p) ]^p
```

where `t ∈ [0, 1]` is the normalized timestep, `p = 7.0` controls the curvature, and `σ_data = 16.0` is the data standard deviation. The schedule distributes timesteps using **midpoint spacing** (`linspace(0, 1, 2N+1)[1::2]`) rather than uniform endpoint spacing, which avoids placing a timestep exactly at t=0 or t=1 where the noise level is degenerate.

| Parameter | Default Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `s_max` | 80.0 (from `DiffusionConfig.S_tmax`) | Starting noise level (maximum σ) |
| `s_min` | 4e-4 | Terminal noise level (minimum σ) |
| `p` | 7.0 | Power-law exponent; higher values concentrate steps at high-noise regime |
| `sigma_data` | 16.0 | Data standard deviation; scales the entire σ range |
| `num_timesteps` | 200 | Number of denoising steps |

The high exponent `p = 7.0` creates a schedule that spends more steps in the high-noise regime where coarse structure is determined, and fewer steps in the low-noise regime where fine details are refined. This is deliberate: early coarse-grained decisions (overall fold, chain arrangement) are more consequential than late fine-grained adjustments (side-chain rotamers).

Sources: [diffusion_schedules.py](chai_lab/model/diffusion_schedules.py#L13-L48), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L821-L829)

## DiffusionConfig: Stochastic Sampler Hyperparameters

The `DiffusionConfig` dataclass controls the stochastic sampling behavior. These parameters directly correspond to Algorithm 2 from Karras et al.'s EDM paper:

| Parameter | Value | EDM Algorithm Role | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `S_churn` | 80 | Stochasticity budget | Total amount of noise injection across all steps |
| `S_tmin` | 4e-4 | Lower σ bound for churn | Below this σ, no stochastic noise is added |
| `S_tmax` | 80.0 | Upper σ bound for churn | Above this σ, no stochastic noise is added |
| `S_noise` | 1.003 | Noise inflation factor | Multiplier on the injected noise std |
| `sigma_data` | 16.0 | Data std | Matches `InferenceNoiseSchedule.sigma_data` |
| `second_order` | True | Enable 2nd-order correction | Uses a second denoiser call for Heun's correction |

> [!TIP]
> The `S_churn = 80` value is notably high, enabling substantial stochastic exploration during sampling. The per-step gamma is capped at `√2 - 1 ≈ 0.414` to prevent instability, and distributed as `min(S_churn / num_timesteps, √2 - 1)`. With 200 timesteps, this yields `γ = min(0.4, 0.414) = 0.4`, meaning the effective noise is increased by 40% at each step before denoising—a significant perturbation that promotes sample diversity.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L242-L248)

## The Denoising Loop: Step-by-Step Decomposition

The core denoising loop implements a modified Euler-Maruyama sampler with Heun's second-order correction. Below is the precise algorithmic trace, mapping each code block to its mathematical operation.

### Initialization

The process begins by drawing atom positions from a **pure Gaussian** scaled by the maximum sigma:

```
x₀ = σ₀ · 𝒩(0, I)   where σ₀ = σ(t=0) ≈ s_max · σ_data
```

This produces coordinates of magnitude `σ₀ ≈ 80 × 16 = 1280 Å` from the origin—effectively unstructured noise. The shape is `(batch_size × num_diffn_samples, num_atoms, 3)`, where multiple samples share the same conditioning but differ in their random initialization.

### Gamma Schedule

For each pair of consecutive sigmas `(σ_curr, σ_next)`, a **churn parameter** γ is computed:

```
γ = min(S_churn / num_timesteps, √2 - 1)   if S_tmin ≤ σ_curr ≤ S_tmax
γ = 0                                       otherwise
```

This γ controls the amount of **stochastic perturbation** added before the denoiser step, enabling exploration of the solution space.

### Per-Step Algorithm

Each denoising step follows this sequence:

**Step 1 — Centering & Random Augmentation.** The atom coordinates are mean-centered and then randomly rotated and translated via `center_random_augmentation`. This is critical because the diffusion model is trained with SE(3)-equivariance; centering removes translational drift while random rotations prevent the model from overfitting to canonical orientations. The translation scale `s_trans = 1.0` adds only a 1 Å perturbation—small enough not to disrupt the structure but sufficient to break rotational symmetry artifacts.

**Step 2 — Stochastic Noise Injection (EDM Algorithm 2, Lines 4–6).** When γ > 0, the current position is perturbed:

```
σ̂ = σ_curr · (1 + γ)
x̂ = x + S_noise · 𝒩(0, I) · √(σ̂² - σ_curr²)
```

This inflates the noise level from `σ_curr` to `σ̂` and adds noise consistent with that inflation. When `γ = 0` (outside the churn range), `σ̂ = σ_curr` and no noise is added, reducing the sampler to a deterministic ODE solver.

**Step 3 — First Denoiser Call & Euler Step (Lines 7–8).** The denoiser network `D(x̂, σ̂)` predicts the clean signal, and the score-like direction is computed:

```
d_i = (x̂ - D(x̂, σ̂)) / σ̂
x ← x̂ + (σ_next - σ̂) · d_i
```

This is the standard Euler step: move from `σ̂` to `σ_next` along the direction that points from the noisy observation toward the denoised estimate, scaled by the noise difference.

**Step 4 — Second-Order Correction (Lines 9–11).** When `second_order = True` and `σ_next ≠ 0`, a **Heun correction** is applied:

```
d_i' = (x - D(x, σ_next)) / σ_next
x ← x + (σ_next - σ̂) · (d_i' + d_i) / 2
```

Instead of using only the gradient at the current point, the second denoiser call evaluates the gradient at the *projected* next point, then averages the two gradients. This trapezoidal rule correction dramatically reduces discretization error at the cost of a second forward pass through the diffusion module.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Step["Single Denoising Step"]
        direction TB
        A["x at σ_curr"] --> B["Center + Random Aug"]
        B --> C["Stochastic Injection<br/>x̂ at σ̂ = σ(1+γ)"]
        C --> D["Denoise #1<br/>D(x̂, σ̂)"]
        D --> E["Euler Step<br/>x₁ = x̂ + (σ_next - σ̂)·dᵢ"]
        E --> F{2nd Order<br/>& σ_next ≠ 0?}
        F -->|Yes| G["Denoise #2<br/>D(x₁, σ_next)"]
        G --> H["Heun Correction<br/>x₂ = x₁ + (σ_next - σ̂)·(dᵢ'+dᵢ)/2"]
        F -->|No| I["x at σ_next"]
        H --> I
    end
```

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L838-L885), [model/utils.py](chai_lab/model/utils.py#L178-L194)

## The Denoiser Interface: _denoise Function

The `_denoise` function serves as the bridge between the iterative sampling algorithm and the exported TorchScript diffusion module. Its signature is:

```python
def _denoise(diff_mod, atom_pos, sigma, ds) -> Tensor
```
