Sources: [all_atom_feature_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/all_atom_feature_context.py#L20-L95), [predict_with_templates.py](examples/templates/predict_with_templates.py#L23-L30), [context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/templates/context.py#L36-L38)

## Template Context Tensor Summary

The `TemplateContext` dataclass holds five frozen tensors that collectively encode structural templates:

| Field | Type | Shape | Default (empty) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `template_restype` | `Int32` | `(T, N)` | Gap token `"-"` | Residue identity at each template position |
| `template_pseudo_beta_mask` | `Bool` | `(T, N)` | `False` | Whether Cβ (or Cα for Gly) coordinates exist |
| `template_backbone_frame_mask` | `Bool` | `(T, N)` | `False` | Whether all N-Cα-C backbone atoms exist for frame computation |
| `template_distances` | `Float32` | `(T, N, N)` | `0.0` | Pseudo-beta pairwise distances; 100.0 for masked pairs |
| `template_unit_vector` | `Float32` | `(T, N, N, 3)` | `0.0` | Rotation-invariant relative position vectors between backbone frames |

Where `T` = number of templates (up to 4), `N` = number of tokens. The `template_mask` property (`template_restype != gap_token`) provides a convenient boolean for determining which template positions carry actual structural information versus padding.

Sources: [context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/templates/context.py#L41-L107)

## Key Design Decisions

**Template scope is protein-only.** The `_get_entity_data()` function explicitly filters for `EntityType.PROTEIN`, and `get_template_context()` only attempts template loading for protein chains. This is because the m8 hit format and the backbone frame / unit vector computations assume polymer backbone geometry.

**Realignment via kalign supersedes m8 coordinates.** Rather than trusting the m8 file's alignment boundaries, the pipeline re-aligns the query against the template subregion using kalign. This ensures correctness when the m8 alignment boundaries don't perfectly correspond to gemmi's residue numbering, at the cost of an additional alignment computation per hit.

**Modified residues are rejected.** Template structures containing modified residues (PTMs, non-standard amino acids) are dropped because per-atom tokenization creates a token count mismatch with the per-residue query sequence. This is a deliberate trade-off: structural coverage is sacrificed to maintain index alignment integrity.

**Distogram masking uses large sentinel values.** Rather than storing a separate mask for the distance matrix, masked positions are filled with 100.0Å, which is guaranteed to exceed the maximum distogram bin edge (50.75Å) and thus land in the "everything too far" bin during `torch.searchsorted`. This avoids an extra mask tensor but couples the masking logic to the binning parameters.

Sources: [load.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/templates/load.py#L234-L258), [load.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/templates/load.py#L324-L330), [m8.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/templates/m8.py#L97-L101), [templates.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/templates.py#L147-L166)

## Next Steps

The template features produced by this pipeline are consumed alongside MSA and pairwise features in the trunk's attention layers. To understand how these template features are integrated into the model's attention mechanism, see [Trunk Recycling and Attention](10-trunk-recycling-and-attention). For the broader context of how template features are generated alongside other feature types, see [Pairwise and Restraint Feature Generators](20-pairwise-and-restraint-feature-generators). For the upstream input that triggers template discovery, see [Feature Context Assembly](8-feature-context-assembly).

# Restraint and Covalent Bond System



The Chai-1 restraint and covalent bond system provides a unified CSV-based interface for encoding three distinct types of prior structural knowledge into the model's feature space: **contact** restraints (residue–residue proximity), **pocket** restraints (residue–chain proximity), and **covalent** bonds (inter-entity chemical linkages). Each type follows a different path through parsing, context assembly, and feature generation, ultimately producing distinct TOKEN_PAIR features that bias the diffusion denoising process toward structurally consistent outputs. Understanding this system is essential for guiding predictions when experimental evidence or domain knowledge about intermolecular contacts is available.

Sources: [restraints.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/restraints.py#L1-L205), [restraint_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py#L1-L137)

## Architecture Overview

The restraint system operates as a three-stage pipeline: **parsing** (CSV → typed interaction objects), **context assembly** (interaction objects → typed restraint groups), and **feature generation** (restraint groups → token-pair tensors). Covalent bonds diverge after parsing — they bypass the `RestraintContext` entirely and instead feed into atom-level bond indices that are resolved to token-pair features by `TokenBondRestraint`. Contact and pocket restraints share the `RestraintContext` pathway but produce asymmetric, structurally distinct feature matrices.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Input
        CSV[".restraints CSV file"]
        FASTA["FASTA entities"]
    end

    subgraph Parsing
        PARSE["parse_pairwise_table()"]
        PI["PairwiseInteraction"]
    end

    subgraph ContextAssembly
        RC["RestraintContext"]
        CR["ContactRestraint"]
        PR["PocketRestraint"]
        BOND["atom_covalent_bond_indices"]
    end

    subgraph FeatureGeneration
        TDR["TokenDistanceRestraint<br/>RBF encoding"]
        TPR["TokenPairPocketRestraint<br/>RBF encoding"]
        TBR["TokenBondRestraint<br/>Binary identity"]
    end

    CSV --> PARSE --> PI
    FASTA --> PARSE
    PI -->|"CONTACT"| CR --> RC
    PI -->|"POCKET"| PR --> RC
    PI -->|"COVALENT"| BOND
    RC --> TDR
    RC --> TPR
    BOND --> TBR
    TDR --> TP["TOKEN_PAIR features"]
    TPR --> TP
    TBR --> TP
```

> [!TIP]
> Covalent bonds are intentionally excluded from `RestraintContext` — the `load_manual_restraints_for_chai1` function explicitly passes through `COVALENT` interactions with a no-op comment "Covalent bonds are handled elsewhere, not as a constraint." This means covalent bonds follow a completely separate data path through `bond_utils.get_atom_covalent_bond_pairs_from_constraints` rather than the restraint context pipeline.

Sources: [restraints.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/restraints.py#L1-L205), [restraint_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py#L89-L110), [token_bond.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_bond.py#L1-L64), [token_dist_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_dist_restraint.py#L1-L273), [token_pair_pocket_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_pair_pocket_restraint.py#L1-L248)

## Restraint File Format

All restraints are specified as CSV files (conventionally with a `.restraints` extension) validated against a strict `PairwiseConstraintDataframeModel` schema via Pandera. Each row defines a single pairwise interaction with the following columns:

| Column | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `restraint_id` | `str` | Yes (unique) | Unique identifier for the restraint |
| `chainA` | `str` | Yes | Subchain ID of partner A |
| `res_idxA` | `str` | Conditional | Residue identifier for A (format: `{name}{pos}`), empty for chain-level |
| `chainB` | `str` | Yes | Subchain ID of partner B |
| `res_idxB` | `str` | Conditional | Residue identifier for B, empty for chain-level |
| `connection_type` | `str` | Yes | One of: `covalent`, `contact`, `pocket` |
| `confidence` | `float` | No (default 1.0) | Confidence score in [0.0, 1.0] |
| `min_distance_angstrom` | `float` | No (≥0) | Minimum distance in Ångströms |
| `max_distance_angstrom` | `float` | No (≥0) | Maximum distance in Ångströms |
| `comment` | `str` | No | Free-text annotation |

The `res_idx` columns use a compound format: `{residue_name}{position}[@{atom_name}]`. For example, `C387` denotes residue Cysteine at 1-indexed position 387; `N437@N` denotes the backbone nitrogen atom of Asparagine at position 437; `@C1` denotes the C1 atom of a non-polymer entity (empty residue name). The parsing function `_parse_res_idx` splits on the `@` delimiter to separate residue identifiers from atom specifiers.

Sources: [restraints.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/restraints.py#L22-L47), [restraints.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/restraints.py#L130-L165)

## Interaction Type Semantics

Each `connection_type` carries distinct structural semantics and validation rules enforced in `PairwiseInteraction.__post_init__`:

**Contact** (`contact`) — Specifies that two specific residues should be within a distance threshold. Both `res_idxA` and `res_idxB` (or their atom names) must be provided. The feature is encoded as a distance threshold in the token-pair matrix and is **asymmetric** (set only at `[left, right]`, not `[right, left]`). Example: `A,C387 ↔ B,Y101` means Cys387 on chain A should be near Tyr101 on chain B.

**Pocket** (`pocket`) — Specifies that a specific residue on one chain should be near all residues of another chain. Partner A is **chain-level** (no `res_idxA`), partner B is **token-level** (must specify `res_idxB`). Atoms must not be specified. The feature matrix sets constraints between the single pocket token and every token in the pocket chain. Example: `B,(chain) ↔ A,C387` means all of chain B should be near Cys387 on chain A.

**Covalent** (`covalent`) — Specifies a covalent chemical bond between atoms of two entities. Both partners should specify atom names via the `@` syntax. Distance bounds are typically set to `0.0` (exact bonding distance). Example: `A,C217@SG ↔ B,@S1` means the sulfur atom of Cys217 on chain A is covalently bonded to atom S1 on chain B.

| Property | Contact | Pocket | Covalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Partner A specificity | Token/Atom | Chain-level | Atom |
| Partner B specificity | Token/Atom | Token-level | Atom |
| Distance encoding | Threshold → RBF | Threshold → RBF | Binary (bond exists) |
| Feature symmetry | Asymmetric | Asymmetric | Symmetric (via `und_self`) |
| Feature generator | `TokenDistanceRestraint` | `TokenPairPocketRestraint` | `TokenBondRestraint` |
| Data pathway | `RestraintContext` | `RestraintContext` | `atom_covalent_bond_indices` |

Sources: [restraints.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/restraints.py#L50-L128), [restraint_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py#L89-L110)

## Parsing and Validation Pipeline

The entry point `parse_pairwise_table` reads a CSV file, validates it against `PairwiseConstraintDataframeModel`, fills missing confidence values with 1.0, and converts each row to a `PairwiseInteraction` instance. The Pandera schema enforces: unique `restraint_id`, non-null chain IDs, `connection_type` must be one of the three enum values, `confidence` in [0, 1], and distance bounds ≥ 0. The `_parse_row` helper further decomposes `res_idx` fields into separate residue identifiers and atom names using `_parse_res_idx`.

The 1-based residue indexing is a critical design choice: `res_idxA_pos` extracts the numeric portion after the first character (the residue single-letter name), returning 1 as default when no position is given. This 1-based index is later converted to 0-based in `load_manual_restraints_for_chai1` via `constraint.res_idxA_pos - 1`.

Sources: [restraints.py](chai_lab/data/parsing/restraints.py#L130-L205), [restraint_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py#L100-L106)

## Context Assembly: From Interactions to Restraint Groups

The `load_manual_restraints_for_chai1` function bridges parsed `PairwiseInteraction` objects to feature-generator-specific `RestraintGroup` dataclasses. It performs three key transformations: (1) **index conversion** from 1-based to 0-based residue indexing, (2) **residue name expansion** from single-letter to three-letter codes using `restype_1to3_with_x`, and (3) **structural decomposition** — contact restraints become `ContactRestraint` groups with explicit left/right token positions, while pocket restraints become `PocketRestraint` groups with distinct chain-level and token-level fields. Covalent interactions are explicitly skipped with the comment "handled elsewhere."

> [!TIP]
> The subchain ID scheme used in restraint files must match the `entity_name_as_subchain` parameter passed to `load_chains_from_raw`. If restraints reference chain IDs by entity name (e.g., `G`, `H`) but `entity_name_as_subchain=False` (which assigns `A`, `B`), the restraint will fail to resolve and all features will be null. The test suite explicitly validates this compatibility matrix.

Sources: [restraint_context.py](chai_lab/data/dataset/constraints/restraint_context.py#L82-L137), [test_restraints.py](tests/test_restraints.py#L45-L126)

## Feature Generation: Contact Restraints

`TokenDistanceRestraint` produces a `TOKEN_PAIR` feature encoded via RBF (Radial Basis Function) with 6 radii. When user-provided `ContactRestraint` groups are available, `generate_from_restraint` resolves each group to a specific token pair by matching `asym_id`, `residue_index`, and `residue_name` (with assertion-enforced uniqueness). The distance threshold is written into the constraint matrix at position `[left_token, right_token]`, then passed through `make_feature` which applies RBF encoding. Without user constraints, the matrix is filled with `ignore_idx = -1.0`.

The generator is registered in the feature factory with `include_probability=1.0`, `size=0.33` (geometric distribution for training-time sampling), `min_dist=6.0`, `max_dist=30.0`, and `num_rbf_radii=6`. The `add_distance_restraint` method enforces that each restraint resolves to exactly one left and one right token — if multiple tokens match, or residue names disagree with the parsed input, an assertion fails.

Sources: [token_dist_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_dist_restraint.py#L42-L273), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L223-L230)

## Feature Generation: Pocket Restraints

`TokenPairPocketRestraint` internally delegates to `TokenDistanceRestraint` for sampling logic but produces a structurally different feature: it sets constraints between a **single pocket token** and **all tokens** in the pocket chain. The `add_pocket_restraint` method first identifies the pocket token (asserting uniqueness), then broadcasts the distance threshold across `restraint_mat[pocket_token_mask, pocket_chain_asym_mask]`. This means a single pocket restraint row in the CSV generates `N` non-null feature entries where `N` is the number of tokens in the pocket chain.

The generator is registered with `size=0.33`, `include_probability=1.0`, `min_dist=6.0`, `max_dist=20.0`, and `num_rbf_radii=6`. Like contact restraints, the feature is asymmetric — constraints flow from the pocket token *to* the pocket chain tokens, not the reverse.

Sources: [token_pair_pocket_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_pair_pocket_restraint.py#L46-L248), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L231-L238)

## Feature Generation: Covalent Bonds

`TokenBondRestraint` takes a fundamentally different approach from the distance-based restraints. It operates on `atom_covalent_bond_indices` — a list of `(left_atom_indices, right_atom_indices)` tensor pairs produced by `get_atom_covalent_bond_pairs_from_constraints`. For each bond, it maps atom indices to token indices via `torch.gather` on `atom_token_index`, then sets `bond_feature[left_token, right_token] = 1`. The feature uses `EncodingType.IDENTITY` (binary) rather than RBF, and `apply_mask` is overridden to return the unmasked feature, ensuring covalent bonds are never masked out regardless of the batch masking strategy.

The resulting feature is a binary `TOKEN_PAIR` matrix where `1` indicates a covalent bond exists between two tokens and `0` indicates no bond. This is critical for glycosylation (NAG–protein bonds) and ligand coordination (e.g., Cys–S–ligand bonds).

Sources: [token_bond.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_bond.py#L1-L64), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L262)

## Inference Integration

At inference time, restraints are passed via the `constraint_path` parameter of `run_inference`. The flow proceeds through `make_all_atom_feature_context`, which reads and parses the restraint file, loads chains from the FASTA input, and assembles the `RestraintContext`. Covalent bond information is simultaneously extracted into `atom_covalent_bond_indices` via `get_atom_covalent_bond_pairs_from_constraints`. The `Collate` class then batches all feature contexts, and the `FeatureFactory` invokes each registered generator to produce the final feature tensors.

```python
# Contact restraint example: residue-residue proximity
candidates = run_inference(
    fasta_file=fasta_path,
    output_dir=output_dir,
    constraint_path=Path("contact.restraints"),
    # ... standard inference parameters
)

# Covalent bond example: protein-glycan linkage
candidates = run_inference(
    fasta_file=Path("1ac5.fasta"),
    output_dir=output_dir,
    constraint_path=Path("1ac5.restraints"),
    # ... standard inference parameters
)
```

Sources: [predict_with_restraints.py](examples/restraints/predict_with_restraints.py#L1-L36), [predict_covalent_ligand.py](examples/covalent_bonds/predict_covalent_ligand.py#L1-L28), [predict_glycosylated.py](examples/covalent_bonds/predict_glycosylated.py#L1-L28)

## Example Restraint Files in Practice

The repository includes three concrete restraint examples demonstrating each interaction type:

**Contact** (`examples/restraints/contact.restraints`): Two residue–residue contacts between antibody heavy/light chains and antigen, with `max_distance_angstrom=5.5` and `confidence=1.0`:
```csv
chainA,res_idxA,chainB,res_idxB,connection_type,confidence,min_distance_angstrom,max_distance_angstrom,comment,restraint_id
A,C387,B,Y101,contact,1.0,0.0,5.5,protein-heavy,restraint_1
C,I32,A,S483,contact,1.0,0.0,5.5,protein-light,restraint_2
```

**Pocket** (`examples/restraints/pocket.restraints`): Two chain-level pocket constraints where chains B and C should be near specific residues on chain A:
```csv
chainA,res_idxA,chainB,res_idxB,connection_type,confidence,min_distance_angstrom,max_distance_angstrom,comment,restraint_id
B,,A,C387,pocket,1.0,0.0,5.5,protein-heavy,restraint_0
C,,A,S483,pocket,1.0,0.0,5.5,protein-light,restraint_1
```

**Covalent — Glycan** (`examples/covalent_bonds/1ac5.restraints`): Two N-linked glycosylation bonds from Asn residues to NAG C1 atoms, with `max_distance_angstrom=0.0`:
```csv
chainA,res_idxA,chainB,res_idxB,connection_type,confidence,min_distance_angstrom,max_distance_angstrom,comment,restraint_id
A,N437@N,B,@C1,covalent,1.0,0.0,0.0,protein-glycan,bond1
A,N445@N,C,@C1,covalent,1.0,0.0,0.0,protein-glycan,bond2
```

**Covalent — Ligand** (`examples/covalent_bonds/8cyo.restraints`): A thioether bond between Cys217 sulfur and ligand S1 atom:
```csv
chainA,res_idxA,chainB,res_idxB,connection_type,confidence,min_distance_angstrom,max_distance_angstrom,comment,restraint_id
A,C217@SG,B,@S1,covalent,1.0,0.0,0.0,protein-ligand,bond1
```

Note the pattern: glycan and ligand entities have empty residue names in `res_idxB` (e.g., `@C1`, `@S1`) because non-polymer entities lack residue-level naming — only atom names are meaningful.

Sources: [contact.restraints](examples/restraints/contact.restraints#L1-L3), [pocket.restraints](examples/restraints/pocket.restraints#L1-L4), [1ac5.restraints](examples/covalent_bonds/1ac5.restraints#L1-L3), [8cyo.restraints](examples/covalent_bonds/8cyo.restraints#L1-L3)

## Subchain ID Compatibility and Error Handling

A critical operational concern is the mapping between chain IDs in the restraint file and the subchain IDs assigned during chain loading. The `entity_name_as_subchain` parameter in `load_chains_from_raw` controls whether subchain IDs are derived from FASTA entity names (e.g., `G`, `H`) or auto-assigned alphabetically (e.g., `A`, `B`). Restraint chain references (`chainA`, `chainB`) must use the same naming scheme. A mismatch causes the feature generators to fail to locate matching tokens, producing all-null feature tensors — silently degrading prediction quality without raising an error.

The `TokenDistanceRestraint` and `TokenPairPocketRestraint` generators both handle missing or unresolvable constraints by falling back to a matrix filled with `ignore_idx = -1.0`, caught via `try/except` with logged errors. This graceful degradation means the model proceeds without the restraint signal rather than crashing, but the user receives no explicit notification that restraints were dropped.

Sources: [test_restraints.py](tests/test_restraints.py#L45-L126), [token_dist_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_dist_restraint.py#L161-L170), [token_pair_pocket_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_pair_pocket_restraint.py#L132-L141)

## Next Steps

- To understand how these features are encoded into the model's input space, see [Pairwise and Restraint Feature Generators](20-pairwise-and-restraint-feature-generators) which covers the RBF encoding, identity encoding, and the base `FeatureGenerator` abstraction.
- For the broader input data pipeline that feeds into restraint parsing, see [FASTA Parsing and Entity Types](13-fasta-parsing-and-entity-types) which defines the entity names referenced by restraint chain IDs.
- To understand how restraint features interact with the diffusion process, see [Diffusion Denoising Process](11-diffusion-denoising-process) which consumes these token-pair features during structure generation.

# Feature Generator Base Design



Chai-1's feature engineering system is built on a disciplined abstract class hierarchy that transforms raw batch data into numerically encoded tensors ready for model consumption. Every feature—whether it's a one-hot residue type, an RBF-encoded distance restraint, or a floating-point reference position—flows through the same `FeatureGenerator` contract: inspect the batch, extract relevant fields, compute the raw tensor, then validate and cast its dtype. This page examines the architectural skeleton that makes that uniformity possible: the `FeatureGenerator` ABC, its `EncodingType` and `FeatureType` enumerations, the masking contract, and the `FeatureFactory` orchestrator.

Sources: [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L1-L114), [feature_type.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_type.py#L1-L17), [feature_factory.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L1-L27)

## FeatureType: The Structural Taxonomy

Before a feature is generated, it must declare *where* it lives in the model's input tensor topology. The `FeatureType` enum partitions all features into eight spatial categories that correspond directly to the model's embedding layers:

| FeatureType | Tensor Rank | Spatial Shape | Example Generator |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TOKEN` | 3 | `(B, N, C)` | `ResidueType`, `ESMEmbeddings` |
| `TOKEN_PAIR` | 4 | `(B, N, N, C)` | `RelativeChain`, `TokenBondRestraint` |
| `ATOM` | 3 | `(B, A, C)` | `AtomElementOneHot`, `RefPos` |
| `ATOM_PAIR` | 4 | `(B, A, A, C)` | `BlockedAtomPairDistances` |
| `MSA` | 4 | `(B, D, N, C)` | `MSAFeatureGenerator` |
| `TEMPLATES` | 5 | `(B, T, N, N, C)` | `TemplateDistogramGenerator` |
| `RESIDUE` | 3 | `(B, R, C)` | (legacy / reserved) |
| `PAIR` | 4 | `(B, R, R, C)` | (legacy / reserved) |

Here **B** = batch, **N** = tokens, **A** = atoms, **D** = MSA depth, **T** = template count, **C** = feature channels. The model's embedding modules consume features grouped by these types—single representations feed token/atom embedders, while pair representations feed pairwise attention modules. This taxonomy ensures the factory can route each generated tensor to the correct downstream consumer without runtime inspection.

Sources: [feature_type.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_type.py#L1-L17)

## EncodingType: The Numerical Representation Contract

Each generator declares an `EncodingType` that governs two critical behaviors: **dtype validation** (via `cast_feature`) and **masking semantics** (via `mask_value`). These six encoding types cover every numerical pattern in the system:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "EncodingType Decision Tree"
        A[Raw Tensor] --> B{Integer indices?}
        B -->|Yes| C{Pairwise outer sum?}
        C -->|Yes| D["OUTERSUM<br>int → one-hot × one-hot"]
        C -->|No| E["ONE_HOT<br>int → one-hot lookup"]
        B -->|No| F{Pre-trained embedding?}
        F -->|Yes| G["ESM<br>float, pass-through"]
        F -->|No| H{Binned distance?}
        H -->|Yes, radial basis| I["RBF<br>float, Gaussian kernels"]
        H -->|Yes, sinusoidal| J["FOURIER<br>float, cosine/sine"]
        H -->|No| K["IDENTITY<br>float, raw values"]
    end
```

The `cast_feature` function enforces dtype constraints at generation time. `ONE_HOT` and `OUTERSUM` require integer dtypes (`torch.long`, `torch.int`, `torch.int16`, `torch.int8`, `torch.uint8`) because their values serve as indices into embedding tables. `RBF` and `FOURIER` require floating-point dtypes (`torch.float16`, `torch.float32`, `torch.bfloat16`). `IDENTITY` casts to `float32` and asserts the absolute maximum is below 100 as a safety check against unscaled inputs. `ESM` is a pass-through that accepts any dtype.

Sources: [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L16-L50)

## The Masking Protocol

Missing or unknown values are an inherent reality of structural biology data—atoms may lack reference coordinates, templates may be absent, and distillation data may not define B-factors. The `FeatureGenerator` base class provides a unified masking protocol through `can_mask` and `mask_value`, with semantics that vary by encoding type:

| EncodingType | `mask_value` | Mechanism | Example Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ONE_HOT` / `OUTERSUM` | `num_classes` | Index beyond last class → zero vector after embedding | Masked residue types, binned distances |
| `RBF` / `FOURIER` | `-100.0` | Large negative sentinel → zero after Gaussian/sinusoidal transform | Distance restraints without constraints |
| `IDENTITY` | Zero tensor with last channel = 1 | Dedicated mask channel appended to feature | Atom positions, deletion values |
| `ESM` | `0.0` | Zero embedding | Masked ESM representations |

For `IDENTITY`-encoded features with `can_mask=True`, the generator appends an extra channel to the output tensor. When a position is masked, the data channels are zeroed and the final mask channel is set to 1, allowing downstream layers to distinguish "value is zero" from "value is unknown." This design is critical for features like `RefPos` and `BlockedAtomPairDistances` where zero is a meaningful coordinate value.

Sources: [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L52-L80)

## FeatureGenerator: The Abstract Contract

The `FeatureGenerator` ABC defines a two-phase generation pipeline that all 20+ concrete generators implement:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Factory as FeatureFactory
    participant Gen as FeatureGenerator
    participant Batch as Input Batch

    Factory->>Gen: generate(batch)
    Gen->>Gen: get_input_kwargs_from_batch(batch)
    Note over Gen: Extracts relevant keys<br/>from batch["inputs"]
    Gen->>Gen: _generate(**kwargs)
    Note over Gen: Subclass implements<br/>raw tensor computation
    Gen->>Gen: make_feature(data)
    Note over Gen: cast_feature() validates<br/>dtype & constraints
    Gen-->>Factory: validated Tensor
```

**Phase 1 — Batch extraction** (`get_input_kwargs_from_batch`): Each subclass declares which keys it needs from the batch dictionary. This indirection decouples the generator from the batch structure, allowing generators to rename, cast, or compose batch fields before computation. For example, `ResidueType` extracts `batch["inputs"]["aatype"]` and casts it to `.long()`, while `RelativeChain` pulls both `token_entity_id` and `token_sym_id`.

**Phase 2 — Computation and validation** (`_generate` + `make_feature`): The subclass computes a raw tensor, then `make_feature` delegates to `cast_feature` for dtype enforcement. The `generate` method orchestrates both phases, so callers never invoke `_generate` directly.

The constructor accepts six parameters that fully characterize a feature's encoding contract: `ty` (spatial type), `encoding_ty` (numerical type), `num_classes` (cardinality for one-hot/bins), `mult` (multiplier for features like atom name characters with `mult=4`), `ignore_index` (sentinel for loss computation, default -100), and `can_mask` (whether masking is supported).

> [!TIP]
> When implementing a custom generator, always call `self.make_feature()` on the raw output tensor rather than returning it directly. This ensures dtype validation fires—skipping it can introduce silent float/int mismatches that only surface as shape errors deep in the model's embedding layers.

Sources: [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L82-L114)

## Two Implementation Patterns

Examining the concrete generators reveals two distinct patterns for implementing the abstract contract:

### Pattern A: Keyword Extraction (Standard)

Most generators follow the template method pattern faithfully—they implement both `get_input_kwargs_from_batch` and `_generate`. The batch extraction method returns a dictionary of named tensors, and `_generate` receives them as typed keyword arguments:

```python
# ResidueType — classic two-method pattern
class ResidueType(FeatureGenerator):
    def get_input_kwargs_from_batch(self, batch) -> dict:
        return dict(aatype=batch["inputs"]["aatype"].long())

    def _generate(self, aatype: Int[Tensor, "b n"]) -> Tensor:
        seq_emb = aatype.clone()
        return self.make_feature(data=seq_emb.unsqueeze(-1))
```

This pattern benefits from `@typecheck` decorators on `_generate` that validate tensor shapes and dtypes at development time, catching dimension mismatches early.

### Pattern B: Direct Override (Identity and RefPos)

Some generators bypass the keyword extraction phase entirely by overriding `generate()` directly. This is used when the computation is simple enough that the indirection adds no value, or when the feature requires special handling that doesn't fit the kwargs pattern:

```python
# Identity — overrides generate() directly
class Identity(FeatureGenerator):
    def generate(self, batch: dict) -> Tensor:
        feat = futils.get_entry_for_key(batch, self.key)
        # ... dimension handling and mask channel appending ...
        return self.make_feature(data=feat)
```

The `Identity` generator is a generic passthrough that uses a configurable `key` (supporting slash-separated nested paths via `get_entry_for_key`) to extract any field from the batch. It handles both scalar features (reshaping from `(B, N)` to `(B, N, 1)`) and vector features (shape `(B, N, D)`), and appends the mask channel when `can_mask=True`.

> [!TIP]
> Prefer Pattern A (keyword extraction) for any generator that processes multiple batch fields or performs non-trivial computation. The `@typecheck`-decorated `_generate` signature serves as living documentation of expected tensor shapes, which is invaluable when debugging feature mismatches across the pipeline.

Sources: [residue_type.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/residue_type.py#L1-L35), [identity.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/identity.py#L1-L49), [ref_pos.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/ref_pos.py#L1-L33), [feature_utils.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_utils.py#L1-L32)

## FeatureFactory: Batch-Level Orchestration

The `FeatureFactory` is the top-level coordinator that transforms an entire batch into a complete feature dictionary. It holds an ordered `dict[str, FeatureGenerator]` mapping feature names to their generators, and its `generate` method iterates over all entries:

```python
class FeatureFactory:
    generators: dict[str, FeatureGenerator]

    def generate(self, batch) -> dict[str, Tensor]:
        return {name: gen.generate(batch) for name, gen in self.generators.items()}
```

The resulting dictionary maps string keys (e.g., `"residue_type"`, `"relative_chain"`) to their computed tensors. Downstream, the model's input modules consume this dictionary, grouping features by `FeatureType` to construct single representations, pair representations, MSA stacks, and template stacks. The factory pattern ensures that adding or removing a feature requires only a dictionary mutation—no changes to the generation loop itself.

Sources: [feature_factory.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L1-L27)

## Constructor Parameter Reference

The `FeatureGenerator.__init__` signature defines six parameters that together fully specify a feature's encoding behavior:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ty` | `FeatureType` | required | Spatial category: TOKEN, TOKEN_PAIR, ATOM, etc. |
| `encoding_ty` | `EncodingType` | required | Numerical encoding: ONE_HOT, IDENTITY, RBF, etc. |
| `num_classes` | `int` | `-1` | Cardinality for ONE_HOT bins; dimension count for IDENTITY |
| `mult` | `int` | `1` | Feature multiplier (e.g., 4 for 4-character atom names) |
| `ignore_index` | `float` | `-100.0` | Sentinel value for loss masking |
| `can_mask` | `bool` | `True` | Whether the feature supports masked/unknown values |

The `mult` parameter is particularly noteworthy for features with multiple sub-components per spatial position. `AtomNameOneHot`, for instance, encodes atom names as 4 characters each, so it sets `mult=4` to signal that each spatial position produces 4 one-hot indices rather than 1.

Sources: [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L82-L95)

## What Comes Next

This page covered the abstract skeleton. The concrete generators that populate this framework fall into two natural groups:

- **[Token and Atom Feature Generators](19-token-and-atom-feature-generators)** — Single-position features like `ResidueType`, `AtomElementOneHot`, `ESMEmbeddings`, `RefPos`, and `Identity` that encode per-token or per-atom properties.
- **[Pairwise and Restraint Feature Generators](20-pairwise-and-restraint-feature-generators)** — Pair-position features like `RelativeChain`, `RelativeEntity`, `TokenBondRestraint`, `TokenDistanceRestraint`, `DockingRestraintGenerator`, and template generators that encode relationships between positions.

# Token and Atom Feature Generators



Chai-1's feature engineering pipeline transforms raw structural and sequence data into rich tensor representations that the model can consume. This page examines the **token-level** and **atom-level** feature generators — the per-position encodings that give the model its fundamental vocabulary of chemical identity, spatial reference, and structural metadata. These generators occupy the critical boundary between raw input data and the embedding layers, converting heterogeneous biological information into uniform, maskable tensors governed by a rigorous type system.

## Feature Type Taxonomy and Encoding System

Every feature generator in Chai-1 is classified along two orthogonal axes: its **FeatureType** (which structural granularity it operates at) and its **EncodingType** (how raw values are numerically represented). The `FeatureType` enum defines eight domains that partition the feature space by structural resolution and relational arity:

| FeatureType | Granularity | Shape Pattern | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ATOM` | Per-atom | `(b, n_atoms, ...)` | Single-atom properties |
| `ATOM_PAIR` | Atom-pair | `(b, n_blocks, bl_q, bl_kv, ...)` | Blocked pairwise atom features |
| `TOKEN` | Per-token | `(b, n_tokens, ...)` | Single-token properties |
| `TOKEN_PAIR` | Token-pair | `(b, n_tokens, n_tokens, ...)` | Pairwise token relationships |
| `MSA` | Per-MSA-row | `(b, depth, n_tokens, ...)` | Multiple sequence alignment features |
| `TEMPLATES` | Per-template | `(b, n_templ, n_tokens, ...)` | Structural template features |

The `EncodingType` enum governs how raw values are cast and masked:

| EncodingType | Input Dtype | Mask Strategy | Typical Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ONE_HOT` | Integer | Class index = `num_classes` (out-of-range) | Categorical features |
| `IDENTITY` | Float | Last channel set to 1.0, zeros elsewhere | Continuous scalar/vector features |
| `RBF` | Float | Value = `-100.0` | Radial basis function encodings |
| `FOURIER` | Float | Value = `-100.0` | Fourier feature encodings |
| `OUTERSUM` | Integer | Same as `ONE_HOT` | Pairwise categorical via outer sum |
| `ESM` | Float | Value = `0.0` | Pre-computed protein language model embeddings |

The `cast_feature` function enforces these dtype contracts at generation time — `ONE_HOT` and `OUTERSUM` require integer types, while `RBF` and `FOURIER` require floating-point. The `mask_value` property on each generator produces the canonical sentinel for missing data according to the encoding type, ensuring downstream embedding layers can distinguish "no data" from "zero value."

Sources: [feature_type.py](/chai_lab/data/features/feature_type.py#L1-L17), [base.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L1-L114)

## The FeatureGenerator Contract

All generators inherit from `FeatureGenerator`, an abstract base class that enforces a two-phase generation protocol. The `generate(batch)` method first calls `get_input_kwargs_from_batch(batch)` to extract relevant tensors from the collated batch dictionary, then passes those kwargs to `_generate(**kwargs)`, which each concrete subclass implements. This separation ensures that batch key lookups are centralized and that the core generation logic receives pre-typed, pre-validated inputs.

Each generator is configured at construction time with five parameters that determine its output shape and masking behavior:

- **`ty`** (FeatureType): The structural granularity, determining which embedding pathway consumes this feature.
- **`encoding_ty`** (EncodingType): The numerical encoding strategy, controlling dtype and masking semantics.
- **`num_classes`**: For `ONE_HOT`, the number of distinct categories (the output channel count after embedding). For `IDENTITY`, the dimensionality of the continuous feature vector.
- **`mult`**: A multiplier on `num_classes`, typically 1, used when a single categorical feature is replicated (e.g., atom name characters encoded 4 times).
- **`can_mask`**: Whether this feature supports masking — i.e., whether a sentinel value can be inserted for missing/invalid entries.

The `make_feature(data)` method is the final gate before a tensor leaves the generator: it calls `cast_feature` to enforce dtype correctness and range safety (e.g., `IDENTITY` features must have absolute max < 100).

> [!TIP]
> The `Identity` generator appends an extra zero-channel to its output when `can_mask=True`, then sets that channel to 1.0 for masked positions. This means the actual output dimension is `num_classes + 1` — the last channel acts as a binary "is this masked?" indicator rather than using a sentinel value. This design avoids ambiguity between a legitimate zero value and a missing value.

Sources: [base.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L58-L114)

## Atom-Level Feature Generators

Atom-level generators produce per-atom features that feed into the atom embedding pathway. These encode the most fine-grained chemical identity and spatial reference information available in the input.

### AtomElementOneHot

**FeatureType**: `ATOM` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 129 (128 + 1 mask)

Encodes the atomic number of each atom as a one-hot vector. The `max_atomic_num` parameter defaults to 128, covering the full periodic table with room to spare. Atomic numbers are clamped to `num_classes` before encoding, so any out-of-range element maps to the last valid index rather than overflowing. The input `atom_ref_element` is drawn directly from the structure context's per-atom element assignment.

```python
# Generation logic (simplified)
seq_emb = torch.clamp(atomic_numbers, max=self.num_classes).unsqueeze(-1)
```

### AtomNameOneHot

**FeatureType**: `ATOM` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 64 × 4 = 256 (with mult=4)

Encodes each atom's name as four separate one-hot vectors, one per character position. Atom names like "CA", "N", "OG1" are decomposed into individual character indices, with each character independently one-hot encoded over `num_chars=64` possible values. The `mult=4` parameter signals to downstream consumers that this feature contains 4 repeated categorical encodings that should be embedded separately and then combined.

### RefPos

**FeatureType**: `ATOM` | **EncodingType**: `IDENTITY` | **Output channels**: 3 (x, y, z) | **can_mask**: `False`

Provides the 3D reference position of each atom, scaled by dividing by 10.0 to bring coordinates into a range suitable for neural network input. An assertion enforces that the maximum L2 norm of the scaled coordinates is below 100, serving as a sanity check against improperly scaled inputs. Unlike most `IDENTITY` features, `RefPos` sets `can_mask=False` because reference positions are expected to always be valid for existing atoms — the atom existence mask handles invalid atoms separately.

```python
feat = original_pos / 10.0  # Å → deca-Ångström scale
assert torch.amax(feat.norm(dim=-1)) < 100.0
```

> [!TIP]
> The `/10.0` scaling in `RefPos` is critical for stable training. Raw Ångström coordinates (typically 0–100) would produce large magnitudes that overwhelm the `IDENTITY` encoding's assertion guard (`abs().max() < 100`). The deca-Ångström scale keeps all coordinate components in roughly the [-10, 10] range, well within the safe interval for embedding.

Sources: [atom_element.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/atom_element.py#L1-L35), [atom_name.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/atom_name.py#L1-L32), [ref_pos.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/ref_pos.py#L1-L33)

## Token-Level Feature Generators

Token-level generators produce per-token features — one value per residue, nucleotide, or ligand token in the input. These encode the coarser-grained biological identity and metadata that the model uses for its primary sequence-level reasoning.

### ResidueType

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 23 (22 + 1 mask)

The foundational categorical feature encoding the residue type at each token position. With `num_res_ty=22`, it covers the 20 standard amino acids plus a gap token and an "X" (unknown) token. The `key` parameter defaults to `"aatype"` but can be overridden to point at alternative batch fields, allowing the same generator class to encode different residue taxonomies. The input is cloned before unsqueezing to avoid mutating the batch data in-place.

### ESMEmbeddings

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `ESM` | **can_mask**: `False`

A passthrough generator that delivers pre-computed ESM (Evolutionary Scale Model) embeddings directly into the token feature stream. Unlike other generators that transform raw data, `ESMEmbeddings` simply validates and forwards the `esm_embeddings` tensor from the batch. The `ESM` encoding type uses `0.0` as its mask value and bypasses the usual dtype casting, since these embeddings are already in their final floating-point form. The embedding dimension is determined by the upstream ESM model (typically 256 or 1280 dimensions).

### MSAProfileGenerator

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `IDENTITY` | **Output channels**: 32 (matches `residue_types_with_nucleotides_order`)

Computes the MSA profile — the per-position frequency distribution across residue types — and delivers it as a continuous `IDENTITY`-encoded feature at the token level. The profile is computed from the *main* (shallow, profile-only) MSA using an optimized `torch.scatter_add` implementation: it accumulates counts for each residue type across the MSA depth dimension, then normalizes by the total count per position. This gives the model a compressed view of evolutionary conservation without requiring the full MSA depth at inference.

```python
# Profile = normalized residue-type frequency across MSA depth
unnormalized_profile = torch.zeros(...).scatter_add(dim=2, index=..., src=...)
profile = unnormalized_profile / unnormalized_profile.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True).clamp_min_(1)
```

### MSADeletionMeanGenerator

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `IDENTITY` | **Output channels**: 1

Averages the MSA deletion counts across the depth dimension of the main MSA, producing a per-token scalar indicating the mean number of deletions at each position. This uses `masked_mean` to properly handle masked MSA rows, ensuring that padding rows don't deflate the average. The output is a single continuous value per token.

### ChainIsCropped

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `IDENTITY` | **Output channels**: 1 | **can_mask**: `False`

A placeholder generator that currently produces all-zeros for every token. Its `can_mask=False` setting means the output will not have a mask channel appended. The generator exists as a structural hook in the feature pipeline — it reads `token_asym_id` from the batch, providing a consistent interface for future implementations that may signal which chains have been truncated by cropping.

### IsDistillation

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 2 (1 + 1 mask)

A binary flag indicating whether each token originates from distillation data (i.e., predicted structures used as training data, as in AlphaFold2's distillation augmentation). The `is_distillation` scalar from the batch is broadcast across all token positions, and the result is cast to `uint8` for one-hot encoding.

### TokenBFactor

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 2 (1 bin boundary + 1 mask)

B-B-factor values into a discrete one-hot encoding. The default bin boundary is `[140.0]`, creating two bins: B-factor ≤ 140 and B-factor > 140. This feature is **only defined for non-distillation data** — for distillation examples or when the stochastic `include_prob` gate excludes a sample, the feature is filled with the mask value. The `include_prob` parameter (default 1.0) randomly drops this feature during training as a data augmentation strategy.

### TokenPLDDT

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 3 (2 bin boundaries + 1 mask)

The mirror image of `TokenBFactor`: binarizes pLDDT (predicted LDDT) scores with default boundaries at `[0.3, 0.7]`, creating three bins. This feature is **only defined for distillation data** — the mask logic is inverted relative to `TokenBFactor`. The same `include_prob` stochastic dropout mechanism applies. Together, `TokenBFactor` and `TokenPLDDT` share the `token_b_factor_or_plddt` batch field, with the `is_distillation` flag determining which interpretation is valid.

### MissingChainContact

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN` | **EncodingType**: `IDENTITY` | **Output channels**: 2 (1 feature + 1 mask)

Identifies tokens belonging to chains that have **no inter-chain atom contacts** within a threshold distance (default 6.0 Å, matching the DockQ contact cutoff). The generator computes all pairwise atom distances, filters for inter-chain atom pairs within the threshold, and then flags tokens on chains where no such contacts exist. For monomeric inputs, the feature is all-zeros. This provides the model with an explicit signal about which chains are spatially isolated — information that is critical for docking scenarios.

Sources: [residue_type.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/residue_type.py#L1-L35), [esm_generator.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/esm_generator.py#L1-L35), [msa.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/msa.py#L139-L197), [is_cropped_chain.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/is_cropped_chain.py#L1-L37), [structure_metadata.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/structure_metadata.py#L1-L144), [missing_chain_contact.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/missing_chain_contact.py#L1-L97)

## Token-Pair Positional Encodings

Several generators produce `TOKEN_PAIR` features that encode relative positional relationships between tokens. These are the spatial and sequential inductive biases that allow the model to reason about chain topology, entity membership, and residue adjacency.

### RelativeEntity

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN_PAIR` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 3

Implements Algorithm 5 from AlphaFold-Multimer. Computes whether token pair *(i, j)* belongs to the same entity (class 1), a different entity (class 2), or is masked (class 0). Entity IDs are first remapped to a zero-indexed range via `torch.unique`, then the relative difference is computed as `entity_id[j] - entity_id[i] + 1`, clamped to [0, 2]. This gives the model a three-way categorical signal about entity co-membership.

### RelativeChain

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN_PAIR` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 2*s_max* + 2 (default: 6)

Also following Algorithm 5 from AF-Multimer. Encodes the **relative chain index** between tokens that share the same entity — i.e., for symmetric copies of the same chain. The parameter `s_max` (default 2) controls the maximum representable chain offset. For token pairs within the same entity, the relative chain offset is clamped to `[-s_max, s_max]` and shifted to `[0, 2*s_max]`. For token pairs across different entities, the feature is set to a dedicated "inter-entity" class at index `2*s_max + 1`. This lets the model distinguish intra-entity chain relationships from inter-entity ones.

### RelativeSequenceSeparation

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN_PAIR` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 66 (default: 2×32 + 2)

Encodes the relative residue index offset between token pairs on the **same chain**. The default `SMALL_SEP_BINS` cover offsets from -32 to +32 (65 bins), with an additional class for inter-chain pairs. The generation uses `torch.searchsorted` to bin the residue index difference, then masks out inter-chain positions (where `asym_id[i] ≠ asym_id[j]`) with the dedicated class. This provides a discretized positional encoding that captures local sequence proximity within a chain.

### RelativeTokenSeparation

**FeatureType**: `TOKEN_PAIR` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` | **Output channels**: 35 (default: 2×16 + 3)

A finer-grained positional encoding that captures the relative **token index** offset (rather than residue index) between tokens on the same residue of the same chain. The `r_max` parameter (default 16) controls the maximum representable token offset. The mask condition requires both same chain (`asym_id` match) AND same residue (`residue_index` match), making this feature active only for multi-atom tokens (e.g., ligand tokens with multiple heavy atoms). Token pairs not meeting this condition receive the sentinel class `2*r_max + 2`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Batch Dictionary] --> B[FeatureFactory.generate]
    B --> C{For each registered generator}
    C --> D[get_input_kwargs_from_batch]
    D --> E[_generate with typed kwargs]
    E --> F[make_feature → cast_feature]
    F --> G[Output: Typed Tensor]
    
    subgraph "Token Generators"
        T1[ResidueType<br/>ONE_HOT · 22 classes]
        T2[ESMEmbeddings<br/>ESM · passthrough]
        T3[MSAProfileGenerator<br/>IDENTITY · 32 dim]
        T4[ChainIsCropped<br/>IDENTITY · 1 dim]
        T5[IsDistillation<br/>ONE_HOT · 1 class]
        T6[TokenBFactor<br/>ONE_HOT · binned]
        T7[TokenPLDDT<br/>ONE_HOT · binned]
        T8[MissingChainContact<br/>IDENTITY · 1 dim]
    end
    
    subgraph "Atom Generators"
        A1[AtomElementOneHot<br/>ONE_HOT · 128 classes]
        A2[AtomNameOneHot<br/>ONE_HOT · 64×4 chars]
        A3[RefPos<br/>IDENTITY · 3 coords]
    end
    
    subgraph "Token-Pair Positional Encodings"
        P1[RelativeEntity<br/>ONE_HOT · 3 classes]
        P2[RelativeChain<br/>ONE_HOT · 2s_max+2]
        P3[RelativeSequenceSeparation<br/>ONE_HOT · binned]
        P4[RelativeTokenSeparation<br/>ONE_HOT · 2r_max+3]
    end
    
    G -.-> T1 & T2 & T3 & T4 & T5 & T6 & T7 & T8
    G -.-> A1 & A2 & A3
    G -.-> P1 & P2 & P3 & P4
```

Sources: [relative_entity.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_entity.py#L1-L48), [relative_chain.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_chain.py#L1-L55), [relative_sep.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_sep.py#L1-L63), [relative_token.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_token.py#L1-L54)

## Atom-Pair Distance Generators

### BlockedAtomPairDistances

**FeatureType**: `ATOM_PAIR` | **EncodingType**: `IDENTITY` | **can_mask**: `True`

Computes pairwise Euclidean distances between atoms in a **blocked** sparse pattern. Rather than materializing the full O(n²) atom-pair distance matrix, it uses pre-computed query and key/value index tensors (`block_atom_pair_q_idces`, `block_atom_pair_kv_idces`) to select only the atom pairs that fall within a spatial block structure. Additionally, atom pairs are filtered to only include atoms sharing the same `atom_ref_space_uid`, which groups atoms that belong to the same reference coordinate frame.

The output concatenates the distance feature with a binary mask channel, producing a 2-channel tensor where `[..., 0]` is the (optionally inverse-squared) distance and `[..., 1]` is 1.0 if the value is valid. The `inverse_squared` transform (`1 / (1 + d²)`) maps large distances toward zero while preserving sensitivity at short range — a physically motivated encoding that emphasizes steric constraints.

### BlockedAtomPairDistogram

**FeatureType**: `ATOM_PAIR` | **EncodingType**: `ONE_HOT` or `RBF` | **Output channels**: varies by bin count

A discrete counterpart to `BlockedAtomPairDistances` that bins distances into a one-hot distogram. Default bins for `ONE_HOT` mode are `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 16]` Å, creating 11 classes (10 bins + 1 mask). Default bins for `RBF` mode are `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]` Å. The same blocked computation and `atom_ref_space_uid` filtering apply, but the continuous distance is discretized via `torch.searchsorted` before encoding. Invalid pairs receive the mask value.

Sources: [blocked_atom_pair_distances.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/blocked_atom_pair_distances.py#L1-L176)

## Identity: The Generic Passthrough Generator

The `Identity` generator is a parameterized passthrough that can adapt to any batch key and feature type. Rather than implementing custom `_generate` logic, it reads a configurable `key` from the batch (supporting nested paths via `/` separators) and forwards the tensor directly as an `IDENTITY`-encoded feature. When `can_mask=True`, it appends the standard zero-channel mask indicator.

This generator serves as the glue between the raw batch tensors produced by the collation pipeline and the typed feature system. Its flexibility means new scalar or vector features can be added to the pipeline by simply registering an `Identity` generator with the appropriate key and dimension, without writing a new subclass.

```python
# Nested key resolution: "inputs/token_asym_id" → batch["inputs"]["token_asym_id"]
sub_keys, sub_dict = key.split("/"), data
for sub_key in sub_keys:
    sub_dict = sub_dict[sub_key]
```

Sources: [identity.py](/chai_lab/data/features/generators/identity.py#L1-L49), [feature_utils.py](/chai_lab/data/features/feature_utils.py#L1-L32)

## Feature Factory: Orchestration Layer

The `FeatureFactory` is the runtime orchestrator that transforms a batch dictionary into a complete feature dictionary. It holds a `dict[str, FeatureGenerator]` mapping and calls `generate(batch)` on each, producing a `dict[str, Tensor]` where each key matches the generator's registration name. This design allows feature sets to be composed declaratively — the same batch can be processed by different factory configurations to produce different feature sets for training vs. inference, or for different model variants.

```python
class FeatureFactory:
    generators: dict[str, FeatureGenerator]
    def generate(self, batch) -> dict[str, Tensor]:
        return {name: gen.generate(batch) for name, gen in self.generators.items()}
```

The complete feature context that feeds the factory is assembled by `AllAtomFeatureContext.to_dict()`, which merges dictionaries from the structure context, MSA context, template context, embedding context, and restraint context into a single flat namespace that generators draw from via `get_input_kwargs_from_batch`.

Sources: [feature_factory.py](/chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L1-L27), [all_atom_feature_context.py](/chai_lab/data/dataset/all_atom_feature_context.py#L68-L96)

## Generator Summary Reference

| Generator | FeatureType | EncodingType | Key Dimensions | Maskable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AtomElementOneHot` | ATOM | ONE_HOT | 129 (128+1) | ✓ |
| `AtomNameOneHot` | ATOM | ONE_HOT | 64×4=256 | ✓ |
| `RefPos` | ATOM | IDENTITY | 3 | ✗ |
| `ResidueType` | TOKEN | ONE_HOT | 23 (22+1) | ✓ |
| `ESMEmbeddings` | TOKEN | ESM | variable | ✗ |
| `MSAProfileGenerator` | TOKEN | IDENTITY | 32 | ✗ |
| `MSADeletionMeanGenerator` | TOKEN | IDENTITY | 1 | ✗ |
| `ChainIsCropped` | TOKEN | IDENTITY | 1 | ✗ |
| `IsDistillation` | TOKEN | ONE_HOT | 2 (1+1) | ✓ |
| `TokenBFactor` | TOKEN | ONE_HOT | 2 (1+1) | ✓ |
| `TokenPLDDT` | TOKEN | ONE_HOT | 3 (2+1) | ✓ |
| `MissingChainContact` | TOKEN | IDENTITY | 1 | ✗ |

| `RelativeTokenSeparation` | TOKEN_PAIR | ONE_HOT | 35 (2×16+3) | ✗ |

| `BlockedAtomPairDistogram` | ATOM_PAIR | ONE_HOT | 11 (default) | ✓ |
