The restraint-specific and docking-specific pairwise generators (`TokenDistanceRestraint`, `TokenPairPocketRestraint`, `DockingRestraintGenerator`, `TokenBondRestraint`) and the MSA-depth generators (`MSAFeatureGenerator`, `MSAHasDeletionGenerator`, `MSADeletionValueGenerator`, `IsPairedMSAGenerator`, `MSADataSourceGenerator`) are covered in detail on [Pairwise and Restraint Feature Generators](20-pairwise-and-restraint-feature-generators) and [MSA Generation and Loading](14-msa-generation-and-loading) respectively. The template generators (`TemplateMaskGenerator`, `TemplateUnitVectorGenerator`, `TemplateResTypeGenerator`, `TemplateDistogramGenerator`) are discussed in the context of [Template Processing Pipeline](16-template-processing-pipeline).


# Pairwise and Restraint Feature Generators



Pairwise and restraint feature generators are the bridge between raw structural context and the model's pair representation. They encode **relational information** — how tokens relate to each other along sequence, chain, and entity axes — and **experimental constraints** that steer the diffusion process toward biologically valid structures. This page dissects every generator that produces `TOKEN_PAIR`, `ATOM_PAIR`, or `TOKEN`-type features with pairwise semantics, tracing the data flow from batch tensors through encoding to the final feature tensor consumed by the trunk.

## Architectural Overview: Two Feature Domains

All generators covered here fall into two functional domains. **Pairwise structural encoders** capture intrinsic relational geometry (sequence separation, chain membership, entity identity, distances). **Restraint encoders** inject external prior knowledge — contacts, pockets, covalent bonds, and docking groups — that bias the model toward desired configurations. Despite their different purposes, both domains share the same `FeatureGenerator` abstraction: they pull named tensors from the batch dictionary, compute an N×N (or blocked N×N) feature, encode it via the type system defined in [Feature Generator Base Design](18-feature-generator-base-design), and return it for collation by the `FeatureFactory`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Pairwise Structural Encoders"
        RS[RelativeSequenceSeparation] --> |TOKEN_PAIR / ONE_HOT| FP[Pair Feature Dict]
        RTS[RelativeTokenSeparation] --> FP
        RC[RelativeChain] --> FP
        RE[RelativeEntity] --> FP
        TCD[TokenCenterDistance] --> FP
        BAPD[BlockedAtomPairDistances] --> |ATOM_PAIR / IDENTITY| FP
        BAPDG[BlockedAtomPairDistogram] --> |ATOM_PAIR / ONE_HOT or RBF| FP
    end

    subgraph "Restraint Encoders"
        TDR[TokenDistanceRestraint] --> |TOKEN_PAIR / RBF| FP
        TPPR[TokenPairPocketRestraint] --> |TOKEN_PAIR / RBF| FP
        TBR[TokenBondRestraint] --> |TOKEN_PAIR / IDENTITY| FP
        DRG[DockingRestraintGenerator] --> |TOKEN_PAIR / ONE_HOT| FP
        MCC[MissingChainContact] --> |TOKEN / IDENTITY| FP
    end

    FP --> FF[FeatureFactory.generate]
    FF --> |dict of str → Tensor| Model[Trunk Pair Input]
```

The `FeatureFactory` orchestrates generation by calling each registered generator's `generate()` method against the same batch, collecting all features into a single dictionary [FeatureFactory](chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L18-L27).

Sources: [feature_type.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_type.py#L1-L17), [feature_factory.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_factory.py#L1-L27), [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L1-L114)

## Pairwise Structural Encoders

These generators produce features that describe the **intrinsic relationships** between token pairs. They operate on batch-level metadata — residue indices, asym IDs, entity IDs — and encode relative offsets as one-hot categorical distributions. The common pattern: compute a pairwise difference matrix via `rearrange(x, "b n -> b n 1") - rearrange(x, "b n -> b 1 n")`, bin or clamp the result, and one-hot encode.

### RelativeSequenceSeparation

`RelativeSequenceSeparation` encodes the signed sequence distance between two tokens **within the same chain**. Inter-chain pairs receive a dedicated sentinel bin. The generator bins offsets using `torch.searchsorted` against a configurable set of separation bins (default: ±32 positions, yielding 67 bins). Critically, the feature is computed only when `asym_id` matches — all inter-chain entries are set to `num_classes - 1`, a dedicated "different chain" class.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sep_bins` | `get_sep_bins(32)` | Bin edges for sequence separation |
| `num_bins` | `None` | Alternative: generates symmetric bins ±`num_bins` |
| Output shape | `(B, N, N, 1)` | ONE_HOT with `len(sep_bins) + 2` classes |
| Feature type | `TOKEN_PAIR` | Consumed by pair trunk |

> [!TIP]
> The extra +2 in `num_classes` accounts for: (1) the sentinel index produced by `searchsorted` for values beyond the last bin edge, and (2) the dedicated inter-chain bin at `num_classes - 1`. When specifying `num_bins=32`, the actual one-hot depth is `2*32 + 2 = 67`.

Sources: [relative_sep.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_sep.py#L1-L63)

### RelativeTokenSeparation

Where `RelativeSequenceSeparation` operates on residue-level offsets, `RelativeTokenSeparation` operates on **token-level** offsets — accounting for ligands, modified residues, and multi-atom token types where token index ≠ residue index. It requires that both the residue index and the chain (asym_id) match between the pair before encoding the relative token separation. Out-of-scope pairs (different residue or different chain) receive the sentinel value `2 * r_max + 2`.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `r_max` | `16` | Maximum token offset to encode explicitly |
| Output shape | `(B, N, N, 1)` | ONE_HOT with `2*r_max + 3` classes |
| Masking logic | `rel_residue == 0 & rel_chain == 0` | Only same-residue, same-chain pairs |

Sources: [relative_token.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_token.py#L1-L54)

### RelativeChain

Following Algorithm 5 of AlphaFold-Multimer, `RelativeChain` encodes the **relative chain index within the same entity**. It computes the pairwise difference of `sym_id` (after remapping to zero-indexed via `torch.unique`), clamps to ±`s_max`, and masks inter-entity pairs to a sentinel bin. This is distinct from `RelativeEntity` — it distinguishes between *copies* of the same entity (e.g., homodimer chains A and B of the same protein sequence).

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `s_max` | `2` | Maximum relative chain offset |
| Output shape | `(B, N, N, 1)` | ONE_HOT with `2*s_max + 2` classes |
| Input keys | `token_entity_id`, `token_sym_id` | Entity and symmetry IDs |
| Inter-entity value | `2*s_max + 1` | Dedicated sentinel for cross-entity |

Sources: [relative_chain.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_chain.py#L1-L55)

### RelativeEntity

`RelativeEntity` provides the coarsest relational encoding: a 3-class one-hot indicating whether a token pair belongs to the **same entity** (class 0), a **different entity** (class 2), or represents a self-pair (class 1, when `rel_entity == 0` after zero-indexing). Entity IDs are remapped to zero-indexed before differencing, then `clamp(+1, 0, 2)` maps the three cases.

| Value | Semantics |
|---|---|
| 0 | Same entity, different token |
| 1 | Self-pair (same token) |
| 2 | Different entity |

Sources: [relative_entity.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/relative_entity.py#L1-L48)

### TokenCenterDistance

`TokenCenterDistance` bridges atom-level coordinates to token-pair features by computing pairwise Euclidean distances between each token's **center atom** (gathered via `token_centre_atom_index`). The resulting distance matrix is binned using `torch.searchsorted` against configurable distance bins, then masked where either token's center atom is absent. Default bins are `[0, 4, 8, 12, 16]`, yielding a 6-class one-hot (5 explicit bins + 1 mask sentinel).

```
all_atom_positions ──► center_atom_coords (via gather on token_centre_atom_index)
                              │
                              ▼
                    cdist(center_atom_coords) ──► bin via searchsorted
                              │
                              ▼
                    mask invalid pairs ──► ONE_HOT encoded TOKEN_PAIR feature
```

This generator is also **composed** by `DockingRestraintGenerator`, which delegates distance computation to `TokenCenterDistance._generate()` internally.

Sources: [token_pair_distance.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_pair_distance.py#L1-L66), [token_utils.py](chai_lab/data/features/token_utils.py#L1-L55)

### BlockedAtomPairDistances and BlockedAtomPairDistogram

These two generators produce `ATOM_PAIR`-type features using a **blocked sparse representation** rather than a full N×N matrix. Instead of computing all atom-atom distances, they use precomputed query/key index tensors (`block_atom_pair_q_idces`, `block_atom_pair_kv_idces`) that define which atom pairs to evaluate — a critical optimization for the atom attention module.

`BlockedAtomPairDistances` outputs raw inverse-squared distances (`1 / (1 + d²)`) concatenated with a validity mask channel, yielding shape `(B, n_blocks, bl_q, bl_kv, 2)`. `BlockedAtomPairDistogram` bins the same distances into discrete categories (one-hot or RBF) for categorical consumption.

Both generators enforce a **same-reference-space** constraint: atom pairs are only valid when their `atom_ref_space_uid` values match, ensuring that distances are only computed between atoms that share a coordinate frame.

| Generator | Encoding | Default Bins | Output Channels |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BlockedAtomPairDistances` | IDENTITY | N/A | 2 (feature + mask) |
| `BlockedAtomPairDistogram` | ONE_HOT | `[0,1,2,3,4,5,6,8,12,16]` | `len(bins)+1` |
| `BlockedAtomPairDistogram` | RBF | `[0,2,4,6,8,10,12,14,16]` | `len(bins)+1` |

Sources: [blocked_atom_pair_distances.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/blocked_atom_pair_distances.py#L1-L176)

## Restraint Feature Generators

Restraint generators encode **user-specified prior knowledge** about desired structural outcomes. They share a common contract: when no constraints are provided (or when constraint resolution fails), they produce a null feature matrix filled with `ignore_idx` (typically `-1.0`), ensuring the model falls back to unbiased prediction. When constraints are present, they resolve chain/residue identifiers into token positions and write constraint values into the N×N feature matrix.

### Constraint Resolution Pipeline

All restraint generators follow the same resolution pipeline from raw text constraints to feature tensors:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Raw .restraints file] --> B[parse_pairwise_table]
    B --> C[PairwiseInteraction objects]
    C --> D[load_manual_restraints_for_chai1]
    D --> E[RestraintContext]
    E --> F[Collator: batch dict keys]
    F --> G[Generator.get_input_kwargs_from_batch]
    G --> H[RestraintGroup dataclasses]
    H --> I[_generate / generate_from_restraint]
    I --> J[RBF or ONE_HOT encoded feature]
```

The parsing layer converts CSV-formatted restraint files into `PairwiseInteraction` objects, which are then resolved into `RestraintContext` during chain loading. The collator places constraint dictionaries under batch keys like `contact_constraints`, `pocket_constraints`, and `docking_constraints`. Each generator's `get_input_kwargs_from_batch` deserializes these back into typed `RestraintGroup` dataclasses before feature computation.

Sources: [token_dist_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_dist_restraint.py#L1-L35), [test_restraints.py](tests/test_restraints.py#L1-L126)

### TokenDistanceRestraint (Contact Restraints)

`TokenDistanceRestraint` encodes **pairwise residue-residue contact constraints** — the most common restraint type. Each `RestraintGroup` specifies a left/right residue pair (identified by subchain ID + residue index + residue name) and a distance threshold. The generator writes the threshold value into `constraint_mat[left_residue_mask, right_residue_mask]`, producing an **asymmetric** feature — the constraint is not mirrored to the transposed position.

Key implementation details:

- **Residue validation**: Both `left_residue_mask` and `right_residue_mask` must select exactly one token each. An assertion fires if multiple tokens match, preventing ambiguous constraints.
- **Name verification**: The residue name in the constraint is validated against the token's parsed residue name via `tensorcode_to_string`, catching mismatched chain/residue specifications early.
- **RBF encoding**: The distance threshold is encoded with radial basis functions (`EncodingType.RBF`, default 5 radii), allowing the model to interpret the constraint as a soft distance prior.
- **Null fallback**: If constraints are `None` or if any exception occurs during resolution, the generator returns a matrix filled with `-1.0`, which the RBF encoding interprets as "no constraint."

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `include_probability` | `1.0` | Probability of including restraints per example |
| `size` | `0.33` | Number of restraints; if `<1`, sampled from `Geometric(size)` |
| `min_dist` / `max_dist` | `10.0` / `30.0` | Distance range for RBF encoding |
| `num_rbf_radii` | `5` | Number of RBF basis functions |
| `query_entity_types` | All | Entity types eligible as constraint "query" side |
| `key_entity_types` | All | Entity types eligible as constraint "key" side |

> [!TIP]
> The `size` parameter has dual semantics: integer values specify an exact count, while float values in `(0, 1)` are interpreted as the parameter of a geometric distribution. This design allows training-time stochasticity (randomly varying the number of constraints per batch) while still supporting deterministic inference with a fixed count.

Sources: [token_dist_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_dist_restraint.py#L1-L273)

### TokenPairPocketRestraint (Pocket Restraints)

`TokenPairPocketRestraint` encodes **pocket constraints** — a qualitatively different relationship from pairwise contacts. Instead of specifying a residue-residue pair, a pocket restraint specifies a **single residue** (the "pocket token") and a **target chain**. The generator then creates constraints between the pocket token and *all* tokens in the target chain, setting each entry to `pocket_distance_threshold`.

This is implemented in `add_pocket_restraint`, which writes `pocket_distance_threshold` into `restraint_mat[pocket_token_residue_mask, pocket_chain_asym_mask]` — a row-vector of constraints from the pocket token to every token on the target chain. Like contact restraints, this feature is **asymmetric**: the reverse direction is not filled.

The `TokenPairPocketRestraint` class internally composes a `TokenDistanceRestraint` instance (with matching hyperparameters) to handle the sampling logic, but overrides the feature generation with its own pocket-specific resolution:

| Aspect | Contact Restraint | Pocket Restraint |
|---|---|---|
| Constraint scope | 1 residue ↔ 1 residue | 1 residue → entire chain |
| Feature symmetry | Asymmetric (one cell) | Asymmetric (one row) |
| Batch key | `contact_constraints` | `pocket_constraints` |
| RestraintGroup fields | `left/right_residue_*` | `pocket_chain/token_*` |

Sources: [token_pair_pocket_restraint.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_pair_pocket_restraint.py#L1-L248)

### TokenBondRestraint (Covalent Bonds)

`TokenBondRestraint` encodes **covalent bond topology** between tokens. It consumes `atom_covalent_bond_indices` — a list of `(left_atom_indices, right_atom_indices)` pairs per batch element — maps atom indices to token indices via `atom_token_index`, and writes `1.0` into `bond_feature[left_token_indices, right_token_indices]`.

Notable design choices:

- **No masking**: `apply_mask` is overridden to return the feature unchanged, since bonds are structural facts rather than soft constraints.
- **Zero-initialized**: The feature starts as all zeros; bonds are explicitly set to 1.0. The absence of a bond is simply the default state.
- **IDENTITY encoding**: Unlike distance restraints that use RBF, bonds are binary (present/absent), making identity encoding natural.

Sources: [token_bond.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/token_bond.py#L1-L64)

### DockingRestraintGenerator

`DockingRestraintGenerator` is the most complex restraint encoder, implementing a **chain-partitioning strategy** for docking tasks. It can operate in two modes:

1. **Training mode** (`_generate_from_batch`): Chains are randomly partitioned into two groups. Token-center distances are computed and provided for **intra-group** pairs while **inter-group** distances are masked. This teaches the model to predict inter-chain interfaces from intra-chain structural cues. Coordinate noise is sampled uniformly from `coord_noise` range. Structure dropout and chain dropout are optionally applied as regularization.

2. **Inference mode** (`_generate_from_restraints`): Explicit `RestraintGroup` objects specify which chains belong to a docking group, along with their center coordinates and noise parameters. Distances are computed between all chain pairs within the group using `add_restraint`, which fills a symmetric constraint matrix and its associated mask.

The generator delegates core distance computation to an internal `TokenCenterDistance` instance, then applies the partition mask or constraint overlay on top:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `dist_bins` | `[0, 4, 8, 16]` | Distance bin edges for ONE_HOT encoding |
| `coord_noise` | `(0.0, 3.0)` | Uniform noise range for coordinates |
| `include_probability` | `0.1` | Probability of including inter-group distances |
| `structure_dropout_prob` | `0.0` | Probability of dropping entire structures |
| `chain_dropout_prob` | `0.0` | Probability of randomly masking chains |
| `entity_types` | All | Entity types eligible for docking |

The `include_probability=0.1` default means that during training, 90% of the time *all* inter-chain distances are masked, forcing the model to learn interface prediction. The remaining 10% provides partial distance information as a teaching signal.

Sources: [docking.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/docking.py#L1-L372)

### MissingChainContact

`MissingChainContact` is a **token-level** (not pair-level) feature that flags chains with no inter-chain contacts. It computes all atom-atom distances, identifies atoms within `contact_threshold` Ångströms of atoms from other chains, and marks tokens belonging to chains that have zero such contacts. This is a diagnostic feature — it signals to the model that certain chains are structurally isolated, which may indicate a docking failure or a genuinely disconnected component.

The generator handles the monomer edge case explicitly: when only one chain exists, all tokens receive `0.0` (no missing contacts), since there are no inter-chain contacts to be missing.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `contact_threshold` | `6.0` | DockQ-compatible atom contact cutoff (Å) |
| Feature type | `TOKEN` | Per-token, not per-pair |
| Encoding | `IDENTITY` | Binary: 0.0 = has contacts, 1.0 = isolated |

Sources: [missing_chain_contact.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/missing_chain_contact.py#L1-L97)

## Encoding and Masking Contract

All pairwise and restraint generators share a unified encoding contract inherited from `FeatureGenerator`. The `mask_value` property and `cast_feature` function ensure consistent dtype handling across encoding types:

| Encoding Type | Mask Value | Dtype | Generators Using It |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ONE_HOT` | `num_classes` (sentinel index) | `long` / `int` | RelativeSep, RelativeToken, RelativeChain, RelativeEntity, TokenCenterDistance, BlockedAtomPairDistogram, DockingRestraint |
| `RBF` | `-100.0` | `float16/32/bfloat16` | TokenDistanceRestraint, TokenPairPocketRestraint |
| `IDENTITY` | Zero tensor with last channel = 1 | `float` | BlockedAtomPairDistances, TokenBondRestraint, MissingChainContact |

The `can_mask` flag on each generator controls whether the identity-encoding mask channel is allocated. For `ONE_HOT` and `RBF` encodings, masking is implicit: sentinel values (`num_classes` or `-100.0`) are decoded as "no information" by downstream embedding layers.

Sources: [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L36-L74)

## Feature Matrix Summary

The table below provides a comprehensive reference for all pairwise and restraint feature generators, their output specifications, and the batch keys they consume:

| Generator | Feature Type | Encoding | Output Shape | Key Batch Inputs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `RelativeSequenceSeparation` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | ONE_HOT | `(B,N,N,1)` | `token_residue_index`, `token_asym_id` |
| `RelativeTokenSeparation` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | ONE_HOT | `(B,N,N,1)` | `token_index`, `token_residue_index`, `token_asym_id` |
| `RelativeChain` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | ONE_HOT | `(B,N,N,1)` | `token_entity_id`, `token_sym_id` |
| `RelativeEntity` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | ONE_HOT | `(B,N,N,1)` | `token_entity_id` |
| `TokenCenterDistance` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | ONE_HOT | `(B,N,N,1)` | `atom_gt_coords`, `atom_exists_mask`, `token_centre_atom_index`, `token_exists_mask` |
| `BlockedAtomPairDistances` | `ATOM_PAIR` | IDENTITY | `(B,bl,bl_q,bl_kv,2)` | `atom_ref_pos`, `atom_ref_mask`, `atom_ref_space_uid`, `block_atom_pair_*` |
| `BlockedAtomPairDistogram` | `ATOM_PAIR` | ONE_HOT/RBF | `(B,bl,bl_q,bl_kv,1)` | Same as above |
| `TokenDistanceRestraint` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | RBF | `(B,N,N,1)` | `contact_constraints`, `token_asym_id`, `token_residue_index`, `subchain_id` |
| `TokenPairPocketRestraint` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | RBF | `(B,N,N,1)` | `pocket_constraints`, same token metadata |
| `TokenBondRestraint` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | IDENTITY | `(B,N,N,1)` | `atom_covalent_bond_indices`, `atom_token_index` |
| `DockingRestraintGenerator` | `TOKEN_PAIR` | ONE_HOT | `(B,N,N,1)` | `docking_constraints`, `atom_gt_coords`, `token_asym_id`, `token_entity_type` |
| `MissingChainContact` | `TOKEN` | IDENTITY | `(B,N,1)` | `atom_gt_coords`, `atom_exists_mask`, `token_asym_id`, `atom_token_index` |

Sources: [feature_type.py](chai_lab/data/features/feature_type.py#L1-L17), [base.py](chai_lab/data/features/generators/base.py#L1-L114)

## Integration with the Inference Pipeline

During inference, restraints flow from user-specified `.restraints` files through the parsing and collation layers into the batch dictionary. The `predict_with_restraints.py` example demonstrates the end-to-end path: a CSV file with columns `chainA, res_idxA, chainB, res_idxB, connection_type, confidence, min_distance_angstrom, max_distance_angstrom, comment, restraint_id` is parsed by `parse_pairwise_table`, resolved into `PairwiseInteraction` objects with `PairwiseInteractionType.CONTACT` or `PairwiseInteractionType.POCKET`, then loaded via `load_manual_restraints_for_chai1` into the `RestraintContext`. The collator places these under the `contact_constraints` and `pocket_constraints` batch keys that the respective generators consume.

The **contact** and **pocket** restraint formats differ in their CSV structure: contact restraints specify residue indices on both sides, while pocket restraints leave `res_idxA` empty and specify a chain-level target. Both formats share the same confidence and distance columns.

Sources: [predict_with_restraints.py](examples/restraints/predict_with_restraints.py#L1-L36), [contact.restraints](examples/restraints/contact.restraints#L1-L3), [pocket.restraints](examples/restraints/pocket.restraints#L1-L4), [test_restraints.py](tests/test_restraints.py#L1-L126)

## Next Steps

With the pairwise and restraint feature generators understood, the feature engineering layer is complete. The next pages in the deep-dive track cover how these features are consumed:

- [Feature Embedding and Token Embedding](9-feature-embedding-and-token-embedding) — how raw feature tensors are embedded into the model's hidden dimension
- [Trunk Recycling and Attention](10-trunk-recycling-and-attention) — how pair features flow through the trunk's triangular attention

# Structure Ranking and Scoring



When Chai-1 generates multiple structure candidates through its diffusion sampling process, it must determine which candidate best represents the true biological assembly. The **ranking and scoring system** orchestrates three independent confidence signals—predicted TM-score (pTM), predicted LDDT (pLDDT), and steric clash detection—into a single aggregate score that drives candidate selection. This page explains how these signals are computed, combined, and used to rank structure predictions.

## Architecture Overview

The ranking pipeline sits at the terminal end of the inference workflow, after the confidence head has emitted its logits and the diffusion module has produced atomic coordinates. Every diffusion sample is independently scored, and the highest-scoring candidate is selected as the predicted structure.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Confidence Head
        PAE[PAE Logits] --> PTM[pTM Scores]
        PLDDT_LOG[lddt Logits] --> PLDDT[pLDDT Scores]
    end

    subgraph Diffusion Output
        COORDS[Atom Coordinates] --> CLASH[Clash Detection]
        COORDS --> FRAMES[Valid Frame Masks]
    end

    FRAMES --> PTM
    PTM --> AGG
    CLASH --> AGG
    PLDDT --> AGG

    AGG["Aggregate Score<br/>0.2×pTM + 0.8×ipTM − 100×clashes"]

    AGG --> SORT["Sort Candidates<br/>Descending"]
    SORT --> BEST[Best Structure]

    style AGG fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style BEST fill:#9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```

The entry point is the `rank()` function in [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py), which produces a `SampleRanking` dataclass containing all sub-scores and the aggregate. This is invoked once per diffusion sample inside the inference loop of [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py).

Sources: [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L1-L126), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L938-L975)

## The SampleRanking Data Model

The `SampleRanking` dataclass is the central artifact of the ranking system. It bundles four categories of scores together:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `asym_ids` | `Int[Tensor, "chain"]` | Sorted unique chain identifiers (1-based) |
| `aggregate_score` | `Float[Tensor, "1"]` | Composite ranking score for the entire sample |
| `ptm_scores` | `PTMScores` | pTM and ipTM at complex, chain, and chain-pair levels |
| `clash_scores` | `ClashScores` | Total, inter-chain, and per-chain-pair clash counts |
| `plddt_scores` | `PLDDTScores` | pLDDT at complex, per-chain, and per-atom levels |

After ranking, the `get_scores()` function flattens these into a plain dictionary of NumPy arrays for serialization to `.npz` files, with keys including `aggregate_score`, `ptm`, `iptm`, `per_chain_ptm`, `per_chain_pair_iptm`, `has_inter_chain_clashes`, and `chain_chain_clashes`.

Sources: [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L16-L32), [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L117-L126)

## Aggregate Score Formula

The aggregate score determines which candidate is "best." It is a weighted combination of pTM scores with a harsh penalty for inter-chain steric clashes:

```
aggregate_score = 0.2 × complex_ptm + 0.8 × interface_ptm − 100 × has_inter_chain_clashes
```

The weighting reveals a clear design intent: **interface quality dominates**. The 0.8 weight on `interface_ptm` (ipTM) versus 0.2 on `complex_ptm` reflects that for multi-chain complexes, the quality of chain-chain interactions is far more informative than the overall fold quality. The clash penalty is binary and punitive—any detected inter-chain clash between polymer chains subtracts 100 points, effectively disqualifying candidates with serious steric violations.

> [!TIP]
> The 80/20 weighting between ipTM and pTM means that for single-chain predictions (where ipTM equals pTM), the formula reduces to `pTM − 100×clashes`. For multi-chain complexes, a strong interface score can overcome a mediocre complex-level score, but clashes are always fatal to the ranking.

Sources: [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L99-L103)

## pTM Scoring: Predicted Template Modeling Score

The pTM (predicted Template Model) score estimates how well the predicted structure would align to the true structure, derived from the model's **Predicted Aligned Error (PAE)** logits. The `PTMScores` dataclass captures four granularity levels:

| Score | Shape | Meaning |
|-------|-------|---------|
| `complex_ptm` | `...` | Overall predicted TM-score for the entire complex |
| `interface_ptm` | `...` | Best interface TM-score across all chains |
| `per_chain_ptm` | `... c` | pTM for each individual chain |
| `per_chain_pair_iptm` | `... c c` | ipTM for each ordered chain pair |

### TM-Score d0 Normalization

All pTM computation depends on the TM-score `d0` normalization constant, computed from the number of tokens:

```
d0 = 1.24 × (n_tokens − 15)^(1/3) − 1.8
```

The value is clamped to a minimum of 19 tokens to avoid undefined behavior for very small chains. This follows the standard TM-score normalization convention.

### Core pTM Computation: `_compute_ptm`

The shared computation engine `_compute_ptm()` works as follows:

1. **Bin weighting**: For each PAE bin, compute `1 / (1 + (bin_center / d0)²)`, which assigns higher weight to small predicted errors—the same weighting used in the actual TM-score formula.
2. **Expected pair TM**: Compute `expectation(logits, bin_weights)` using softmax over bins, yielding a per-pair expected TM contribution.
3. **Query-key masking**: Only pairs where the query has a valid frame and both query/key tokens exist contribute.
4. **Aggregation**: Sum weighted expected TM scores per query, normalized by the number of key tokens.
5. **Optimistic selection**: Take `torch.max` over query rows to select the most optimistic alignment—the row whose predicted alignment yields the highest TM-score.

### Complex pTM vs. Interface pTM

The distinction between `complex_ptm` and `interface_ptm` lies in which tokens serve as query vs. key:

- **complex_ptm**: All tokens are both query and key. This measures the overall fold quality of the entire assembly.
- **interface_ptm**: For each chain `c`, tokens in `c` are the query and tokens in all *other* chains are the key. The maximum over chains is returned, capturing the strongest interface signal.

The `per_chain_pair_iptm` extends this to every ordered chain pair (i → j), using tokens in chain `i` as query and tokens in chain `j` as key. For memory efficiency, this is computed in a for-loop rather than batched when the tensor size would exceed 2³² elements.

Sources: [ptm.py](chai_lab/ranking/ptm.py#L1-L222)

## pLDDT Scoring: Predicted Local Distance Difference Test

The pLDDT score estimates the local accuracy of atomic positions, derived from the model's **lddt logits**. Unlike pTM which operates at the token level on PAE, pLDDT operates at the atom level on predicted distance errors.

The `PLDDTScores` dataclass provides three granularity levels:

| Score | Shape | Meaning |
|-------|-------|---------|
| `complex_plddt` | `...` | Masked mean pLDDT over all atoms |
| `per_chain_plddt` | `... c` | Masked mean pLDDT per chain |
| `per_atom_plddt` | `... a` | Per-atom pLDDT expectations |

The computation is straightforward: `expectation(logits, bin_centers)` applies softmax to the logits and computes the weighted sum with bin center values as weights. For the complex-level score, a `masked_mean` averages over all valid atoms. For per-chain scores, the chain masks from `get_chain_masks_and_asyms()` are applied before averaging.

Note that pLDDT scores are **not** part of the aggregate ranking formula—they are reported alongside the ranking for diagnostic purposes and written as B-factors (scaled to 0–100) in the output CIF files.

Sources: [plddt.py](chai_lab/ranking/plddt.py#L1-L82), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L978-L979)

## Clash Detection: Steric Violation Scoring

Clash detection identifies atoms that are unphysically close to each other, a critical quality check especially for multi-chain interfaces. The `ClashScores` dataclass captures:

| Score | Shape | Meaning |
|-------|-------|---------|
| `total_clashes` | `...` | Total clash count (intra + inter, double-counting corrected) |
| `total_inter_chain_clashes` | `...` | Sum of clashes across all chain pairs |
| `chain_chain_clashes` | `... n_chains n_chains` | Per chain-pair clash matrix |
| `has_inter_chain_clashes` | `...` | Boolean: whether any polymer chain pair has problematic clashes |

### Pairwise Distance Computation

The core `_compute_clashes()` function computes all pairwise atom distances via `cdist`, then flags any pair where: (1) both atoms exist, (2) they are not the same atom, and (3) their distance is below `clash_threshold` (default **1.1 Å**).

### Chain-Level Aggregation

Raw atom-atom clashes are aggregated into a chain-chain matrix using `scatter_add_` operations: first mapping atoms to their chain (via `atom_asym_id`), then accumulating clashes per chain pair. The diagonal (intra-chain clashes) is compensated for double-counting by dividing by 2, and the off-diagonal (inter-chain) is similarly halved to account for matrix symmetry.

### Inter-Chain Clash Criteria

A chain pair is flagged as having inter-chain clashes if **any** of these conditions hold:

1. **Absolute count**: The pair has ≥ `max_clashes` (default 100) clashes
2. **Relative ratio**: Clashes exceed `max_clash_ratio` (default 0.5) of the smaller chain's atom count
3. **Polymer restriction**: Both chains must be polymer types (Protein, RNA, DNA, or Polymer Hybrid)

> [!TIP]
> The polymer-only filter means that ligand-polymer or ligand-ligand clashes do not contribute to the `has_inter_chain_clashes` flag, even though they are counted in `chain_chain_clashes`. This prevents small-molecule proximity from penalizing the aggregate score.

Sources: [clashes.py](chai_lab/ranking/clashes.py#L1-L164)

## Frame Computation for pTM Validity

The `frames.py` module provides the `valid_frames_mask` that gates which tokens participate in pTM computation. A token can contribute to pTM only if it has a well-defined local reference frame—three non-collinear atoms that define an orientation.

The `get_frames_and_mask()` function combines two sources of frame definitions:

1. **Backbone frames**: Pre-defined N-Cα-C frames for standard amino acid residues, provided via `token_backbone_frame_mask` and `token_backbone_frame_index`
2. **Single-atom frames**: For tokens without backbone frames (e.g., ligand atoms), the function constructs frames by finding the two nearest atoms within the same residue and chain, then checking for collinearity

The collinearity check uses `abc_is_colinear()`, which computes the angle at atom B in the A-B-C triplet. If the angle is less than 25° or greater than 155°, the triplet is deemed collinear and the frame is rejected. This ensures that only geometrically meaningful frames influence the pTM calculation.

Sources: [frames.py](chai_lab/ranking/frames.py#L1-L173)

## Integration in the Inference Pipeline

The ranking system is invoked inside `run_folding_on_context()` in [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py), after the confidence head has produced its logits for each diffusion sample. The call sequence for each sample is:

1. **Frame computation**: `get_frames_and_mask()` determines which tokens have valid reference frames
2. **Ranking**: `rank()` computes the full `SampleRanking` from atom coordinates, token metadata, PAE logits, and lddt logits
3. **Output**: The aggregate score is logged, the CIF file is written with pLDDT as B-factors, and scores are saved to `.npz`

After all samples are scored, the `StructureCandidates.sorted()` method reorders candidates by descending `aggregate_score`, making the first candidate the model's best prediction. When multiple trunk samples are used, `StructureCandidates.concat()` merges candidates from different trunk runs before sorting.

```
Score=0.8241, writing output to .../pred.model_idx_0.cif
Score=0.7903, writing output to .../pred.model_idx_1.cif
...
```

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L938-L1004), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L53-L92)

## Shared Ranking Utilities

The `utils.py` module provides foundational operations used across all scoring submodules:

| Function | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `get_chain_masks_and_asyms()` | Extracts per-chain boolean masks and sorted unique asym IDs from token/atom tensors |
| `get_interface_mask()` | Identifies token pairs across chains within an interface distance threshold |
| `expectation()` | Computes softmax-weighted expectation: `softmax(logits) · weights` |
| `num_atoms_per_chain()` | Counts valid atoms per chain using chain masks |
| `chain_is_polymer()` | Determines if each chain contains polymer entity types (Protein, RNA, DNA, Polymer Hybrid) |

The `expectation()` function is particularly critical—it is the shared mechanism by which both pTM and pLDDT convert categorical logit distributions into scalar scores. For pLDDT, weights are bin center values; for pTM, weights are TM-score bin weights `1/(1+(d/d0)²)`.

Sources: [utils.py](chai_lab/ranking/utils.py#L1-L87)

## Score Output Files

Each diffusion sample produces two output files in the output directory:

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `pred.model_idx_{N}.cif` | Atomic coordinates with pLDDT (0–100 scale) as B-factors |
| `scores.model_idx_{N}.npz` | NumPy archive with all ranking scores as arrays |

The `.npz` file contains the following keys, as produced by `get_scores()`:

- `aggregate_score` — the composite ranking score
- `ptm` — complex-level pTM
- `iptm` — interface pTM
- `per_chain_ptm` — per-chain pTM array
- `per_chain_pair_iptm` — chain-pair ipTM matrix
- `has_inter_chain_clashes` — boolean clash flag
- `chain_chain_clashes` — per chain-pair clash count matrix

Sources: [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L117-L126), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L985-L988)

## Next Steps

The aggregate score relies on three distinct metric systems, each with its own mathematical foundations and implementation nuances. To deepen your understanding:

- **[pTM, pLDDT, and Clash Metrics](23-ptm-plddt-and-clash-metrics)** — detailed mathematical derivations and interpretation guidelines for each metric
- **[CIF Output and Chain Naming](22-cif-output-and-chain-naming)** — how ranked predictions are materialized into structural files
- **[Confidence Prediction and Scoring](12-confidence-prediction-and-scoring)** — the upstream module that produces the PAE and lddt logits consumed by ranking

# CIF Output and Chain Naming



Chai-1 writes predicted structures in **ModelCIF** format—a standardized extension of mmCIF designed for computational models. The CIF output subsystem is responsible for translating raw coordinate tensors, token-level metadata, and per-atom confidence scores into a fully compliant `.cif` file with correct chain identifiers, entity grouping, chemical component annotations, and embedded quality metrics. This page explains how chain names are assigned, how entities are deduplicated, how different biomolecule types are serialized, and how the output pipeline integrates with the broader inference workflow.

## From Inference to CIF: The Output Pipeline

The CIF writing step is the final stage of the inference pipeline. After diffusion denoising produces atomic coordinates and the confidence head emits pLDDT/PAE/PDE logits, the system iterates over each diffusion sample, computes ranking scores, and writes one `.cif` file per sample. The entry point is `save_to_cif`, which orchestrates coordinate rearrangement, PDB context reconstruction, and delegation to the lower-level writer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Diffusion Denoising<br/>(atom_pos tensor)"] --> B["Confidence Prediction<br/>(pLDDT, PAE, PDE)"]
    B --> C["Per-Sample Loop"]
    C --> D["rank() → SampleRanking"]
    D --> E["save_to_cif()"]
    E --> F["pdb_context_from_batch()"]
    F --> G["new_context_to_cif_atoms()"]
    G --> H["get_chains_metadata()"]
    H --> I["Entity Deduplication<br/>& AsymUnit Creation"]
    I --> J["Atom Iteration &<br/>model.Atom Creation"]
    J --> K["pLDDT QA Metrics<br/>(non-ligand only)"]
    K --> L["modelcif.System →<br/>dumper.write()"]
```

The `save_to_cif` function accepts the predicted coordinates (shape `[1, n_atoms, 3]`), the full output batch dictionary, the output path, a mapping of asym IDs to entity names, and optional B-factor (pLDDT) tensors. It rearranges the batch dimension away, reconstructs a `PDBContext` from the batch dictionary, and passes everything to `new_context_to_cif_atoms` for the actual serialization. The output directory is created automatically if it does not exist. [save_to_cif](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L144-L158), [call site in inference](chai_lab/chai1.py#L1034-L1049)

## Chain Naming: Auto-Generated vs. FASTA-Derived

Chain naming is controlled by the `fasta_names_as_cif_chains` flag in `run_inference` (exposed as `--fasta-names-as-cif-chains` in the CLI). This flag determines whether chains receive sequential auto-generated identifiers or retain the entity names from the input FASTA file.

### Auto-Generated Chain Letters

When `fasta_names_as_cif_chains=False` (the default), the system uses `get_chain_letter()` to map each 1-indexed `asym_id` to a string from a structured vocabulary:

| Priority | Pattern | Range | Count |
|----------|---------|-------|-------|
| 1 | Single uppercase | A–Z | 26 |
| 2 | Single lowercase | a–z | 26 |
| 3 | Double letter | AA–zz | 2,704 |

The vocabulary is built as `_CHAIN_VOCAB`: first all 52 single-letter codes (A–Z then a–z), then all 52×52 two-letter combinations in lexicographic order. This supports up to **2,808 unique chains**—far beyond typical use cases. The mapping is strictly 1-indexed: `asym_id=1` → `"A"`, `asym_id=2` → `"B"`, ..., `asym_id=27` → `"a"`, `asym_id=53` → `"AA"`. [_CHAIN_VOCAB and get_chain_letter](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L39-L47)

### FASTA-Derived Chain Names

When `fasta_names_as_cif_chains=True`, each chain is named using the `entity_name` field from the corresponding FASTA header. This is critical for restraint workflows where restraints reference chains by name—using auto-generated names would break the correspondence. The system validates that entity names are unique before proceeding with inference. [validation in run_folding_on_context](chai_lab/chai1.py#L621-L632)

The actual name assignment happens at the `save_to_cif` call site, where a dictionary comprehension builds the `asym_entity_names` mapping:

```python
asym_entity_names={
    i: (
        chain.entity_data.entity_name
        if entity_names_as_chain_names_in_output_cif
        else get_chain_letter(i)
    )
    for i, chain in enumerate(feature_context.chains, start=1)
}
```

This dictionary flows into `get_chains_metadata`, where each `AsymUnit` receives its `id` and `details` from the entity name. [asym_entity_names construction](chai_lab/chai1.py#L1041-L1049)

## Entity Deduplication and Chemical Component Mapping

Not every chain becomes a distinct entity in the CIF file. The `get_chains_metadata` function implements **entity deduplication**: chains with identical sequences and entity types share a single `Entity` object. This mirrors how the PDB groups identical sequences under one entity ID.

### Deduplication Key Construction

The entity key is computed differently based on entity type:

| Entity Type | Entity Key | Deduplication Behavior |
|-------------|-----------|----------------------|
| PROTEIN | `(type, *sequence)` | Identical protein sequences share one entity |
| RNA | `(type, *sequence)` | Identical RNA sequences share one entity |
| DNA | `(type, *sequence)` | Identical DNA sequences share one entity |
| LIGAND | `(type, asym_id)` | **Each ligand is always a unique entity** |
| MANUAL_GLYCAN | `(type, *sequence)` | Identical glycan sequences share one entity |

Ligands are never deduplicated because two different SMILES strings may represent the same molecule, and the system cannot reliably determine equivalence. Each ligand therefore gets its own Entity with a unique key incorporating its `asym_id`. [entity_key construction](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L93-L98)

### Chemical Component Type Mapping

Each residue in an entity is represented by an IHM `ChemComponent` subclass, selected by the `_to_chem_component` function based on entity type:

| Entity Type | IHM Class | Canonical Code Handling |
|-------------|-----------|------------------------|
| PROTEIN | `LPeptideChemComp` | 3-letter → 1-letter via `restype_3to1` + gemmi lookup |
| DNA | `DNAChemComp` | Strips leading "D" (e.g., DA→A for canonical) |
| RNA | `RNAChemComp` | Uses 3-letter code as-is |
| LIGAND | `NonPolymerChemComp` | ID = residue name + asym_id suffix |
| MANUAL_GLYCAN | `SaccharideChemComp` | Uses 3-letter residue name |

For proteins, the canonical one-letter code is resolved through gemmi's tabulated residue database, ensuring correct handling of non-standard amino acids. For DNA, the convention follows wwPDB practice where the canonical code drops the "D" prefix (e.g., "DA" → "A"). [_to_chem_component](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L120-L139)

## Atom Serialization and Ligand Handling

The core serialization loop in `new_context_to_cif_atoms` iterates over every atom, skipping those masked by `atom_exists_mask`. For each surviving atom, it extracts coordinates, resolves the parent chain's `AsymUnit`, determines the atom name, and creates a `model.Atom` instance.

### Ligand Atom Name Disambiguation

Ligand residues present a naming challenge: multiple atoms may share the same element-based name (e.g., two carbon atoms both named "C"). The system solves this with a counter-based suffix: for each `(asym_id, atom_name)` pair in a ligand, a running count is appended, producing names like `C_1`, `C_2`, `O_1`. Non-ligand atoms retain their standard PDB names (CA, CB, N, etc.). The `het` flag is set to `True` for all ligand atoms, marking them as HETATM entries. [ligand atom naming](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L206-L213)

### Residue Numbering

Residue sequence IDs in the output CIF are **1-indexed**, converted from the 0-indexed internal representation by adding 1: `seq_id = int(token_residue_index) + 1`. This follows mmCIF convention where residue numbering starts at 1. [seq_id computation](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L222)

## pLDDT Quality Metrics: Dual Representation

Chai-1 writes pLDDT confidence values in two complementary ways within the same CIF file:

1. **B-factor field (`biso`)**: Every atom receives its per-atom pLDDT score (scaled to 0–100) as the B-factor value. This enables immediate visualization in molecular viewers like PyMOL and ChimeraX, which color structures by B-factor.

2. **ModelCIF QA metric**: For non-ligand chains, token-centre pLDDT values are attached as `_LocalPLDDT` QA metrics at the residue level. The token centre is CA for proteins and C1' for nucleic acids. This provides the standardized ModelCIF representation that programmatic tools can parse. Ligands are excluded from QA metrics because they lack a meaningful token-centre convention. [pLDDT as biso and QA metric](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L224-L244), [_LocalPLDDT class](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L31-L34)

> [!TIP]
> When consuming Chai-1 CIF output programmatically, prefer the ModelCIF QA metrics for residue-level pLDDT (they are explicitly per-residue and exclude ligand noise) and the B-factor field for atom-level visualization. The two representations use the same underlying scores but differ in granularity and scope.

## PDBContext: The Structural Metadata Backbone

The `PDBContext` dataclass serves as the bridge between the batch tensor dictionary produced during inference and the CIF serialization logic. It extracts and organizes all token-level and atom-level metadata needed for CIF writing:

| Field | Level | Purpose in CIF Writing |
|-------|-------|----------------------|
| `token_asym_id` | Token | Maps tokens → chains |
| `token_residue_index` | Token | Residue numbering (seq_id) |
| `token_entity_type` | Token | Chemical component selection |
| `token_residue_names` | Token | Sequence reconstruction |
| `token_centre_atom_index` | Token | pLDDT QA metric anchoring |
| `atom_token_index` | Atom | Maps atoms → parent tokens |
| `atom_ref_element` | Atom | Element symbol (type_symbol) |
| `atom_exists_mask` | Atom | Skip masked atoms |
| `atom_ref_name_chars` | Atom | Atom name resolution |

The dataclass provides two cached properties: `token_res_names_to_string` (converts encoded residue names to strings) and `asym_id2entity_type` (builds a mapping from chain ID to entity type, excluding padding asym_id=0). The `pdb_context_from_batch` factory function extracts the first batch element (index `[0]`) from each tensor and validates that all tensors reside on CPU. [PDBContext](chai_lab/data/io/pdb_utils.py#L15-L64)

## ModelCIF Assembly Structure

The final CIF file follows the ModelCIF hierarchical structure:

```mermaid
flowchart BT
    subgraph System
        MG["ModelGroup<br/>name='pred'"]
    end
    subgraph MG
        M["AbInitioModel<br/>name='pred_model_1'"]
    end
    subgraph M
        A1["Atom objects<br/>(x, y, z, biso, het)"]
        QA["_LocalPLDDT<br/>QA metrics"]
    end
    subgraph Assembly["Assembly<br/>name='Assembly 1'"]
        AU1["AsymUnit<br/>Chain A"]
        AU2["AsymUnit<br/>Chain B"]
    end
    subgraph AU1
        E1["Entity<br/>(shared sequence)"]
    end
    subgraph AU2
        E2["Entity<br/>(unique ligand)"]
    end
    M --> Assembly
    AU1 --> E1
    AU2 --> E2
```

The system title is set to `"Chai-1 predicted structure"` and the author is `"Chai Discovery team"`. Each diffusion sample produces one model within a single model group named `"pred"`. The assembly encompasses all asymmetric units (chains), and entities are shared across chains where deduplication applies. [ModelCIF system construction](chai_lab/data/io/cif_utils.py#L246-L255)

## Output File Naming and Multiple Samples

For each diffusion sample, two files are written to the output directory:

| File | Format | Content |
|------|--------|---------|
| `pred.model_idx_{idx}.cif` | ModelCIF | Atomic coordinates, chain metadata, pLDDT metrics |
| `scores.model_idx_{idx}.npz` | NumPy archive | Ranking scores from `SampleRanking` |

The sample index `idx` ranges from 0 to `num_diffn_samples - 1`. When multiple trunk samples are requested (`num_trunk_samples > 1`), outputs are further organized into `trunk_{trunk_idx}/` subdirectories. The aggregate score is printed to stdout for each sample. [output file writing](chai_lab/chai1.py#L1029-L1052)

> [!TIP]
> The `StructureCandidates` object returned by `run_inference` contains all CIF paths, ranking data, and confidence tensors. Its `.sorted()` method reorders candidates by aggregate score (descending), making it straightforward to select the top prediction: `candidates.sorted().cif_paths[0]`.

- [Structure Ranking and Scoring](21-structure-ranking-and-scoring) — How aggregate scores are computed before CIF writing
