# pTM, pLDDT, and Clash Metrics



Chai1's confidence and quality assessment system produces three complementary metric families—**pTM** (predicted Template Modeling score), **pLDDT** (predicted Local Distance Difference Test), and **Clash** metrics—that together power the aggregate ranking of structure candidates. These metrics are computed downstream of the confidence prediction head and operate on distinct signal types: pTM interprets the Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) distribution through the TM-score lens, pLDDT extracts per-atom localization confidence from the LDDT logits, and clash detection performs geometric verification on the final atomic coordinates. The aggregate score that determines the best candidate is a weighted formula: `0.2 × pTM + 0.8 × ipTM − 100 × has_inter_chain_clashes`, heavily prioritizing interface quality and penalizing steric violations.

Sources: [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L88-L93), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L897-L903)

## Metric Architecture Overview

The three metric modules share a common architectural pattern: each exposes a `get_scores()` entry point that returns a typed dataclass, each decomposes scores into complex-level, per-chain, and per-chain-pair granularities, and each relies on shared utilities in `ranking/utils.py` for chain mask construction and expectation computation. The ranking orchestrator in `rank.py` calls all three `get_scores()` functions, assembles the `SampleRanking` dataclass, and computes the aggregate score.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Confidence Head
        PAE["PAE Logits<br>... n n bins"]
        LDDT["LDDT Logits<br>... a bins"]
        COORDS["Atom Coords<br>... a 3"]
    end

    PAE --> PTM_MODULE["ptm.py<br>get_scores()"]
    LDDT --> PLDDT_MODULE["plddt.py<br>get_scores()"]
    COORDS --> CLASH_MODULE["clashes.py<br>get_scores()"]

    PTM_MODULE --> PTM_SCORES["PTMScores<br>• complex_ptm<br>• interface_ptm<br>• per_chain_ptm<br>• per_chain_pair_iptm"]
    PLDDT_MODULE --> PLDDT_SCORES["PLDDTScores<br>• complex_plddt<br>• per_atom_plddt<br>• per_chain_plddt"]
    CLASH_MODULE --> CLASH_SCORES["ClashScores<br>• total_clashes<br>• total_inter_chain_clashes<br>• chain_chain_clashes<br>• has_inter_chain_clashes"]

    PTM_SCORES --> AGG["Aggregate Score<br>0.2·pTM + 0.8·ipTM − 100·has_clashes"]
    CLASH_SCORES --> AGG
    AGG --> SR["SampleRanking"]

    subgraph Shared Utilities
        UTILS["utils.py<br>• expectation()<br>• get_chain_masks_and_asyms()<br>• num_atoms_per_chain()<br>• chain_is_polymer()"]
    end

    PTM_MODULE -.-> UTILS
    PLDDT_MODULE -.-> UTILS
    CLASH_MODULE -.-> UTILS
```

> [!TIP]
> The aggregate score's 0.2/0.8 weighting between pTM and ipTM means that for multi-chain complexes, interface quality dominates the ranking. For single-chain predictions where ipTM equals pTM, the formula reduces to `pTM − 100·has_clashes`, making clash detection the sole differentiator when present.

Sources: [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L50-L93), [utils.py](chai_lab/ranking/utils.py#L1-L87)

## pTM: Predicted Template Modeling Score

The pTM metric translates the model's PAE (Predicted Aligned Error) distribution into a TM-score estimate. The TM-score is a length-dependent measure of structural similarity that ranges from 0 to 1, where values above 0.5 suggest correct fold topology. Chai1 computes four pTM variants, each querying the PAE logits against different subsets of tokens to measure structural confidence at different scopes.

### The d0 Normalization Function

The foundational computation is the TM-score **d0** parameter, which scales the distance penalty by the number of tokens:

```
d0(n) = 1.24 × (n − 15)^(1/3) − 1.8
```

This formula, clamped to a minimum of 19 tokens, produces a distance threshold that grows sublinearly with sequence length—longer chains tolerate larger absolute deviations. The d0 value converts raw PAE distances into the TM-score's normalized distance metric.

Sources: [ptm.py](chai_lab/ranking/ptm.py#L28-L31)

### Core Computation: `_compute_ptm`

The internal `_compute_ptm` function implements the pairwise TM-score expectation. It takes PAE logits of shape `(... n n bins)`, a set of query tokens, a set of key tokens, and bin centers representing distance values. The computation proceeds as:

1. **Bin weighting**: Each distance bin center is weighted by `1 / (1 + (d/d0)²)`, the TM-score distance weighting function applied element-wise to all bins.
2. **Expected TM per pair**: The softmax of PAE logits produces per-bin probabilities; multiplying by bin weights and summing yields the expected TM contribution for each query-key token pair.
3. **Query-level aggregation**: Each query token's TM score is the sum of its pairwise expected TM values divided by the number of key tokens.
4. **Optimistic selection**: The final pTM is the **maximum** query-level TM score across all queries, selecting the most favorable alignment orientation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    PAE[PAE Logits<br>softmax] --> PROBS[Per-bin Probabilities]
    BINS[Bin Centers d] --> W["Weight: 1/&lpar;1+&lpar;d/d<sub>0</sub>&rpar;<sup>2</sup>&rpar;"]
    PROBS --> E_TM["Expected TM<br>Σ prob·weight"]
    W --> E_TM
    E_TM --> Q_TM["Query TM<br>Σ per-key / n_keys"]
    Q_TM --> MAX["max over queries<br>→ pTM"]
```

> [!TIP]
> The `max` operation in step 4 is critical: pTM reports the best-case alignment rather than an average. This makes pTM an optimistic estimate of how well the predicted structure would align to the true structure under the most favorable superposition.

Sources: [ptm.py](chai_lab/ranking/ptm.py#L34-L66)

### pTM Variants

| Variant | Query Scope | Key Scope | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| **complex_ptm** | All tokens with valid frames | All tokens | Global structural confidence for the entire complex |
| **interface_ptm (ipTM)** | One chain at a time | All tokens *outside* that chain | Best inter-chain alignment quality |
| **per_chain_ptm** | One chain at a time | Same chain | Per-chain internal fold confidence |
| **per_chain_pair_iptm** | One chain at a time | All other chains individually | Pairwise interface quality matrix |

**complex_ptm** uses the simplest query/key configuration: all existing tokens with valid frames query against all existing tokens. This measures the overall confidence in the entire structural arrangement.

**interface_ptm** restricts each query chain to key tokens from *other* chains only, then takes the maximum over all chains. This isolates the confidence in inter-chain docking arrangements, which is the most informative signal for multi-chain complexes. The formula: `ipTM = max_c pTM(query=c, key=∁\{c})`.

**per_chain_ptm** constrains both query and key to the same chain, measuring how confidently each individual chain is folded regardless of inter-chain arrangement.

**per_chain_pair_iptm** computes a full chain×chain matrix where entry (i,j) is the pTM when chain i queries against chain j. This is the most granular interface metric. For memory efficiency, it defaults to a loop implementation over chains rather than batched computation, switching to batched mode only when the total tensor size is below 2³² elements.

Sources: [ptm.py](chai_lab/ranking/ptm.py#L69-L186)

### The `PTMScores` Dataclass

The `get_scores()` function assembles all four variants into a single `PTMScores` dataclass:

```python
@dataclass
class PTMScores:
    complex_ptm: Float[Tensor, "..."]           # scalar
    interface_ptm: Float[Tensor, "..."]          # scalar
    per_chain_ptm: Float[Tensor, "... c"]        # one value per chain
    per_chain_pair_iptm: Float[Tensor, "... c c"]  # chain × chain matrix
```

The per_chain_pair_iptm matrix is asymmetric: entry (i,j) reflects how well chain i aligns relative to chain j, which differs from (j,i) when chains have different sizes.

Sources: [ptm.py](chai_lab/ranking/ptm.py#L14-L24), [ptm.py](chai_lab/ranking/ptm.py#L189-L222)

## pLDDT: Predicted Local Distance Difference Test

The pLDDT metric estimates per-atom local structural accuracy by computing the expected value of the LDDT score from the model's binned logits. Unlike pTM which operates on token-level PAE, pLDDT operates at atom resolution and measures the confidence that local inter-atomic distance neighborhoods are correct.

### Core Computation

The computation is elegantly simple: apply softmax to the LDDT logits to get per-bin probabilities, then compute the weighted sum using bin center values as weights. This yields the expected LDDT score per atom.

```python
def plddt(logits, mask, bin_centers, per_residue=False):
    expectations = rank_utils.expectation(logits, bin_centers)  # softmax + weighted sum
    if per_residue:
        return expectations           # per-atom scores
    else:
        return masked_mean(mask, expectations, dim=-1)  # scalar average
```

The `expectation()` utility in `ranking/utils.py` performs `softmax(logits) · weights`, summing over the bin dimension. For pLDDT, the weights are simply the bin center values themselves (not the TM-score weighting used in pTM), producing a value proportional to the expected distance accuracy.

Sources: [plddt.py](chai_lab/ranking/plddt.py#L26-L34), [utils.py](chai_lab/ranking/utils.py#L43-L49)

### pLDDT Variants

| Variant | Granularity | Shape | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| **complex_plddt** | Scalar (masked mean) | `...` | Overall structure quality |
| **per_atom_plddt** | Per-atom | `... a` | Atom-level confidence mapping |
| **per_chain_plddt** | Per-chain (masked mean per chain) | `... c` | Chain-level quality comparison |

**per_chain_plddt** works by constructing a chain mask tensor of shape `(... c a)` via `get_chain_masks_and_asyms()`, then repeating the logits across the chain dimension and computing the masked mean for each chain independently.

### Bin Center Derivation

In the inference pipeline (`chai1.py`), the LDDT bin centers are derived as:

```python
_bin_centers(0, 1, plddt_logits.shape[-1])
```

This creates `no_bins` evenly-spaced centers via `torch.linspace(0, 1, 2*no_bins+1)[1::2]`, placing each center at the midpoint of its bin. The range [0, 1] corresponds to the normalized LDDT scale. When reported in the `StructureCandidates` dataclass, per-atom pLDDT is converted to per-token by averaging within tokens, and the raw expectation values are stored for downstream use.

Sources: [plddt.py](chai_lab/ranking/plddt.py#L37-L82), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L919-L932)

### The `PLDDTScores` Dataclass

```python
@dataclass
class PLDDTScores:
    complex_plddt: Float[Tensor, "..."]       # scalar average
    per_atom_plddt: Float[Tensor, "... a"]    # per-atom scores
    per_chain_plddt: Float[Tensor, "... c"]   # per-chain averages
```

Sources: [plddt.py](chai_lab/ranking/plddt.py#L14-L22)

## Clash Metrics: Steric Quality Assessment

Clash metrics perform post-hoc geometric validation on the predicted atomic coordinates, detecting steric clashes that indicate physically implausible structures. Unlike pTM and pLDDT which interpret model confidence outputs, clash detection is a deterministic geometric computation on the final coordinates.

### Core Clash Detection: `_compute_clashes`

The foundational operation computes a boolean matrix of atom pairs that are too close:

1. **Pairwise distances**: Compute all pairwise Euclidean distances via `cdist(atom_coords)`.
2. **Valid pair mask**: Exclude self-interactions (diagonal) and pairs where either atom is masked out.
3. **Threshold**: Mark a pair as clashing if `distance < clash_threshold` (default **1.1 Å**).

The result is a boolean matrix of shape `(... a a)` indicating all clashing atom pairs.

Sources: [clashes.py](chai_lab/ranking/clashes.py#L29-L41)

### From Atom-Atom to Chain-Chain Clashes

The `get_scores()` function aggregates atom-atom clashes into chain-level statistics through a series of scatter operations:

1. **Build `clashes_a_a`**: Boolean → int32 matrix of atom-atom clashes.
2. **Scatter to `clashes_a_chain`**: For each atom, sum clashes grouped by chain identity (using `atom_asym_id` shifted from 1-based to 0-based).
3. **Scatter to `clashes_chain_chain`**: Aggregate atom-chain clashes into a chain×chain matrix.
4. **Compensate doubling**: The diagonal (intra-chain) entries are counted twice due to symmetry, so divide by `(1 + I)` where I is the identity matrix—this halves diagonal entries while leaving off-diagonal unchanged.
5. **Extract inter-chain**: Zero out the diagonal to isolate inter-chain clashes, then sum and divide by 2 for symmetry.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    AA["clashes_a_a<br>(a × a)"] --> AC["clashes_a_chain<br>(a × c)<br>scatter_add by asym_id"]
    AC --> CC["clashes_chain_chain<br>(c × c)<br>scatter_add by asym_id"]
    CC --> DIAG["Diagonal compensation<br>÷ (1 + I)"]
    DIAG --> TOTAL["total_clashes<br>Σ / 2"]
    DIAG --> INTER["inter_chain_chain<br>diagonal zeroed"]
    INTER --> INTER_TOTAL["total_inter_chain_clashes<br>Σ / 2"]
    INTER --> HAS["has_inter_chain_clashes<br>via threshold logic"]
```

Sources: [clashes.py](chai_lab/ranking/clashes.py#L72-L138)

### Inter-Chain Clash Determination: `has_inter_chain_clashes`

The boolean `has_inter_chain_clashes` flag uses a dual-criteria threshold to determine whether inter-chain clashes are significant enough to flag the entire structure:

| Criterion | Threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Absolute count** | ≥ `max_clashes` (default 100) | Large absolute number of clashes regardless of chain size |
| **Relative ratio** | ≥ `max_clash_ratio` (default 0.5) of smaller chain's atom count | Disproportionate clashes for small chains |
| **Polymer restriction** | Both chains must be polymers (protein/RNA/DNA/hybrid) | Ignore clashes involving ligands or water |

A chain pair is flagged if **either** the absolute count or the relative ratio is exceeded, and **both** chains are polymers. The final `has_inter_chain_clashes` is `any()` reduction over all chain pairs—meaning even a single problematic polymer-polymer interface triggers the flag.

> [!TIP]
> The polymer-only restriction means that ligand chain clashes never trigger the penalty. This is intentional: ligands are often in tight binding pockets where many atoms are close to the protein surface, which would produce false-positive clash flags under the same thresholds used for polymer-polymer interfaces.

Sources: [clashes.py](chai_lab/ranking/clashes.py#L44-L70), [utils.py](chai_lab/ranking/utils.py#L71-L87)

### The `ClashScores` Dataclass

```python
@dataclass
class ClashScores:
    total_clashes: Int[Tensor, "..."]                    # all clashes (intra + inter)
    total_inter_chain_clashes: Int[Tensor, "..."]        # inter-chain only
    chain_chain_clashes: Int[Tensor, "... n_chains n_chains"]  # per-pair matrix
    has_inter_chain_clashes: Bool[Tensor, "..."]         # penalty flag
```

Sources: [clashes.py](chai_lab/ranking/clashes.py#L14-L27)

## Aggregate Score Composition

The aggregate score in `rank()` combines pTM and clash metrics into a single scalar:

```python
aggregate_score = (
    0.2 * ptm_scores.complex_ptm
    + 0.8 * ptm_scores.interface_ptm
    - 100 * clash_scores.has_inter_chain_clashes.float()
)
```

The weighting scheme has important implications:

| Scenario | Score Behavior | Practical Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-chain, good interface, no clashes | ~0.8 × ipTM dominates | ipTM is the primary quality signal |
| Multi-chain, poor interface, no clashes | Score drops with ipTM | Interface quality determines rank |
| Any complex with inter-chain clashes | −100 penalty applied | Clash-bearing structures sink to bottom |
| Single-chain structure | 0.2×pTM + 0.8×pTM = pTM | Reduces to complex_ptm alone |

The `get_scores()` function converts the `SampleRanking` dataclass to a flat numpy dictionary for downstream consumption, exposing: `aggregate_score`, `ptm`, `iptm`, `per_chain_ptm`, `per_chain_pair_iptm`, `has_inter_chain_clashes`, and `chain_chain_clashes`.

Sources: [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L88-L126)

## Integration with the Inference Pipeline

The metrics are computed after the confidence head produces its three output logit tensors. In `run_folding_on_context()`, the confidence head is invoked per diffusion sample, producing `pae_logits`, `pde_logits`, and `plddt_logits`. These are converted to score tensors via softmax-einsum with bin centers, then fed into `rank()` along with atom coordinates and token metadata.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CH as Confidence Head
    participant INF as Inference Pipeline
    participant RANK as rank()
    participant OUT as StructureCandidates

    CH->>INF: pae_logits, pde_logits, plddt_logits
    INF->>INF: softmax_einsum → pae_scores, pde_scores, plddt_scores
    INF->>INF: get_frames_and_mask()
    INF->>RANK: atom_coords, masks, logits, bin_centers
    RANK->>RANK: ptm.get_scores(pae_logits, ...)
    RANK->>RANK: plddt.get_scores(lddt_logits, ...)
    RANK->>RANK: clashes.get_scores(atom_coords, ...)
    RANK->>RANK: aggregate_score = 0.2·pTM + 0.8·ipTM − 100·clashes
    RANK->>OUT: SampleRanking dataclass
    OUT->>OUT: sorted() by aggregate_score descending
```

The PAE and PDE bin centers both use `_bin_centers(0.0, 32.0, 64)` (64 bins spanning 0–32 Å), while LDDT uses `_bin_centers(0, 1, n_bins)` spanning the normalized [0, 1] range. Frame computation via `get_frames_and_mask()` provides the `valid_frames_mask` that determines which tokens participate in pTM calculations—tokens without valid local frames (e.g., isolated atoms without neighbors for frame construction) are excluded from the alignment search.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L897-L980), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L865-L895)

## Comparative Summary

| Aspect | pTM | pLDDT | Clash |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Input Signal** | PAE logits (token×token) | LDDT logits (per-atom) | Atom coordinates |
| **Operates On** | Token pairs | Individual atoms | Atom pairs |
| **Score Range** | [0, 1] | [0, 1] (normalized) | Non-negative integers |
| **Key Formula** | TM-score weighting `1/(1+(d/d₀)²)` | Bin center expectation | Euclidean distance < threshold |
| **Chain Awareness** | Full asymmetry decomposition | Per-chain averaging | Chain scatter + polymer filter |
| **Primary Granularity** | Chain pair matrix | Per-atom | Chain pair matrix |
| **Role in Ranking** | 20% complex + 80% interface | Not in aggregate score | −100 penalty flag |
| **Module** | [ptm.py](chai_lab/ranking/ptm.py) | [plddt.py](chai_lab/ranking/plddt.py) | [clashes.py](chai_lab/ranking/clashes.py) |

Note that pLDDT does **not** contribute to the aggregate ranking score despite being computed and stored—it serves as a per-atom confidence map useful for visualization and local quality assessment, but the ranking decision is driven entirely by pTM/ipTM and clash penalties.

Sources: [ptm.py](chai_lab/ranking/ptm.py#L1-L222), [plddt.py](chai_lab/ranking/plddt.py#L1-L82), [clashes.py](chai_lab/ranking/clashes.py#L1-L164), [rank.py](chai_lab/ranking/rank.py#L1-L126)

## Next Steps

- For how these metrics feed into the broader sample selection and CIF output pipeline, see [Structure Ranking and Scoring](21-structure-ranking-and-scoring).
- For the confidence head architecture that produces the PAE and LDDT logits consumed by these metrics, see [Confidence Prediction and Scoring](12-confidence-prediction-and-scoring).
- For the frame computation that determines which tokens have valid structural frames for pTM, see [frames.py](chai_lab/ranking/frames.py).

# Memory Management and Device Strategy



Chai-1's inference pipeline processes massive tensor representations — pairwise token features, MSA stacks, atom-level diffusion coordinates — that can easily exceed GPU memory if naively loaded all at once. The codebase addresses this through a **transient device migration** architecture: model components and intermediate tensors are moved to GPU only when actively computing, and immediately returned to CPU afterward. This page dissects the three pillars of that strategy — module lifecycle management, data movement control, and strategic cache eviction — so you can reason about memory behavior when folding large complexes or running on constrained hardware.

## The Core Abstraction: ModuleWrapper and Transient Migration

The central memory-saving mechanism is the `ModuleWrapper` class, which wraps TorchScript-compiled model components and exposes a `forward` method with two memory-controlling parameters: `move_to_device` and `return_on_cpu`. When `move_to_device` is set, input data is recursively transferred to the target device right before the forward call; when `return_on_cpu` is set, the output is moved back to CPU immediately after computation. This means no caller needs to manually track where data lives — the wrapper enforces the contract.

The `forward` method resolves the correct compiled graph variant by dynamically selecting `forward_{crop_size}` based on the padded model size (one of 256, 384, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048). Each size corresponds to a separately exported static graph, avoiding dynamic-shape overhead inside the JIT runtime.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L104-L122), [utils.py](chai_lab/data/collate/utils.py#L10-L11)

## Component Caching and Lazy Loading

Model components are loaded via `load_exported`, which implements a **CPU-first loading strategy**: when the target device is not `cuda:0`, the JIT module is first loaded onto CPU and then transferred to the target device. This avoids CUDA OOM errors that can occur when `torch.jit.load` directly materializes large parameter buffers on the GPU.

The module-level dictionary `_component_cache` stores loaded `ModuleWrapper` instances by their component key. Once a component is loaded, it is never re-read from disk. The context manager `_component_moved_to` leverages this cache to transiently move a cached module to the active device, yield it for computation, and then move it back to CPU — a round-trip that is far cheaper than deserializing from disk repeatedly.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as Inference Loop
    participant CM as _component_moved_to
    participant Cache as _component_cache
    participant Disk as Local Filesystem
    participant GPU as CUDA Device
    participant CPU as System RAM

    Caller->>CM: enter("trunk.pt", device=cuda:0)
    alt Component not in cache
        CM->>Disk: torch.jit.load (CPU-first)
        Disk-->>CM: JIT Module on CPU
        CM->>Cache: store ModuleWrapper
    end
    CM->>Cache: retrieve ModuleWrapper
    CM->>GPU: module.to(cuda:0)
    CM-->>Caller: yield module (on GPU)
    Note over Caller: Forward pass executes
    Caller->>CM: exit context
    CM->>CPU: module.to("cpu")
```

This pattern is applied consistently across all five model components — `feature_embedding.pt`, `bond_loss_input_proj.pt`, `token_embedder.pt`, `trunk.pt`, `diffusion_module.pt`, and `confidence_head.pt` — each entering and exiting the GPU within a single `with` block.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L124-L141), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L606-L616)

## The low_memory Flag: Two Operating Modes

The `run_inference` function accepts a `low_memory` boolean (defaulting to `True`) that governs how aggressively the pipeline moves intermediate tensors off the GPU. This flag propagates into `run_folding_on_context` and controls behavior at every major pipeline stage.

| Mode | Batch Placement | Intermediate Features | Module Outputs | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `low_memory=True` | CPU (default) | Moved to GPU per-module via `move_to_device` | Returned to CPU via `return_on_cpu` | Consumer GPUs (≤24 GB VRAM) |
| `low_memory=False` | GPU immediately | Already on GPU | Kept on GPU | High-VRAM servers (≥80 GB) |

In low-memory mode, the collated batch remains on CPU after construction. Each model component's `forward` call uses `move_to_device=device` to transfer only the required inputs to GPU for the duration of that call, and `return_on_cpu=True` to bring outputs back. This means that at any point, only one model component and its immediate inputs occupy GPU memory — peak usage is bounded by the largest single component rather than the sum of all components.

When `low_memory=False`, the entire batch is moved to GPU upfront via `move_data_to_device(batch, device=device)`, and module outputs stay on GPU. This eliminates the overhead of repeated CPU↔GPU transfers but requires sufficient VRAM to hold all intermediate representations simultaneously.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L590-L595), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L620-L631)

## Recursive Data Migration: move_data_to_device

The utility function `move_data_to_device` performs recursive, type-dispatched device transfer across arbitrarily nested data structures. It handles `torch.Tensor` (via `.to(device)`), `dict`, `list`, `tuple`, and `dataclass` instances — the latter by reconstructing the dataclass with all fields migrated. This is the workhorse that enables both the `ModuleWrapper.forward` parameter and the batch-level migration in non-low-memory mode.

The recursive nature matters because the batch dictionary produced by `Collate` contains deeply nested structures: `batch["inputs"]` is a flat dict of tensors, but `batch["features"]` is a dict of named feature tensors, and future extensions could nest further. A simple `tensor.to()` call would miss non-tensor containers; the recursive dispatch ensures nothing is left behind.

> [!TIP]
> When extending the pipeline with new data structures, ensure they are either plain tensors/dicts/lists or dataclasses. The `move_data_to_device` function will raise `NotImplementedError` for unsupported types — this is intentional and catches bugs early rather than silently leaving data on the wrong device.

Sources: [tensor_utils.py](chai_lab/utils/tensor_utils.py#L254-L278)

## Strategic Cache Eviction Points

Beyond the component-level migration pattern, the pipeline includes explicit `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` calls at three critical junctures where peak memory pressure is known to occur:

1. **Before folding begins** — clears any residual allocations from feature context assembly.
2. **After trunk recycles complete** — the trunk module is the most memory-intensive component (pairwise attention over all tokens), and its fragmented GPU memory must be reclaimed before the diffusion loop begins.
3. **After the diffusion loop completes** — before confidence prediction, the `static_diffusion_inputs` dict (which holds trunk outputs, pair representations, and atom masks) is explicitly `del`'ed, then the cache is emptied. This is the single largest memory release in the entire pipeline.

Additionally, after confidence prediction and scoring, all output data — `inputs`, `atom_pos`, `plddt_logits`, `pae_logits` — is explicitly moved to CPU before writing CIF files. This ensures the GPU is free for subsequent trunk samples in the outer loop.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L578-L579), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L682-L683), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L810-L812), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L895-L898)

## Static Model Sizing and Padding Strategy

Memory consumption is also controlled at the input level through **static model sizing**. The `AVAILABLE_MODEL_SIZES` list defines seven discrete token counts (256, 384, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048), and the `Collate` class pads every input to the smallest size that accommodates the actual token count. Atom counts are derived as `23 × n_tokens` (23 atoms per token maximum), ensuring alignment to 32-atom blocks for the blocked atom-pair attention mechanism.

This padding has a direct memory implication: an input with 300 tokens is padded to 384, consuming memory proportional to the padded size rather than the actual size. The trade-off is that static graph shapes enable TorchScript optimization and eliminate dynamic-shape dispatch overhead. The `raise_if_too_many_tokens` guard rejects inputs exceeding 2048 tokens, providing a hard ceiling on peak memory.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["Input: N tokens"] --> B{N ≤ 2048?}
    B -- No --> C["UnsupportedInputError"]
    B -- Yes --> D[Pad to smallest<br/>AVAILABLE_MODEL_SIZES ≥ N]
    E["Static JIT graph<br/>forward_N_selected"]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Memory proportional<br/>to padded size]
```

Sources: [utils.py](chai_lab/data/collate/utils.py#L10-L40), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L235-L245)

## Memory-Aware Distance Computation

The `cdist` function in `tensor_utils.py` demonstrates a subtler memory optimization: when computing pairwise Euclidean distances on CUDA, it checks whether the total number of point pairs exceeds a threshold (2,147,400,000). If so, it falls back to a naive implementation that avoids the memory spike of `torch.cdist`'s internal buffer allocation. The naive version computes differences via broadcasting and uses in-place operations (`pow_`, `add_`, `sqrt_`) to minimize intermediate allocations.

This matters during ranking and scoring, where pairwise distance matrices over thousands of atoms can approach the multi-gigabyte range. The threshold was calibrated to prevent OOM on 24 GB GPUs during batch-32 inference scenarios.

Sources: [tensor_utils.py](chai_lab/utils/tensor_utils.py#L17-L47)

## Device Selection and ESM Embedding Placement

The `run_inference` entry point accepts an optional `device` string parameter, defaulting to `"cuda:0"`. This device is used for all model components and is also passed to `make_all_atom_feature_context` as the `esm_device` parameter for ESM embedding generation. ESM inference runs on the same device as the folding pipeline, which means it competes for GPU memory during the feature assembly phase. On memory-constrained setups, ESM embeddings can be precomputed and loaded from disk (by setting `use_esm_embeddings=False` and providing cached embeddings) to avoid this contention.

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L530-L566)

## End-to-End Memory Flow

The diagram below shows the complete device residency lifecycle for a single trunk sample in low-memory mode:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph CPU_Resident
        A[Collated Batch] --> B[Feature Embedding Input]
        B --> C[Embedded Features on CPU]
        C --> D[Token Embedder Input]
        D --> E[Token Representations on CPU]
        E --> F[Trunk Input]
        F --> G[Trunk Outputs on CPU]
    end

    subgraph GPU_Transient["GPU (Transient per Stage)"]
        H[Feature Embedding<br/>module + inputs]
        I[Token Embedder<br/>module + inputs]
        J[Trunk Module<br/>+ recycled reprs]
        K[Diffusion Module<br/>+ static inputs]
        L[Confidence Head<br/>+ single sample]
    end

    B --> H --> C
    D --> I --> E
    F --> J --> G
    G --> K
    G --> L
    K --> M[Diffusion outputs → CPU]
    L --> N[Confidence outputs → CPU]
```

> [!TIP]
> When running multiple trunk samples (`num_trunk_samples > 1`), the outer loop in `run_inference` calls `run_folding_on_context` repeatedly. Since `_component_cache` persists across calls, module loading cost is amortized — only the device migration round-trip repeats. However, feature context data remains in memory for the full duration; for very large inputs, consider whether multiple trunk samples are necessary.

## Summary of Memory Control Mechanisms

| Mechanism | Scope | Overhead | Memory Saved |
|---|---|---|---|
| `low_memory=True` (default) | Entire pipeline | CPU↔GPU transfers per stage | ~60-70% peak VRAM reduction |
| `_component_moved_to` context | Per-model-component | `.to()` round-trip per stage | Only 1 component on GPU at a time |
| `_component_cache` | Cross-call persistence | None (avoids disk I/O) | Avoids duplicate loads |
| `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` | 3 strategic points | Brief stall | Reclaims fragmented memory |
| Static model sizing | Input padding | Over-padding for small inputs | Enables JIT optimization |
| `cdist` threshold fallback | Pairwise distances | Slower naive computation | Avoids multi-GB buffer spikes |
| Explicit `del` + CPU move | Post-diffusion | None | Frees largest intermediates |

Sources: [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L104-L141), [chai1.py](chai_lab/chai1.py#L530-L898), [tensor_utils.py](chai_lab/utils/tensor_utils.py#L17-L47), [utils.py](chai_lab/data/collate/utils.py#L10-L40)

---

**Next steps**: To understand how the diffusion noise schedule interacts with memory during the iterative denoising loop, see [Diffusion Noise Schedule](25-diffusion-noise-schedule). For the trunk recycling mechanism that repeats GPU-intensive attention under the same memory constraints, see [Trunk Recycling and Attention](10-trunk-recycling-and-attention).

# Diffusion Noise Schedule



The diffusion noise schedule governs how Chai-1 traverses from pure noise to structured atomic coordinates during inference. It defines the sequence of noise levels (σ values) that the denoising network progressively resolves, and it controls the stochastic perturbation strategy that determines sample diversity and quality. This page dissects the mathematical formulation, the power-interpolation mechanism, and the concrete integration into Chai-1's stochastic sampler.

## Core Abstraction: InferenceNoiseSchedule

The noise schedule is encapsulated in a single frozen dataclass — `InferenceNoiseSchedule` — with four parameters that jointly define a continuous σ(t) curve mapping normalized time t ∈ [0, 1] to noise levels:

| Parameter | Default | Role |
|-----------|---------|------|
| `s_max` | 160.0 (schedule) / 80.0 (DiffusionConfig) | σ at t = 0, the maximum noise level (pure noise) |
| `s_min` | 4e-4 | σ at t = 1, the minimum noise level (near-clean) |
| `p` | 7.0 | Power exponent controlling the interpolation curvature |
| `sigma_data` | 16.0 | Data scale factor; final σ = sigma_data × interpolated_value |

The schedule is constructed via two methods: `get_schedule` produces a discrete σ trajectory for a given number of timesteps, while `get_noise_for_times` computes σ for arbitrary normalized time values. Both ultimately delegate to the `_power_interpolation` function.

Sources: [diffusion_schedules.py](/chai_lab/model/diffusion_schedules.py#L12-L34)

## Power Interpolation: The Mathematical Kernel

The heart of the schedule is `_power_interpolation`, which defines a smooth, parametric curve between `val_0` (at t = 0) and `val_1` (at t = 1):

```
f(t) = (t · val_1^(1/p) + (1-t) · val_0^(1/p))^p
```

This is a **generalized power mean** of order 1/p. When p > 1, the curve spends more time near `val_0` (high noise) before transitioning toward `val_1` (low noise). With p = 7, the interpolation is heavily skewed — the schedule lingers in high-noise regions where coarse structural features are resolved, then rapidly traverses low-noise regions where fine atomic details emerge. The final σ values are obtained by scaling this interpolation by `sigma_data`:

```
σ(t) = sigma_data · f(t)
```

This two-stage design (interpolate then scale) decouples the shape of the schedule from the absolute noise magnitude, allowing `sigma_data` to be tuned independently to match the data distribution's variance.

Sources: [diffusion_schedules.py](/chai_lab/model/diffusion_schedules.py#L37-L49)

## Timestep Discretization: Midpoint Lattice

The `get_schedule` method generates discrete timesteps using a **midpoint lattice** strategy rather than uniform endpoint spacing:

```python
times = torch.linspace(0, 1, 2 * num_timesteps + 1, device=device)[1::2]
```

This creates `2N + 1` equally-spaced points on [0, 1], then selects every other point starting from index 1 — yielding N points at positions 1/(2N+1), 3/(2N+1), 5/(2N+1), …, (2N-1)/(2N+1). These are the midpoints of N equal subintervals, which provides a more balanced sampling of the σ curve compared to endpoint-inclusive linspace. The default `num_timesteps = 200` produces 200 σ values, with the first being the noisiest and the last being nearly clean.

Sources: [diffusion_schedules.py](/chai_lab/model/diffusion_schedules.py#L21-L26)

## DiffusionConfig: Sampler Hyperparameters

While `InferenceNoiseSchedule` defines the σ trajectory, the `DiffusionConfig` class in `chai1.py` controls the **stochastic sampling** behavior applied during the denoising loop:

| Parameter | Default | Role |
|-----------|---------|------|
| `S_churn` | 80.0 | Total stochasticity budget; controls how much random perturbation is injected across all steps |
| `S_tmin` | 4e-4 | Lower σ threshold for stochastic perturbation — below this, no noise is added |
| `S_tmax` | 80.0 | Upper σ threshold for stochastic perturbation — above this, no noise is added |
| `S_noise` | 1.003 | Scale factor on the noise injected at each stochastic step |
| `sigma_data` | 16.0 | Data scale, passed to `InferenceNoiseSchedule` |
| `second_order` | True | Whether to use the second-order (Heun's) correction for improved accuracy |

> [!TIP]
> The `S_tmax` parameter serves dual purpose: it defines both the upper bound for stochastic churn in the sampler AND the `s_max` value passed to `InferenceNoiseSchedule`. This coupling means the schedule's starting noise level and the sampler's stochastic window are intentionally aligned — the sampler only adds perturbation within the same σ range that the schedule traverses.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L242-L248)

## Integration: The Stochastic Sampler Loop

The noise schedule is consumed within `run_folding_on_context` to drive the full denoising process. The integration follows a variant of the **stochastic sampler from Karras et al.** (Algorithm 2), which combines deterministic Euler steps with optional stochastic perturbation:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Initialize atom positions:<br/>x₀ = σ[0] · N(0, I)"] --> B["Iterate over (σ_curr, σ_next, γ_curr)"]
    B --> C["Center coordinates<br/>(random augmentation)"]
    C --> D{"σ_curr in [S_tmin, S_tmax]?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["γ = min(S_churn / N, √2 - 1)"]
    D -- No --> F["γ = 0"]
    E --> G["Stochastic perturbation:<br/>σ̂ = σ_curr + γ · σ_curr<br/>x̂ = x + S_noise · ε · √(σ̂² - σ_curr²)"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["First denoising:<br/>d = (x̂ - D(x̂, σ̂)) / σ̂"]
    H --> I["Euler step:<br/>x' = x̂ + (σ_next - σ̂) · d"]
    I --> J{"second_order AND σ_next ≠ 0?"}
    J -- Yes --> K["Second denoising:<br/>d' = (x' - D(x', σ_next)) / σ_next"]
    K --> L["Heun correction:<br/>x = x' + (σ_next - σ̂) · (d' + d) / 2"]
    J -- No --> M["x = x' (Euler only)"]
    L --> N{More steps?}
    M --> N
    N -- Yes --> B
    N -- No --> O["Return final atom positions"]
```

The key mechanics are:

**Schedule instantiation.** The `InferenceNoiseSchedule` is constructed with `s_max = DiffusionConfig.S_tmax` (80.0), `s_min = 4e-4`, `p = 7.0`, and `sigma_data = 16.0`. The resulting σ trajectory determines the sequence of noise levels the model traverses.

**Gamma computation.** For each step, the stochasticity factor γ is computed as `min(S_churn / num_timesteps, √2 - 1)` when the current σ falls within the window `[S_tmin, S_tmax]`, and zero otherwise. The `√2 - 1` upper bound prevents the perturbation from overshooting into instability.

**Stochastic perturbation.** When γ > 0, the current positions are noised to a slightly higher level σ̂ = σ_curr(1 + γ), then the denoiser is applied from that perturbed state. This injection of controlled randomness is what generates diverse structural samples from the same trunk representation.

**Second-order correction.** When enabled, a second denoiser evaluation at σ_next provides a corrected gradient estimate (Heun's method), improving the accuracy of each step at the cost of one additional forward pass per timestep.

Sources: [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L775-L830)

## Schedule Shape and Its Implications

The interaction between the power interpolation (p = 7) and the midpoint discretization produces a schedule that is heavily concentrated in the high-σ regime. With `sigma_data = 16.0` and the default schedule range, the initial σ values are on the order of 16 × 80 = 1280, while the final values approach 16 × 4e-4 ≈ 0.0064. This six-order-of-magnitude span ensures that the denoiser first resolves large-scale structural topology (backbone arrangement, domain packing) before attending to atomic-level precision (bond lengths, side-chain rotamers).

| Regime | σ Range | Structural Features Resolved |
|--------|---------|------------------------------|
| High noise | σ > 100 | Global topology, chain arrangement |
| Medium noise | 10 < σ < 100 | Secondary structure, domain folding |
| Low noise | σ < 10 | Side-chain packing, bond geometry |
| Near-clean | σ < 1 | Atomic precision, hydrogen bonds |

> [!TIP]
> Reducing `num_diffn_timesteps` below the default 200 trades sample quality for speed, but because the power interpolation is concentrated in the high-noise regime, the schedule remains well-behaved even at lower step counts. The γ values scale inversely with `num_timesteps`, so fewer steps automatically receive larger perturbations per step, partially compensating for the coarser traversal.

Sources: [diffusion_schedules.py](/chai_lab/model/diffusion_schedules.py#L21-L34), [chai1.py](/chai_lab/chai1.py#L775-L790)

## Relationship to the Broader Pipeline

The noise schedule sits at the boundary between the trunk representation and the final atomic output. It operates on the **structure branch** of the model — consuming `token_single_structure_input`, `token_pair_structure_input_feats`, and their trunk-refined counterparts — and produces the atom coordinates that feed into the confidence head. The schedule's design is therefore independent of the MSA, template, and feature embedding stages, but its output quality directly determines the confidence predictions and ranking scores downstream.

For the full denoising pipeline context, see [Diffusion Denoising Process](11-diffusion-denoising-process). For how the resulting structures are evaluated, see [Confidence Prediction and Scoring](12-confidence-prediction-and-scoring) and [pTM, pLDDT, and Clash Metrics](23-ptm-plddt-and-clash-metrics).
